News.title: German chancellor Merz vows to stay in office amid ‘disaster’ after double election blow with far-left AND far-right win
News.content:
Next

GERMANY’s chancellor has vowed to stay in office – despite describing the elections as as a “disaster” for his party.

Friedrich Merz, leader of Christian Democratic Union (CDU), responded to the projected losses in two state elections to both far-left and far-right parties.



Merz said: “Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right.”

In the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, preliminary results indicated that the CDU would just about creep over the 5 per cent threshold to enter the state’s parliament.



However, exit polls suggest the party has missed the threshold in its worst-ever state score, with far-right group The Alternative for Germany (AfD) securing the most votes instead.

In Berlin, the ruling CDU are expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left).

Merz called the recent results a “disaster” as he promises to continue fighting for economic changes in Germany.

He faces intensifying scrutiny amid poor approval ratings and rumours of being replaced in a mid-term “chancellor swap”.



Speaking on state election night on Sunday, he said that he would move forward with his coalition government’s plans to push through a bill of economic, tax and welfare reforms.

He said: “The reforms have to come. I am taking on this responsibility, because I want to move our country forward.

“What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness and patience.

“I will demonstrate this as CDU party chairman and, above all, as chancellor of our country.

“I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that, with the fascination of authoritarianism, is penetrating ever deeper into our society.”



AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel said: “We are the strongest force and have reached the mainstream of the population.”

The party’s other co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, gleefully mocked Merz, saying voters had given his own party a “very clear result”.

Chrupalla also called on the chancellor to resign.

Earlier this month, the AfD won a staggering 43.8 per cent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, in a historic state election.

This saw CDU suffer a horrible loss as their vote was cut in half.



Merz is expected to lose leadership of the CDU party due to terrible election results, which would automatically stop him from running for Chancellor again in 2029.

His decline in popularity has created a sense of instability in Germany.

Known as Europe’s top economic powerhouse, the country has been riddled with issues of deindustrialisation, sluggish growth and rising energy costs.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Many speculate that if Merz leaves office early, it would give momentum to other far right parties across Europe.

It comes as France, Italy, Spain and Poland are all expected to hold elections next year with nationalist parties growing in popularity.

News.title: Man, 82, dies after violent beach brawl with another bather over sunbed in Greece
News.content:
BEACH TRAGEDY Man, 82, dies after violent beach brawl with another bather over sunbed in Greece







Next

A PENSIONER has died after reportedly getting into a brawl over a sunbed on a beach in Greece.

The victim, 82, was heard getting into a heated argument with another man over the use of loungers at Vouliagmeni beach, near Athens.



It escalated into a violent fight, which then spiralled when bystanders got involved.

One witness said the scene was pure “chaos” and that he could hear screams from the other end of the beach.



He told Greek outlet Kathimerini that he saw a man and a woman beating the victim before efforts were made to revive him with CPR.

The younger man, 76, has since been arrested and charged with causing fatal bodily harm.

A 21-year-old woman who was with him was released from custody.

Bystanders told Ta Nea daily newspaper that she had a bloodied and swollen face.

One witness said the victim appeared to be waiting for other people and had reserved the seat that caused the fight.

A friend of the alleged assailant claims that he was buying a ticket while the 76-year-old went to find a lounger.



He said his friend got into an argument the older man, who allegedly said: “Do you know who I am? I’m from the navy.”

The witness claims that the brawl left his friend with injuries.

During the fight, the 82-year-old collapsed.

He received CPR and a defibrillator was reportedly used on him before paramedics arrived.

The man was rushed to hospital where he later died.



An investigation has been launched into what sparked the brawl and caused the man’s death.

News.title: Labour slam Sir Jim Ratcliffe for claiming Britain is ‘on the slide’ and risks going broke while living in Monaco
News.content:
JIM JIBES Labour slam Sir Jim Ratcliffe for claiming Britain is ‘on the slide’ and risks going broke while living in Monaco







Next

MANCHESTER United owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe warned Britain risks going broke as Labour ministers hit back at his claim the country is “on the slide”.

The billionaire businessman blamed high taxes, mass immigration and the soaring benefits bill for Britain’s decline.



Treasury minister Torsten Bell responded by accusing him of “hating his own country”.

And Labour chair Bridget Phillipson said Sir Jim had lost the “moral high ground” by criticising Britain while living in Monaco and supporting Brexit.



She told the BBC: “I do think you lose the moral high ground in the argument you make, Jim Ratcliffe, that is, by making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile.”

She added: “And of course, he was also someone, as I understand it, who was a big supporter of Brexit.”



The row comes as Britain struggles to hang on to some of its wealthiest taxpayers.

Hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos, one of Britain’s biggest individual taxpayers, is moving his residency to Greece amid fears of further Labour tax rises.

Betfred founder Fred Done, whose family paid £400million in tax last year, has also complained about the burden on the wealthy and said he would “not wish to be reborn” in Britain.

Sir Jim, whose fortune is estimated at around £15billion, also warned: “If you tax everybody to death, they’re all going to leave.”

News.title: Brothers who kidnapped ‘wealthy’ man in honeytrap plot forced to slash ransom when his friends ‘couldn’t afford it’
News.content:
Next

TWO brothers who held a man at gunpoint for hours believing he was wealthy were forced to lower their ransom after his friends could not afford it.

The pair threatened to kill Ali Almafraji if they did not receive £30,000 by sunrise, before realising nobody had the money.



Bilal, 28, and Zachariya Rakik, 26, kidnapped the victim after luring him to a south-east London Nando’s restaurant with a fake dating profile.

The crooks then climbed into the victim’s car wearing balaclavas and began the harrowing ordeal.



Almafraji was then threatened with an imitation handgun, unaware it was not real, which they waved in the air and threatened to shoot him with.

The brothers took over Almafraji’s car and began driving him around Lewisham while calling his contacts demanding the money.



They threatened if they did not receive the money by sunrise then they would shoot the man dead.

However, after repeated calls to the man’s friends, they soon realised nobody had the money.

At that point they were forced to reduce the ransom, until they eventually settled at just £2000.

Friends, however, quickly foiled the plans of the brothers by ringing police and passing on the car registration plate.



The Met Police’s Flying Squad later ambushed the car at 4:20am, which was all caught on video.

The dramatic footage shows officers swooping in and saving Almafraji following the traumatic ordeal.

The pair were sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court to a combined total of more than 14 years.

Judge Yale said: “You put a collapsing timeframe on the threats, making it plain to Mr Almafraji and his friends that he would be killed if the money wasn’t raised by first light.”

Bilal was jailed for seven years and two months, and Zachariya for seven years and one month.

News.title: Patrick Clancy’s new wife reveals she’s pregnant during emotional 60 Minutes interview after Lindsay’s mistrial
News.content:
Next

PATRICK Clancy’s new wife has revealed she is pregnant with their first child during the couple’s first emotional TV interview together.

Patrick and his wife Dr. Rachel Danis appeared on 60 Minutes on Sunday night, speaking openly about his grief, their relationship and the conspiracy theories that have surrounded him since Lindsay killed their three children.



Lindsay strangled Cora, five, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan with exercise bands inside the family’s Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023.

Her defense team argued that she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.



But the blockbuster case ended in a dramatic mistrial earlier this month after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict following seven days of deliberations.

In one of the most revealing moments of the interview, Rachel confirmed the couple are expecting their first child together.



Correspondent Ross Douthat asked, “And you guys are starting a family?”

“Yeah,” Rachel simply replied.

Patrick, who married fertility doctor Rachel, 37, earlier this year, said their new child would grow up knowing about Cora, Dawson and Callan.

“I can’t wait to tell them about their brothers and sister,” he said.



Pregnancy rumors first circulated after the couple were recently spotted out on a walk in New York, with Rachel showing a noticeable bump.

The Clancy case was described on 60 Minutes as a “national obsession.”

Patrick recalled how Lindsay first began struggling with insomnia in October 2022, months before the killings.

“I didn’t know how to manage a postpartum illness,” he said.

“I’m sure there are things I didn’t see. I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive.”



Patrick spoke candidly about rebuilding his life in the shadow of unimaginable grief and admitted he became suicidal after the deaths, at one point unsure whether he would live to see his 35th birthday.

He also described the agonizing four days that Callan remained alive in the hospital after the killings.

“That night I really thought there was a chance that Callan would live,” Patrick said.



“And I remember just thinking, just gimme one, just gimme one kid, and I would raise him as best I could.

“I would give him the best life I possibly could. I would tell him about his brother and sister, and I was holding out hope for that.”

But he said he realized he would not survive and he was grateful for the days he had with him.

Through tears, Patrick recalled telling his son, “I’m so sorry.”

“I got to hold him, I got to lay down next to him, and he died in my arms,” he said.



Despite everything that happened, Patrick, 36, insisted Lindsay is not a “monster” and said refusing to forgive her would leave him “eaten up inside, forever.”

Patrick also recalled a day driving past the children’s school

He said Lindsay, who remains in Tewksbury Hospital, never asked for his forgiveness, but he chose to give it to her.

Patrick also opened up about taking the stand during her murder trial and suffering what he described as a “massive, traumatic panic attack” when his harrowing 911 call was played in court.

“My heart was pounding and they put me in an ambulance,” he said.



“They offered me some medication, but I said, ‘I don’t want it, I want to go back and I want to finish this. So I can be done with this.’

“I went back and I finished the testimony.”

The biggest bombshells from the interview Rachel revealed she is pregnant with their first child

Patrick said their baby will grow up knowing about Cora, Dawson and Callan

Patrick revealed he was suicidal after his children died

He recalled holding Callan as he died in his arms in hospital

Patrick said he has forgiven Lindsay and insisted she is not a “monster”

He suffered a “ massive, traumatic panic attack ” when his 911 call was played at Lindsay’s trial

massive, traumatic panic attack when his 911 call was played at Lindsay’s trial Patrick hit back at the conspiracy theories surrounding him

Lindsay’s anxiety had worsened after the birth of Callan, and she was prescribed medications including Zoloft and Ativan.

Her treatment continued to change as her insomnia and anxiety became more severe, while her parents began traveling from Connecticut to help care for the children as Patrick worked from a home office.

Her private writings later documented a months-long decline in her mental health.



By December, Lindsay had told Patrick about suicidal thoughts and unwanted thoughts of harming the children, and she was admitted to McLean Hospital for several days.

After she returned home, Patrick believed she was improving.

On January 24, 2023, Patrick returned from running an errand and picking up takeout for the family before discovering his children in the basement and Lindsay on the ground after jumping out of a window.

She survived but is now paralyzed from the waist down.

“I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time,” he told 60 Minutes.



“And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day. But I think I did the best I could.”

Patrick also revealed that he later asked Lindsay whether she remembered what had happened.

“I asked her if she remembered it. She said it was like a dream,” he said.

“I try not to think about that night, very often.”

Lindsay later told him during an emotional phone call that she had heard a man’s voice ordering her to kill the children and then herself.



Patrick has faced a torrent of baseless conspiracy theories from internet sleuths, including claims that he was somehow involved in the deaths of his children.

Online detectives have picked apart his movements on the night of the killings, his divorce from Lindsay and his subsequent relationship and marriage to Rachel.

There is no evidence Patrick had anything to do with the children’s deaths, and he has never been charged with any crime.

“It’s deeply harmful to the legacy of my children,” he said of the online speculation.

“It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health, and it’s done real harm to real people.”



His lawyers have fiercely hit back at the claims, warning those spreading false allegations that they could face legal action.

Rachel also defended her husband as she addressed the intense scrutiny surrounding their relationship.

“I don’t understand how the story’s been so twisted,” she said.

“But I would hope people know that Pat is, as I said before, the most selfless father and supportive partner.”

Rachel also recalled how the pair first met in February 2024.



“And I was just a girl that met a guy running in Central Park on a really cold Saturday,” she said.

“And I don’t think there’s anything wrong with that.”

The couple went on to marry in April this year after Patrick relocated to New York following the tragedy.

Patrick also opened up about the grief he continues to live with and revealed that he still speaks to his children.

“I talk to them all the time,” he told Douthat.



Asked what he says to them, Patrick replied, “Help me. All the time.”

“Do they help you?” Douthat asked.

“I like to believe they do,” Patrick said.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“It’s a way I stay connected to them.”

The 60 Minutes interview comes as prosecutors continue to weigh whether Lindsay will face a second murder trial in the coming months.

Men women and children who justly fear for their future and desperately want their country back.



The only people who can deliver this priceless reward are the politicians who genuinely believe in sovereignty, the rule of law and the nation state.

News.title: Girl, 17, fighting for her life after horrific motorbike crash as cops appeal for witnesses
News.content:
BIKE SMASH Girl, 17, fighting for her life after horrific motorbike crash as cops appeal for witnesses







Next

A 17-YEAR-OLD girl is fighting for her life after a motorbike crash as police are appealing for witnesses to the horror smash.

The teen is in a life-threatening condition after an incident involving the bike and a van in Wiltshire.



The girl was riding a Yamaha YZF125 motorcycle on Lyndhurst Road in Landford on Saturday morning when the crash took place.

It is believed at around 11.20am the bike collided with a Ford Transit van at a crossroad junction.



Police are now appealing for any witnesses, or those who may have dashcam footage of the crash, to get in touch.

In a statement, Wiltshire Police said: “We are appealing for any witnesses, or anyone who may have dash cam footage of the incident or the vehicles involved prior to the collision.



“Contact our Serious Collision Investigation Team on 01225 694597, quoting log 124.”

News.title: Horror as ten lions found dead after ‘poisoning’ at popular wildlife reserve in Tanzania
News.content:
'POISON' PROBE Horror as ten lions found dead after ‘poisoning’ at popular wildlife reserve in Tanzania







Next

TEN lions were found dead at a wildlife reserve in Tanzania after allegedly being poisoned.

The lions’ bodies were tragically discovered in the Ngorongoro wildlife reserve on Friday, the Conservation Area Authority said in a statement.



The area’s management authority said: “Preliminary findings suggest the ‌animals may have died after ingesting poison.”

They have launched an investigation to determine the cause of the killings and identify the culprits.



The Ngorongoro Conservation Area is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the country’s top tourist attractions.

Among the wide range of wildlife are lions, elephants, buffaloes and endangered black rhinos.

The diverse landscape, which features highland plains, savanna, and forest, was designated as a multi-use area in 1959.

According to the UNESCO World Heritage Convention, semi-nomadic Maasai pastoralists live alongside local wildlife in the reserve.

They said: “The property has global importance for biodiversity conservation due to the presence of globally threatened species, the density of wildlife inhabiting the area, and the annual migration of wildebeest, zebra, gazelles and other animals into the northern plains.

“Extensive archaeological research has also yielded a long sequence of evidence of human evolution and human-environment dynamics, including early hominid footprints dating back 3.6 million years.”



Poisoning has sadly been a significant threat to large carnivores across East Africa, often due to conflicts between the predators and livestock owners.

Just last month, four suspects were arrested by police investigating the deaths of 18 elephants in Kenya, but have since been released on bail.

The tourism and wildlife ministry said officials confiscated various materials including chemicals.



Initial speculation hinted at the use of cyanide poisoning linked to eating pesticide-contaminated tomatoes from farms bordering Amboseli National Park.

Early lab tests suggest a toxic substance is likely involved, the ministry stated on Saturday.

However, many wildlife experts question the pesticide theory, noting the absence of deaths among other animal species.

Frank Pope, CEO of conservation organisation Save the Elephants, told the BBC that land use has replaced ivory as the main threat to Amboseli’s elephants.

He said: “People are moving into areas where there’s enough water to grow crops, and fertile soils, and those are the very areas that the elephants tend to use as well.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

In early January, Lion Guardians, a Kenyan organisation said six lions were lost in a poisoning incident near the Kenya-Tanzania border.

The discovery of 30 dead vultures in the area implied that poisoning was the likely cause of death.

News.title: Ofsted graded inspections must be halted amid 'risk to life', union demands
News.content:
Ofsted graded inspections must be halted amid 'risk to life', union demands

Paul Whiteman, NAHT's general secretary, said: 'The clear theme emerging across all the feedback we have received is that this Ofsted framework is even more stressful than the one that preceded it'

View Image A new inspection system was intended to address fears over wellbeing following the tragic death of 53-year-old primary school headteacher Ruth Perry in 2023 (Image: PA)

Ofsted's graded inspections must be halted, a major union has demanded amid warnings of "a risk to life".

‌



The call for action from the biggest school leaders' union - NAHT - comes almost 12 months on since the introduction of a revised inspection system.

‌



England's school watchdog replaced the old regime - an overall single-word grade ranging from 'outstanding' to 'inadequate' - with a new 5-point grading scale last year.

‌



It was intended to address fears over wellbeing following the tragic death of 53-year-old primary school headteacher Ruth Perry in 2023.

She had been told her school - Caversham primary school in Reading, Berkshire - was being downgraded from "outstanding" to "inadequate", the lowest possible rating.

A coroner at the time had said an Ofsted inspection "likely contributed" to her mental health deterioration and death.

‌



NAHT said it had raised concerns at the start of a new framework that replacing an overall single-word grade would not ease the intolerable pressure on leaders.

The union said a survey of more than 5,000 of its members - conducted in June - found nearly three quarters (72%) felt the direction of travel on inspection had worsened.

It has led NAHT to call for the government to halt the inspection system - and conduct a review.

‌



Paul Whiteman, NAHT's general secretary, said: "The clear theme emerging across all the feedback we have received is that this Ofsted framework is even more stressful than the one that preceded it.

"It poses a real and present danger to the well-being and mental health of school leaders and teachers, possibly even a risk to life."

"We warmly welcome the new Education Secretary's recent words stating how seriously she takes leader wellbeing and her determination to get not just the Ofsted framework, but the whole culture of accountability, right."

‌



He added: "Really fundamental changes to inspection are needed, and we stand ready to work with the new government to achieve that.

"In the meantime, there remains a risk to the safety of school leaders, which is why we are calling for graded inspections to be halted."

An Ofsted spokeswoman said: “Ofsted exists to raise standards for children and to provide clear reporting to parents.

‌



“Over the last three years, we have worked closely with teaching unions to deliver significant reforms to how Ofsted inspections work, to reduce unnecessary pressure on teachers. And we involved parents to make sure our new-look inspection reports worked for them – presenting clear, colour-coded grades and detailed information about the school.

“We will continue to engage closely with trades unions – but we will also continue to grade schools.”

Speaking earlier this month, the new Education Secretary Lucy Powell committed to working with headteachers and others to "make sure that we get this Ofsted framework, but also the culture, the whole regime, right".

‌



She told LBC in early September: "There's nothing that is more concerning to me as Education Secretary than the idea that our accountability regime in this country would lead to a headteacher to taking their own life.

"It's just absolutely awful and that is not at all what we should be about, the kind of culture and atmosphere that that is created here.

She added: "So, I take incredibly seriously teacher, headteacher wellbeing and yes, of course we need an accountability structure and regime to continue school improvement.

Article continues below

"But I want to see one that that is much more kind of supportive and understanding of the great jobs that the majority, in fact, you know, almost all headteachers are doing around the country and support them with that."

News.title: Three sisters who died off Brighton beach drowned say police in new statement
News.content:
Three sisters who died off Brighton beach drowned say police in new statement

Sisters Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, who were recovered from the sea off Brighton, died by drowning, Sussex Police said

View 3 Images Joseph Jacobson and his daughters (L-R): Jane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters (Image: Family Handout/PA Wire)

The three sisters whose bodies were recovered from the sea off the coast of Brighton died by drowning, with police finding no evidence of criminality or third-party involvement.

‌



Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, were recovered from the water near Madeira Drive on May 13. The women, who were from the Uxbridge area of London, were named by Sussex Police.

‌



An inquest into their deaths opened in May at Brighton and Hove Coroner's Court and is expected to resume in early October. The inquest previously heard that post-mortem examinations had given a provisional cause of death as "yet to be ascertained". On Sunday, Sussex Police said post-mortem examinations had confirmed that "all three women died by drowning".

‌



View 3 Images Flowers left at the scene where the bodies of three sisters were recovered from the sea off Brighton beach (Image: Anahita Hossein-Pour/PA Wire)

The force also said the police investigation into the sisters' deaths had concluded, finding no evidence of criminality or third-party involvement.

During the investigation, Sussex Police officers, supported by other forces, reviewed hundreds of hours of CCTV footage, took statements from witnesses across the country and conducted further enquiries to establish the sisters' movements before their deaths.

‌



The investigation found the three women were dropped off by taxi at Madeira Drive at 10.20pm on May 12. Police found no evidence that they visited any nightclubs or businesses in the area that evening.

The women were found to have entered the water near the area where their bodies were recovered the following morning, "wearing everyday clothing".

With the police investigation now concluded, the inquest will resume to determine the facts surrounding where, when and how the three sisters died.

‌



An inquest hearing in May was told that Ms Adetoro was brought ashore by an RNLI crew and pronounced dead by a paramedic at the scene.

View 3 Images Floral tributes for the sisters (Image: Adam Gerrard/Daily Mirror)

Christina Walters was recovered from the sea by an RNLI lifeboat, while Rebecca Walters was washed ashore on Brighton beach. Both were also pronounced dead by paramedics.

‌



Following the sisters' deaths, their father, Joseph Jacobson, said there were days when the grief felt "unbearable", but he held on to the memories they shared and "the bond that death can never take away".

Chief Superintendent Adam Hays said: "From the outset of this complex and challenging investigation, we have been acutely aware of the speculation surrounding this incident, the public’s unanswered questions and their desire for answers.

"Our priority throughout has been uncovering the truth for the loved ones of Jane, Rebecca and Christina, because at this incident’s core there has always been a grieving family coming to terms with an unthinkable tragedy and loss. Our investigation has been thorough.

Article continues below

"Our extensive enquiries intentionally considered concerns raised by black communities surrounding the deaths of black people in or near bodies of water, as we worked to understand who the three women were and the factors that could have led to them being found on the beach that morning.

"However, our enquiries have now concluded, pending any new information coming to light. Jane, Rebecca and Christina’s tragic deaths sparked a national outpouring of grief, and I would like to thank everyone who supported our investigation by coming forward with information.

"We will now support the coronial process and ask that the sisters’ family continue to be given privacy to come to terms with their loss."

News.title: RNLI warned of cyber attack after volunteers abused for saving migrants by far-right thugs
News.content:
RNLI warned of cyber attack after volunteers abused for saving migrants by far-right thugs

Online security experts have warned that the identities of RNLI members could have been leaked or fallen into the wrong hands

View 2 Images RNLI volunteers were labelled as traitors online by far-right thugs for rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel (Image: Barry Williams/PA Wire)

RNLI members have been warned they may have been hit with a cyberattack amid a heightened threat from far-Right agitators.

‌



Volunteers for the organisation were told their data may have been stolen by hackers - just days after they suffered online and physical abuse for rescuing 120 migrants from a dinghy in the English Channel.

‌



Online security experts have warned that the identities of RNLI members could have been leaked or fallen into the wrong hands after a cyber-attack on a third-party software provider. In a letter accompanying the autumn copy of its Lifeboat magazine, the charity warned supporters that their "name, contact details and records of interactions with the RNLI" could have been breached in the raid on Beacon CRM.

‌



View 2 Images Balaclava-clad followers have protested in both Dover and Portsmouth in recent weeks

The RNLI said it was advised last month by the provider to "assume that data held within its systems was taken" in a cyber-attack that affected around 1,500 charities in late July.

"At this stage we're not aware of any misuse of your personal information and have no evidence that your information has been published or shared," the charity added.

‌



The RNLI has suspended its services in Portsmouth since its staff were subjected to relentless abuse and branded "traitors" by anti-migrant protesters.

Peter Sparkes, the charity's chief executive, condemned abuse of its volunteers as "wholly unacceptable in civilised society", adding that the RNLI worked to save lives at sea irrespective of whose they are.

The latest data breach has fuelled concerns that lifeboat volunteers will face "doxxing", which involves the publication online of a person's home address.

‌



Dr William Allchorn, a senior research fellow at Anglia Ruskin University's International Policing and Public Protection Research Institute, said that those on the far-Right could exploit the data breach.

He told the Sunday Telegraph: "They use open source maritime tracking and endto-end encryption, but beyond that I don't know how sophisticated their set up is."

"It is the chill effect," he added. "For those on the fringes of the movement this information could be quite key."

‌



Andy Burnham hit out at "appalling" abuse directed at hero crews after they were labelled as traitors online by far-right thugs for rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel and bringing a dinghy to safety in Portsmouth, Hants.

Hundreds of protesters blocked roads overnight on September 6 and vowed to stop migrants from leaving the port.

The boat, reported to be carrying about 140 migrants, is thought to have made one of the longest journeys of any small boat and landings as far west as Hampshire are rare.

‌



The Mirror later revealed two RNLI heroes were named and pictured online by Portsmouth protestors who condemned them as "collaborators" and "traitors" for rescuing asylum seekers.

The RNLI issued security advice warning volunteers and staff not to wear the charity’s branding because of “unacceptable abuse”.

A spokesman for the RNLI said: "Beacon CRM works with many charities and organisations across the UK and Ireland, and while they cannot confirm exactly which records were accessed or downloaded, it advised all affected organisations, including the RNLI, to assume that data held within its systems was taken.

Article continues below

"At this stage, there is no evidence that information relating to RNLI supporters has been published, shared online or otherwise misused."

News.title: Earl Spencer in tears as he admits pictures of Diana 'break him'
News.content:
Earl Spencer in tears as he admits pictures of Diana 'break him'

Diana, Princess of Wales' brother, Earl Charles Spencer, became visibly emotional during a new interview as he was interrogated about his late sister and their memories

View 4 Images Earl Spencer became emotional as he spoke about Diana, Princess of Wales (Image: Jeff Overs/BBC/PA Wire)

Earl Spencer was left in tears as he spoke candidly about his late sister, Diana, Princess of Wales. In recent days, the Earl, 62, has made a string of allegations against his former in-laws, the Royal Family, including King Charles.

‌



In a new interview, the aristocrat was asked by Laura Kuenssberg about his late sister following claims that His Majesty said Diana "would soon be forgotten," following her tragic death in 1997. Buckingham Palace, in a rare statement, strongly refuted Charles's claims.

‌



During his interview with Kuenssberg at his ancestral home, Althorp, the Earl paused and became emotional when asked about the childhood memories he shares with Diana.

‌



View 4 Images The Earl spoke about growing up at Sandringham with the late Princess (Image: Jeff Overs/BBC/PA Wire)

He said: "My memories of Diana tend to be from our happy childhood days, in our home before this, which was Park House in Sandringham, in Norfolk. Even though we had the rupture of my parents' divorce, it was such a happy home. Just those days there, carefree days… not an instance, but a period of life."

Diana and Charles' parents, John, Eighth Earl Spencer, and The Honourable Frances Shand Kydd, rented Park House on the late Queen Elizabeth's private Sandringham estate. John had a close tie to the late Queen, having served as an equerry to her and her father, King George VI. They moved to Althorp in 1975, when John inherited the title of Earl from his father.

‌



Charles went on to add: "It really breaks me up when I look at old photographs of Diana as a child, and then think what happened to her, it's terribly sad." When asked how much he misses his sister, he told Laura: "Every day. That's the thing with sibling loss. You never get over it."

View 4 Images Charles said he has 'never' gotten over the death of Diana (Image: Channel 4)

It was at this moment that Charles' eyes started to fill with tears as Laura brought the interview to a halt. Earlier this week, Charles' book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is currently being serialised ahead of its release on Tuesday, has made a string of claims against The House of Windsor.

‌



He also suggests that his nephews, Diana's sons, Princes William and Harry, will not be shocked by his book. He said: "I don't like to talk about what I've been speaking about to William and Harry but this will not be a surprise to them I will tell you that. These words will not be a surprise to them."

Charles also addressed the two princes, walking behind Diana's coffin ahead of her funeral. William was just 15, and Harry was 12, just weeks before his 13th birthday. He claims to have argued with the then-Prince Charles, Diana's former husband, over the decision.

View 4 Images The Earl has made a series of allegations about his former brother-in-law, the now King Charles (Image: John Stillwell/PA Wire)

‌



He claimed: "I said, 'Well, of course not, sir, she wouldn't want it'. And then he said, 'Well, I walked behind Lord Mountbatten's coffin.' And I said, 'Yes, but you were 30, and he wasn't your mother'."

Following the claims that His Majesty said people would "soon forget" the late Princess, Buckingham Palace said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

In retaliation, the Earl claimed to have been "gaslit" by His Majesty, adding that the statement was a "poor imitation of the 'recollections may vary,'" quote which Her Late Majesty famously used during the fallout from Harry and Meghan's infamous Oprah Winfrey interview.

Article continues below

Earl Spencer insists he is "telling the truth" in the book, adding that as a historian, it is his "duty as an eyewitness to history", to share the story of his sister.

Like this story? For more of the latest showbiz news and gossip, follow Mirror Celebs on TikTok , Snapchat , Instagram , Twitter , Facebook , YouTube and Threads .

News.title: Residents near fire-hit Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone evacuated over safety fears
News.content:
Residents near fire-hit Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone evacuated over safety fears

Residents living near the fire-damaged Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone have been evacuated amid concerns over the building's structural safety

View 3 Images Fire damage on the walls of the Grand Burstin Hotel (Image: Cover Images)

Dozens of residents living near a fire-damaged hotel in Kent have been evacuated amid fears that the building's structure may have been weakened.

‌



Emergency services were called to a fire at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Marine Parade, Folkestone, shortly after 1am on Saturday, Kent Fire and Rescue Service said. The blaze is believed to have started in the basement.

‌



While the cause of the fire remains under investigation, officers believe it may have been started deliberately, Kent Police said. About 280 people were evacuated from the hotel at the time, and no injuries were reported.

‌



On Saturday evening, 90 people were moved from nearby Pavilion Court in Marine Terrace after safety inspectors raised concerns that the intensity of the fire may have weakened the building's structure, Folkestone and Hythe District Council said.

View 3 Images A fire broke out at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone in the early hours of Saturday (Image: Cover Images)

Folkestone's housing team is working to arrange alternative accommodation for affected residents while the hotel undergoes further assessments and any necessary work to make it safe.

‌



Susan Priest, chief executive at Folkestone and Hythe District Council, said on Saturday evening: "This has been an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes.

"The extent of support of organisations including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks."

Kent Fire and Rescue Service said at 11.30am on Sunday that firefighting operations were complete.

‌



View 3 Images About 280 people were evacuated from the hotel (Image: Cover Images)

A spokesperson for Britannia Hotels Group said: "We’d like to extend our sincere thanks to the fire service for their swift and professional response to the incident at the Grand Burstin Hotel yesterday, as well as our hotel team for their tremendous efforts in ensuring a quick and safe evacuation for all.

"Engineers and building inspectors are now on site conducting structural assessments and our team is working hard to assist all guests with their immediate needs. We remain in close contact with all relevant authorities and we appreciate everyone’s patience and understanding during this developing situation."

Article continues below

Anyone who witnessed the incident or has relevant CCTV or dashcam footage from the area, particularly between 10pm on Friday and 12.30am on Saturday, is asked to contact Kent Police on 01843 222289, quoting reference 46/155727/26.

News.title: Can Andy Burnham build a strong US-UK relationship? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Can Andy Burnham build a strong US-UK relationship? Take our poll and have your say

The Prime Minister will meet the US President next week in New York City but Andy Burnham has previously shared strong remarks against Donald Trump

View 3 Images Andy Burnham will meet Donald Trump next week (Image: ADAM VAUGHAN/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

Andy Burnham is set to come face-to-face with Donald Trump for the first time next week.

‌



The two leaders will cross paths at the UN general assembly in New York, as Burnham's steps up his presence on the world political stage. Trump and Burnham have spoken to each other at least twice on the phone since the new PM entered Downing Street in July.

‌



The US President even described Burnham as "a very nice guy" last week but the PM made unflattering comments on Trump in the past.

‌



In a post from 2021, Burnham, who was the Mayor of Greater Manchester at the time, said: "Any UK politician who gave Trump the time of day should be ashamed right now." This was after the January 6 Capitol riots.

North Korea launches double ballistic missiles into the sea as Pyongyang escalates weapons testing READ MORE :

View 3 Images Trump and Burnham have spoken over the phone twice (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

In 2017, Burnham, who was also the Manchester Mayor at this time, said the US leader would not be welcome in the city.

‌



Labour chair Bridget Phillipson however suggested these past comments will be not get in the way of a strong UK-US relationship.

She said: "Look, I think what you've just described there is politics, and the President knows that. And this is not far from unique, and people will express views at different points on different topics, and that's no bar to having a strong relationship."

‌



Phillipson added: "But of course, like there are differences of opinion, we don't have the same political outlook, but the relationship between the UK and the US goes beyond any one President, any one Prime Minister. It's something that has stood the test of time over many centuries."

The Prime Minister has previously defended his old remarks on Trump. Last month, the PM said: "I've had a habit of saying what I feel over the years, and I'll continue to do that.

"But, at the same time, I am somebody who works with people, tries to find common ground, and obviously that's what I should be doing in this job in the British public's interest, and I will always take that approach.

‌



View 3 Images The relationship between Starmer and Trump was strained over Iran and Greenland (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

"I'm looking forward actually to my first meeting. We had a good phone call on my first day in office and looking forward to meeting in person."

Relations between the White House and Sir Keir's government later became increasingly strained over the Iran conflict and disagreements about Trump's threats to annex Greenland.

Article continues below

Liberal Democrats leader Sir Ed Davey, an outspoken critic of the US president, urged the Prime Minister to take a firmer line in his dealings with the White House.

He said: "There is a danger that the new prime minister could be Keir Starmer, but with just better social media, that's not going to help anybody, is it? We need to see some teeth in his relationship with the White House. I want him to stand up to Trump. It's really clear that’s the only language the president respects."

News.title: BBC presenter Maryam Moshiri in heartbreaking 'rest of my life' admission after incurable cancer diagnosis
News.content:
BBC presenter Maryam Moshiri in heartbreaking 'rest of my life' admission after incurable cancer diagnosis

The BBC News presenter revealed that she was diagnosed in November 2024

View Image Maryam Moshiri has spoekn openly about her cancer diagnosis (Image: ITV)

Maryam Moshiri says she is finally understanding the physical and psychological impact of her incurable cancer diagnosis. The 49-year-old confirmed earlier this month that she had been diagnosed with polycythaemia vera (PV).

‌



PV - also known as erythrocytosis - is a rare blood cancer that causes your body to make too many red blood cells. There is no cure, although it can be managed and treated effectively.

‌



Only around 8,000 people in the UK have it, making it incredibly rare. Maryam revealed in an interview on BBC, she said she had spent a long time struggling to come to terms with the diagnosis.

‌



"I've been living with this for two years, and so I've managed to kind of get to a place where I understand its impact psychologically and physically on me," she explained.

"And also, I guess, I'm ready to come out and talk about it to try and help people who may have the same diagnosis or may be living with something very similar, chronic condition. The prognosis is good as long as I stay on an even keel with the medication. You know, I could live for many decades like this."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



When asked how she had come to terms psychologically with the illness, she answered: "It's really hard. When you first get a diagnosis like this, Lucy, you, you know, you kind of feel sorry for yourself.

"I remember going through a period of, 'Why me? Why has it happened to me?' But then also you feel kind of guilty because you're like, "Well, I have a chronic cancer, but I'm not going to die, you know? If I treat this cancer as it should be and get the right medical treatment, then I could live, you know, a pretty normal life'.

"It's just knowing that for the rest of my life, I'm going to be under medical care."

‌



On living with the disease, Maryam admitted some days she feels "really not well". She said: "You feel really not very well, very tired, like someone's taken your battery out. And at that point, I think you hunker down, and you just think to yourself, 'This day will be over soon, and I'll feel better again.'

"Because it's very much a disease where you'll have good times, bad times, periods where you're feeling well and periods where you are extremely unwell. And I think everyone's journey is different."

Blood cancer symptoms

Blood cancer is the fifth most common cancer in the UK, with over 40,000 people diagnosed each year. According to Dr Chun Tang, a GP at Pall Mall Medical, many cases are detected too late, often because the early signs are vague and easily overlooked.

‌



Currently, an estimated 250,000 people are living with the condition in the UK. Statistically, one in every 16 men and one in every 22 women will develop the disease in their lifetime.

While many know that persistent fatigue, unexplained weight loss, and frequent infections can be signs of cancer, Dr Tang stresses that blood cancer often presents in much more subtle ways.

“People tend to associate cancer with lumps or dramatic symptoms. But with blood cancer, you might just feel 'off', and that’s dangerous,” says Dr Tang. Lesser-known symptoms include night sweats, itchy skin, dizziness, or headaches, bruising easily or unusual bleeding such as gums or frequent nosebleeds. Shortness of breath and pale washed out looking skin are other indicators, too.

Article continues below

“These symptoms can mimic other conditions like iron deficiency or even stress,” Dr Tang explains. “But if they persist, it’s crucial to get them checked.”

Detecting blood cancer can start with a simple blood test.

“Too many people blame tiredness on a busy life. We need to flip that thinking,” said Dr Tang. “If your body is sending you signals, listen.”

News.title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
News.content:
Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history".

In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true".

Among claims made in Swan Song about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

News.title: Specialist courts for rape cases to be rolled out across England and Wales
News.content:
Labour promised in its 2024 manifesto to halve violence against women and girls within a decade.

"For too long, victims of rape and serious sexual offences have felt let down by our justice system," Burnham said.

"Prosecution rates for rape remain shamefully low, with many victims waiting years for justice. This is not good enough."

The changes were "long overdue" and would make a "significant difference" but focusing on prosecution alone would not be enough, he added.

"So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place," the prime minister said.

Nichols spoke publicly for the first time about being raped when she accused the then Justice Secretary, David Lammy, of using crime victims as a "cudgel" to push through his reforms of the legal system.

She was criticising the Courts and Tribunals Bill's plans to limit jury trials to cases with a likely prison sentence of three years or more.

She said she had waited 1,088 days to go to court, with every day being "agony" and the "trauma" made worse by her role in public life.

Her attacker, she said, was acquitted at crown court but subsequently ordered to pay compensation after she won a civil case against him.

"It is because I have been raped that I am as passionate as I am about what it means for a justice system to be truly victim-focused," she said.

"It is because I have endured every indignity that our broken criminal justice system could mete out that I care what kind of reform will actually deliver justice for survivors and victims of crime more widely."

Responding to news of the specialist courts being rolled out, the Conservatives said tackling delays to criminal rape trials was "long overdue" and they pushed Labour to commit to scrapping plans to restrict jury trials.

"The fact that victims have been withdrawing their cases because they have taken too long has been a disgrace," said shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy.

"Labour need to get courts sitting throughout the year, end the delays and clear the backlog â not undermine our right to a trial by jury."

Last year another charity, the Salford Survivor Project, said victims of rape and sexual assault were being "failed by the system" as court backlogs reached a record high.

The long delays for cases to go to trial were having a serious impact on victims' mental health, it said.

Also last year, a woman who says she was sexually assaulted by a taxi driver on her 21st birthday told BBC News she had dropped the case because of court delays.

She reported the alleged incident in early 2022 and gave evidence in court in December 2023 but the case was adjourned until September 2024 when the judge fell ill.

"I made the decision, even though I hate the statement, to drop the case," she said. "I couldn't let this hurt me further."

The Crown Prosecution Service said that, without her testimony, the case had been dropped because of insufficient evidence.

News.title: Union calls for halt to graded Ofsted inspections over health concerns
News.content:
England's biggest school leaders' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections, saying they could pose a "risk to life" for school staff.

The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said the change to inspections, rolled out nationally just under a year ago, had been severely harmful to school leaders' welfare.

It said schools should instead be rated using short narrative reports that set out their strengths and areas they could improve.

Ofsted said it had worked closely with unions and parents to develop the new report card inspection system, and would continue to grade schools.

Ofsted, England's schools' inspectorate, introduced the report card system to replace its previous one or two-word judgements last November, following the death of head teacher Ruth Perry, who took her own life after Ofsted downgraded her school from "outstanding" to "inadequate".

An inquest ruled that an Ofsted inspection had contributed to her death in January 2023.

That led to a change in how Ofsted assessed schools, bringing in report cards designed to grade schools on several areas, rather than focusing on one overall grade for the whole school.

News.title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of expected first Trump meeting
News.content:
"Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said at a Q&A with members at party conference.

"So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won."

Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.

In the wake of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.

The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.

The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.

Burnham has spoken with Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intends to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home" including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine.

News.title: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth last year
News.content:
Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.

The podcaster and author, 35, had two children with British boy band star Tom Parker before he died in 2022, aged 33, after being diagnosed with terminal brain cancer.

She is now in a relationship with Will Lindsay and last June revealed the "earth-shattering news" that they had lost their baby Phoenix.

On Sunday, a post on her Instagram account showed a photo of a newborn baby's arm next to a pink sign with the word River. "Welcome to the world, River. Our little bit of hope," the caption said.

Celebrities including The Saturdays singer Rochelle Humes, TV presenter Susanna Reid and reality TV star Holly Hagan-Blyth have congratulated Kelsey Parker on social media.

"Congratulations angel," Rochelle Humes wrote.

"Oh my goodness â this is so wonderful â welcome River," Susanna Reid said.

Hagan-Blyth commented "I am SO happy for you xxxx".

Kelsey Parker's Instagram bio says "turning life's hardest moments into hope".

Last year she posted a poem online after the loss of her stillborn baby.

It was called Born Sleeping, Forever Loved, and began "the world grew quiet as you arrived, So loved, so longed for, yet not alive. Our precious boy, our angel light, Born with wings, took silent flight".

News.title: Jailed teacher convicted of sexual abuse secretly released early in Indonesia, BBC finds
News.content:
In January this year, after hearing that Bechi may have been released early, BBC undercover reporters attended an annual prayer event at the Shiddiqiyyah Islamic boarding school in East Java.

The reporters saw Bechi wearing a mask and sitting beside his father. Just before he appeared on stage, filming and photography was prohibited, a marked difference from previous years.

Then in March, BBC reporters again captured Bechi on hidden camera at another prayer event for Eid at his family home located in the same compound as the school.

The BBC sought comment from Bechi, his mother and the Shiddiqiyyah school but there has been no response.

The students who testified, including the girl he was convicted of sexually assaulting, were placed under witness protection and Indonesian law requires them to be informed of Bechi's release.

But they were not informed, Ira and another former student who testified told the BBC. They were stunned by the undercover footage of Bechi because they believed he was still in prison.

The ministry said that victims need not be informed because Bechi remains on parole, but the witness protection agency disputed this, saying the victims must still be informed.

Ayu Masuroh says she was never abused by Bechi but she started investigating the allegations of abuse against him after hearing about them from schoolmates. She lives close to the school and says she is frightened about Bechi being out of prison.

"He hates me. His supporters have threatened to kill me many times. I will never feel safe here. I don't feel safe living in Indonesia."

Speaking publicly for the first time, she told the BBC she collected testimonies from at least 10 other female students, all of whom alleged that they were sexually assaulted or raped by Bechi.

According to her, some said Bechi told them they were "chosen", and one of them said Bechi raped her after calling her for a "personal interview".

These accounts were part of the closed-door trial, which alleged years of abuse at the school, according to court records seen by the BBC.

News.title: Brigitte Bardot's ballet flats and diamond rings to be sold at auction
News.content:
Personal possessions of late actress Brigitte Bardot â from Repetto ballet flats and diamond rings to her copy of the Kama Sutra â are being sold at auction on Monday with proceeds going to her animal charity.

Fans of the iconic figure, who died last December at the age of 91, have been coming en masse to contemplate the nearly 300 lots on display at the Drouot sale rooms in central Paris.

The items are from Bardot's two homes in Saint-Tropez as well as her Paris flat, parts of which are recreated in the display.

"Each item on sale bears the trace of an encounter, an involvement, a moment of happiness, a stage of her life. They tell the story of the woman as well as the legend," said her secretary for many years, Frank Guillou.

Bardot is seen today as one of the most important female personalities of the late 20th century. As a model and actress from the 1950s, she became an emblem of modern femininity and the sexual revolution before later taking up the cause of animal rights.

But later in life she was also criticised for making homophobic slurs and was fined multiple times for inciting racial hatred.

News.content:
It may well be decades away, but do you know how much money you will get when you stop working?

News.title: Homes evacuated over fears fire at seaside hotel weakened building's structure
News.content:
Speaking to the BBC, John Dighton, who was evacuated from Pavilion Court, said that he was told to leave his flat at about 19:00 on Saturday.

The 50-year-old said: "We don't know how long we will be out for but we have grabbed stuff for a couple of days.

"The worst thing is the not knowing. We are at a hotel over the road from the flats."

Ross Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC on Saturday how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00.

He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying.

"We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions."

Kevin Crawford, 91, and his wife Kathleen, 82, said they had booked in for a two-week stay at the hotel.

The couple, from London, told the BBC that they were in their room on the sixth floor when they heard a fire alarm.

"We saw the fire but we thought the fire brigade had it under control," said Kevin.

"We managed to sleep through it. At the time, we didn't realise how bad the fire was."

The council's chief executive, Susan Priest, said on Saturday: "The extent of support of organisations, including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army, has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks.

"This was an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes."

News.title: The deadly new drugs making Scotland's fight against addiction even harder
News.content:
Efforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous.

In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses.

Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe.

"The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science.

News.title: Billionaire Man United owner loses moral high ground after tax exile, Labour chair says
News.content:
The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Bridget Phillipson said she would take the billionaire businessman's comments that the UK was "on the slide" with a "pinch of salt".

Sir Jim, the founder of petrochemical giant Ineos and Manchester United's co-owner, told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020 and said "things would have to get better" in the UK for him to return.

When questioned over the remarks, Phillipson said Sir Jim loses "the moral high ground" by "making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile".

Pushed on whether it bothers her that people who create jobs and pay a lot of tax were leaving the UK, the minister said she was "optimistic about our country's prospects".

Other high profile billionaires have left the UK, including including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently the UK's third biggest taxpayer, hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

But, Philipson argued the country was in a good position ahead of the Budget next month, and Andy Burnham has shown a "sense of hope and optimism whilst recognising that many families are still struggling and there is more to do."

"Of course, there are challenges, including big international headwinds, but I fundamentally believe that we are in a strong position going into this budget because of the decisions taken over the last two years, and I believe our country's best days lie ahead of us," she said.

Philipson declined to speculate over whether there would be tax rises in the Budget on 28 October, and said the government remained committed to being disciplined about its spending rules.

News.title: Tens of thousands of fridge freezers left at docks as household collections suspended
News.content:
People have reported storing broken fridges and freezers in their gardens for months because some council collections have been suspended.

It follows the closure of specialist treatment facilities and a wider shortage of capacity to process cooling appliances, the Local Government Authority (LGA) said.

Recycling company Unimetals, which had dozens of sites in the UK, filed for liquidation in 2025 leaving tens of thousands of fridge freezers at Newport Docks.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was working to manage the capacity shortages.

Almost a quarter of Welsh councils say they have suspended household collections of fridge-freezers due to a shortage of space at disposal sites.

Cardiff is one of these and Lee Young, who lives in the city, has been trying to get rid of his broken fridge-freezer for two months.

"I tried to take it to the recycling centre in July but was told it wasn't accepted. Someone said the council would collect it, but they won't either."

It has been sitting in his back garden ever since and he does not know when council collections will resume.

News.title: Human extinction fears make me want to flee AI and live on an island
News.content:
Since headlines broke about claims AI advancement could lead to human extinction, James Downs has felt his anxiety rising.

"It makes me almost feel powerless. Like, what can I do as an individual?" said the mental health campaigner from Cardiff.

This sense of fear has led him to check his phone for more news.

"And the more you look at it the more your attention's drawn to the negative or scary things and the worse and worse it can seem," said the 37-year-old.

Earlier this month, a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned AI was advancing so quickly he believed there was a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

Then computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC that the claim was "not unreasonable", external.

On Tuesday, amid rising public concerns about the risks, the boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe.

News.title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
News.content:
Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living.

The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump.

Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy.

"Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said.

The policy would cost about Â£2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding."

In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from Â£3 to Â£1, and reduce rail fares by 10%.

He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs.

Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already.

"Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them."

Sir Ed also ruled out scrapping the state pension triple lock after party grandee and former business secretary Sir Vince Cable said at a fringe event it was unsustainable and should be "phased out".

Speaking at Q&A on the conference stage, Sir Ed said the policy had been introduced by the Lib Dems during the Conservative coalition to address inequalities and there was still work to do to tackle pensioner poverty.

"It has not finished the job," he told party members, who were split in a show of hands about whether the triple lock should be scrapped if the Lib Dems win power.

The triple lock guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but critics say it is unaffordable and unfair to younger people.

News.title: JLR suppliers call for shift to aerospace
News.content:
Major Jaguar Land Rover suppliers have urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.

In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market".

The intervention comes nearly a fortnight after JLR announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs.

The Treasury said it recognised the uncertainty facing workers and was supporting the automotive sector through grants, lower energy costs and investment in electric vehicle production.

JLR has its global headquarters in Coventry and plants in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood.

Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.

News.title: Maddy Cusack 'more than a number on a shirt' as anniversary falls during inquest delay
News.content:
Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fun.

Olivia Cusack says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life", while for Emily Reilly, her cousin Maddy's the one who "used to get us in trouble with my dad".

But as they come to remember the former Sheffield United footballer on the third anniversary of her death, they're still waiting for answers.

An inquest examining what happened to Maddy Cusack, who was 27 when she was found unconscious at her home in Derbyshire, started in June and should've finished in July.

But it has been paused for months while her former club Sheffield United looks for documents linked to her medical records.

It means her family will have to wait until at least December to hear more evidence, a wait Olivia describes as "extremely overwhelming".

"It is very emotional and you can find yourself frustrated at times," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"They're very difficult days."

A federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent reportedly shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas, early Sunday afternoon during the latest instance of government violence allegedly tied to President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign.

The unidentified victim was hit once in the torso and rushed to a local trauma center, where he was in serious but stable condition, Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Robert Luckritz said during a news conference. He couldn’t confirm whether the man was shot in the front of his body or from behind.

Officials said city police officers weren’t present during the shooting, which took place near a highway overpass in the 800 block of Anderson Square around 12:55 p.m. local time.

Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said she was told the shooter “is an ICE agent,” and Mayor Kirk Watson said he was “very angry” over the shooting.

“Part of what makes me angry about this, part of what makes me so unhappy about it, is that we live in a time where there's a politics of fear, where people are trying to create fear,” Watson said.

open image in gallery A car at the scene of the shooting in Austin, Texas, appears to have bullet holes in it ( Reuters )

Watson said there was “no reason for us to be surprised” by the shooting, given “the nature of ICE and how it’s doing its business” in other cities. He called for an independent, third-party investigation, saying it “would not be appropriate” to let ICE conduct the probe.

Davis said, “I trust the Texas Rangers, and I trust [the Texas Department of Public Safety]...to work alongside us and to get — to get answers. Absolutely.”

Spokespersons for ICE and the Department of Homeland Security didn’t immediately return inquiries from The Independent.

Photographs taken at the scene show a dark blue Toyota Corolla with damage along its passenger side and what appear to be two bullet holes in the rear window.

The police chief said she couldn’t confirm a report that the car was sideswiped and that the ICE agent fired multiple shots through its rear windshield.

“That's not what I'm hearing. I'm hearing that it was out on foot...there was a small foot pursuit,” she said, adding that “this is all very preliminary” and that she hadn’t been briefed by federal officials.

open image in gallery Austin Mayor Kirk Watson says there’s ‘no reason for us to be surprised’ by the shooting, given ‘the nature of ICE and how it’s doing its business’ ( The City of Austin, Texas/ATXN )

Democratic U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, whose district covers the shooting scene, said, “I think the obvious should be said, that there is a reason that people in Austin and across the country are deeply suspicious of anything that ICE has said.”

“People in the community don't know all the facts, but people are hurting and upset because they see how ICE has shot and, in some cases, even killed people with impunity in other parts of the country,” he said.

Casar also called on ICE to end what he called its “surge of officers here” and to instead “be focused on transparently working on issues of crime, not what they've been doing consistently here in Austin before this event.”

The mayor said local officials “have seen an increase, we believe, in the number of incidents where ICE has detained somebody, stopped somebody, those sorts of instances.”

“And it happened in a relatively brief period of time,” Watson said. “I think in one week we saw it go from: count them on one hand to in the thirties, and that happened in less than a couple of days.”

open image in gallery US Rep. Greg Casar says ‘there is a reason that people in Austin and across the country are deeply suspicious of anything that ICE has said’ ( The City of Austin, Texas/ATXN )

The incident in Austin follows a string of immigration-related shootings by federal law-enforcement officers carrying out Trump’s pledge to conduct the “largest mass deportation program in history,” which has a reported goal of expelling 1 million people a year.

In Minneapolis, two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot while separately protesting ICE operations in January, leading to the ouster of then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who falsely accused them of domestic terrorism.

ICE officers also allegedly killed Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Colombian national Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, during separate traffic stops in July, even though neither was the target of an investigation.

Their slayings led Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to order a temporary halt to vehicle stops by ICE. Trump immediately criticized the directive, leading Mullin to countermand it the following day.

Reports also revealed that the ICE officer who allegedly shot Durán Guerrero, David Brouilette, had a history of mental illness that led military recruiters to reject him before he went off his medications and was able to enlist in the Maine National Guard and later join the Army in January 2010.

Brouilette was deployed to Afghanistan from May 2012 to February 2015, with an immediate relative telling The Associated Press that the tour of duty "destroyed him."

"They took someone who was extremely mentally ill and turned him into a killing machine," the relative said.

News.content:
