At just 22 years old, Eman David has spent much of her life in and out of hospital.

Diagnosed with kidney failure at seven, she was handed a lifeline in 2014 when she had a successful kidney transplant, which allowed her to finally enjoy her childhood.

But in 2021, she received the heartbreaking news that her body had started to reject the organ and that she would need another transplant. Six years later, she is still waiting.

“Right now I’m just doing maths at college. But I can’t focus on anything but dialysis and the transplant and when they’re going to call me.”

“I’m always looking at my phone, I’m always thinking that it’s them [the hospital] calling me.”

Ms David, from Manchester, is one of 8,700 patients in the UK waiting for an organ transplant – a record high – with nine people a week dying while waiting to get a lifesaving call, according to NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT). At this rate, it could mean 468 deaths by next summer if nothing changes.

The situation has reached crisis point and is now so concerning that NHSBT, the body responsible for organ donation, has had to take the “unprecedented” move to trigger its “urgent” organ donation response plan.

John Richardson, assistant director of Organ and Tissue Donation and Transplantation, told The Independent: “In organ donation, it’s unprecedented that we’ve moved to this footing; it’s the highest list we’ve seen. Up to nine people each week will die waiting for an organ transplant, so it is significant.”

open image in gallery Eman David is still waiting for a donor three years on ( Patient Handout )

Despite a change in the law to introduce opt-out donations – which assumes people have opted in to donate organs unless they have explicitly stated otherwise – families can still decline a deceased relative’s wishes. The latest data shows family consent rates have dropped from 67 per cent in 2020-21 to 57 per cent last year.

Mr Richardson explained the issue likely driving this is that people do not make their wishes clear by registering to donate, and so families who don’t know what their loved one wanted can often decline donation.

That leaves people like Ms David in limbo and facing lengthy waits.

‘Dialysis just drains you’

She is one of the 80 per cent of transplant waiting list patients waiting for a kidney, with 7,200 currently in limbo.

Ms David and her parents were first told she would need a transplant and weekly dialysis when she was seven.

“Since then I’ve just had to basically live at Manchester Royal Infirmary. I think I missed about two, three years of primary school.”

At 11, Ms David and her family got some hope, and she received a kidney from a donor.

“My life changed so much, you know; I finally was able to travel. I remember that a year after my transplant, I went to Spain. I’d be more active. I get tired a lot because I even wanted to eat without restrictions.”

However, in 2021, doctors discovered that her body was rejecting her kidneys, which were functioning at just 15 per cent, and she would need to go back on dialysis.

“It wasn’t really scary because I was thinking like, “What do you mean it’s not working?” I was doing all these blood tests, all these tubes taken out on me, you know. I was thinking, ‘Is this going to ruin my education again?’”

“Dialysis just drains you.”

Initially, she was too ill to even be eligible for a transplant, but she was eventually placed on the waiting list in 2023. She is still waiting.

Fiona Loud, policy director at Kidney Care UK, and a kidney transplant recipient herself, said: “It’s experiences like Eman’s that really highlight the impact that waiting for a transplant can have. To be waiting in limbo for so many of her formative years is heartbreaking. It really hits home that every number on that waiting list is a person with hopes and dreams just waiting for that life-changing call.

“We hope that after reading Eman’s story, people will understand more about the difference organ donation can make and register their decision to be a donor.”

open image in gallery Becca Moore, 31, has been waiting for a new kidney for 18 months ( Handout )

Becca Moore, 31, was treated for recurring urine infections (UTI) during childhood due to a condition which means her urine travels the wrong way from her bladder to her kidneys, causing organ damage.

When she turned 16, the infections “came back with a vengeance” and UTIs made her so sick she was unable to properly take her GCSEs.

After a few years of stable health, she was admitted to hospital in 2008 with a significant UTI and suspected sepsis, a blood infection that can be fatal. The UTIs had done such damage to her kidneys that she needed dialysis.

“It was devastating. My life turned upside down. I worked so hard.”

“When I got my GCSE results, I was told, ‘You ain’t gonna make anything good’. I’d been so poorly during them that I didn’t do the best I should have, or what they expected of me.

“However, I worked myself up working in care homes, daycare centres, and I’d really conquered a job that I absolutely loved. I was a deputy manager of a supported living unit for adults with learning disabilities and mental health issues.”

She added, “I’d gone from having nothing with GCSEs to get where I wanted to be, then losing it again, due to my illness that I didn’t understand. So it did affect me...I had quite severe anxiety. I thought I was going to die.”

In July 2019, Ms Moore received a transplanted kidney from her cousin who was a match. However, devastatingly, in 2023, her body rejected the kidney.

Again in 2025, when her health deteriorated further, she began haemodialysis treatment, where a machine filters waste products and excess fluid from the blood.

Ms Morten has to travel to the hospital for this three times a week and her closest treatment centre is three hours away.

While she waits for a transplant, Ms Moore has been able to move to home dialysis, which has allowed her to work again and go on her honeymoon this month. However, she desperately needs an organ donor.

Chief executive of Kidney Research UK, Fiona Carragher, said: “We all have the power to help turn the tide. Saying yes to organ donation, recording your decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register and making your loved ones aware of your decision is vital if we are to reduce those waiting times.

“But we also must do more, and science holds the answers. It is only through research that we’ll be able to make more kidneys suitable for transplant and find ways to make transplanted kidneys work better and last longer, giving patients the best possible chance of a healthier future.”

Kenyan growers who produce black tea for British supermarket shelves have warned that climate impacts are damaging crop harvests and further diminishing their already "scarce" household incomes.

The East African nation currently provides half of all black tea consumed across Britain, but local farmers face increasingly unpredictable weather patterns, lower crop yields and quality, alongside escalating operational expenses over recent years.

These compounding issues have driven up global tea costs, leaving supermarket shoppers in the UK paying noticeably higher prices for their favourite beverage.

Yet impoverished farmers at the start of the supply chain see little financial gain from higher market prices. Harvesting smaller crops while spending more to maintain them, growers watch as intermediaries, brokers and large corporate firms continue absorbing the vast majority of total profits.

Across the western Kenyan regions of Kericho and Bomet, many local agricultural workers say they cannot cover basic family living expenses, let alone invest in essential protective measures to build future climate resilience on their farms.

These areas are experiencing severe weather volatility this year, including heavy rainfall during usually dry January periods, unseasonal heat in July, intense storm activity and prolonged drought conditions.

open image in gallery Kenyan farmers who grow tea sold in UK supermarkets have warned that climate impacts are hitting yields and their already 'scarce' incomes ( PA )

Nelson Ngeno, manager of Fintea, a union of tea farming cooperatives based in Kericho, said farmers are “really scared” as their livelihoods are “cut short” by the changing conditions.

Production across Fintea’s five cooperatives fell by 30% in May and June this year compared to what their farmers usually harvest during those months, he said.

“Climate is really affecting our farmers,” Mr Ngeno said. “There has been a complete change as far as the weather is concerned.

“It is very serious.”

In January, an unprecendented hail storm damaged thousands of tea plants in the district of Kabartegan, with Fintea estimating losses of 20,000 to 30,000kg daily over four months as the plants recovered.

Lilian Mutai Levin Langot, from the village of Kesebet, was among some 500 tea farmers who lost significant earnings when the storm wiped out her farm.

The 48-year-old smallholder farmer told the Press Association: “It was scary. The hailstones hit everything. On the tea plants, only the stems remained.

“I could not pick anything. It meant there was no income. There was nothing. We just had to survive.”

While she normally earns around 120,000 Kenyan Shillings (Kes) annually (£692), this will likely drop to no more than 90,000 Kes (£520) in 2026.

Ms Langot said she has taken out a loan to get through the year but has still struggled to pay for healthcare fees, school fees for her son and the upkeep of her infant granddaughter.

And having bought a cow and calf to diversify her income, the farmer said she was unable to buy enough feed, so the cow stopped producing milk, and both eventually died.

“It was so hard,” she said, adding that she is “very worried” about such a storm happening again.

“It will be so bad on us,” she said. “When we see the rain, we are just hoping: ‘Don’t let it be the hailstones. Let it just be the rain’.”

Meanwhile, Paul Kipsigei Koech, 50, who lives in nearby Chepchabas, told PA that he is earning so little from his tea farm that he can only provide one meal of mushed-up maize each day for his seven children, wife and elderly father.

Extreme weather events are now happening “once a year”, he said. “You can’t predict like we usually do in the previous (years).”

This, alongside the rising cost of living, is putting further pressure on his ability to make ends meet, with his current income sitting at around 3,000 to 4,000 Kes (£17 to £23) a month, equivalent to less than £1 a day.

“The income is really low to support the entire family,” he said, adding that he is also 80,000 Kes (£462) in debt.

“It is not enough. It is very scarce,” he said. “There is no breakfast. No lunch.”

Asked what he would spend the money on if he received a higher price for his produce, Mr Koech said he would pay the fees so his children – the youngest of which is six – could go to school and eventually help to support the family.

open image in gallery Kenya, which supplies half of all the black tea consumed by Britain, has seen farmers facing unpredictable climate conditions, lower production and quality levels, and rising input costs in recent years ( PA )

“I do not want them to come back to pick tea. I want them to go forward and even get different jobs than what I do,” he said.

Meanwhile, Gladys Maiywa, 50, also from Chepchabas, also earns around 3,000 Kes (£17) a month to support her eight children and sometimes less depending on the weather.

She similarly has sunk 19,000 Kes (£109) in debt to pay for school fees and has an overdraft in the bank of 3,000 Kes.

“It’s very difficult,” she said. “If we get droughts for one, two or three months, we don’t get money. We can’t harvest anything.”

Ms Maiywa said she would spend additional income on her children, their education and build a new home to replace the basic hut they all currently live in.

“I want to see an increase to the rate of pay for our tea,” she added.

And Philip Kitur, a 66-year-old farmer based near Kericho Town, said he has produced 50 per cent less tea than usual for July as climate change and unfair trade practices hit his income.

He said: “A long time ago, the weather was very, very reliable but now the weather patterns have changed.”

His income “just covers the production costs right now”, he said, adding that he has to look for other means of earning money to cover his household’s needs.

“I expect to see less profit this year because of the dry period. We don’t know what’s to come,” he said. “It is very painful.”

open image in gallery These areas are seeing more volatile and extreme weather this year, including wetter conditions in January when it is usually dry, hot temperatures in July when cooler conditions are expected, storms and drought. ( PA )

Their stories come against a wider backdrop of Fintea seeing a drop in the amount of tea it sells on Fairtrade terms from around 5 per cent five years ago to less than 1 per cent today.

This means its farming cooperatives receive less money from “premium payments”, which they can use to invest in climate resilience measures or social impact projects.

Supermarket Lidl last week announced it would be sourcing more tea from Fintea on Fairtrade terms and pay additional money to boost farmers’ incomes, for a new tea called “Way To Go!”, which will hit shelves on Tuesday.

Fintea said the commitment means the percentage of tea it sells on Fairtrade terms may increase to around 2.6 per cent in the coming years.

But Fairtrade is urging more businesses to source tea on Fairtrade terms as the organisation marks the start of its annual “Fairtrade Fortnight” campaign on Monday.

Kerrina Thorogood, partnerships director at the Fairtrade Foundation, said: “Today, just one in five tea farmers in Kenya earns enough income each month to support their families with the essentials.

“As a result, many struggle to invest in their farms, adapt to climate change, and plan for the future.

“Addressing this challenge requires businesses to take responsibility for the prices they pay.”

Hints of an “autumn bounce” were seen in the housing market in September, as the average price tag on a home increased month on month for the first time since May, according to a property website.

The average price of a home coming on the market increased by 0.7% or £2,441 month on month in September, Rightmove said.

Across Britain, the average price tag on a home in September is £367,440, it added.

open image in gallery Rightmove’s map shows average asking price changes across Britain (Rightmove/PA)

This September’s asking price bounce is bigger than the average for the month over the past 10 years, at 0.5%.

September is traditionally a busier period for the housing market as people return from summer holidays, Rightmove said.

It added that heatwaves and the World Cup also created conditions for a particularly quiet summer this year, giving some potential scope for a bigger rebound.

But typical prices remain 0.8% below a year earlier, and 2.3% lower than the start of the summer.

Rightmove also said it is a challenging and crowded market for sellers, with the number of homes available on the market for sale at a 12-year high for the time of year and buyer affordability still stretched.

The Bank of England kept interest rates unchanged at 3.75% last week – but average fixed mortgage rates have still been increasing in recent weeks amid rises in swap rates, which are used to price mortgages.

Finance experts said last week that fixed mortgage rates are influenced by financial markets’ expectations for what will happen, adding that home buyers are expected to be cautious and price-sensitive in the months ahead.

open image in gallery

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Rightmove said buyer demand is below this time last year as buyers grapple with affordability challenges.

Colleen Babcock, property expert at Rightmove, said: “Property prices have largely underperformed against the long-term average this year, but September is an exception.

“While buyers and sellers are returning to the market after the summer holidays to potentially fuel an autumn bounce, sellers face stiff competition from a 12-year high number of other homes for sale.

“With a large crowd of sellers chasing a smaller number of buyers, realism on pricing or a high-quality finish are absolutely key to attracting a buyer and making a sale.”

Rightmove’s analysis indicated that a home for sale typically has around a six in 10 (61%) chance of finding a buyer – but this varies significantly across Britain.

In Scotland, nine in 10 (91%) homes for sale are finding a buyer, which is partly due to Scotland’s buying and selling practices, the website said.

In the North West of England, 71% of homes are finding a buyer, compared with 56% in the South East and 42% in London, the analysis indicated.

Rightmove’s analysis also indicated that 74% of homes sold so far this year were priced right first time and did not need a later asking price reduction.

Ms Babcock added: “It’s encouraging to see more buyers returning to the market as we move into autumn, with activity picking up as usual after a subdued summer.

“Whilst almost two-thirds of homes are still successfully finding a buyer, the chances of selling vary significantly depending on where you live.

“Over 90% of homes that come to market for sale are selling in Scotland versus less than half in London, meaning those who want to sell will have to set their pricing according to local market conditions.

“Buyers continue to have plenty of choice and mortgage rates are increasing, so competitive pricing is still the biggest factor in attracting interest and securing a sale.

“Sellers who get the initial asking price right are giving themselves the best chance of standing out in a crowded market.”

Matt Smith, a mortgage expert at Rightmove, said: “This month’s traditional uplift in buyer activity shows there’s still a strong underlying desire to move, but volatility in mortgage rates remains a significant challenge for many.

“Mortgage rates have risen again over the past month, adding further pressure to monthly budgets, and the uncertainty over what may happen to rates in the medium term is likely holding back some potential movers.”

Kevin James, managing director at Bradleys Estate Agents in the south west of England, said: “The summer months delivered better activity than expected in our areas, particularly for sellers who adapted their expectations to the affordability pressures in the market, and listened to advice to price realistically.

“As families now return from their holidays and the new school year begins, we’re seeing the traditional autumn uplift in demand.”

Marc von Grundherr, director of Benham and Reeves, said: “Pricing correctly from day one is absolutely vital, particularly in London where buyers have a huge amount of choice and very little patience for homes that look over-ambitious on price.

“That can sometimes mean having a difficult conversation with a seller at the outset, but an experienced agent should be prepared to have it.

“Launch too high and you risk wasting the strongest period of buyer interest, only to reduce later once the property has already started to look stale.

“Price is only part of the equation.

“Presentation matters, flexibility around viewings matters and, above all, sellers need to listen to the feedback the market is giving them.”

Signs of an "autumn bounce" appeared in the housing market during September as average asking prices rose month on month for the first time since May, according to Rightmove.

The property website reported that the average price tag on a home put up for sale increased by 0.7 per cent, or £2,441, in September. This brings the national average asking price across Britain to £367,440.

This month’s increase exceeds the decade-long average September rise of 0.5 per cent. September is traditionally a more active period for the property sector as prospective buyers return from summer holidays.

Rightmove noted that heatwaves and the World Cup had resulted in a particularly quiet summer this year, creating the potential conditions for a larger rebound.

However, average prices remain 0.8 per cent lower than at the same point a year ago, and are 2.3 per cent below levels recorded at the start of summer.

It remains a challenging and crowded marketplace for prospective sellers, with the total number of homes available for sale reaching a 12-year high for this time of year, while buyer affordability remains stretched.

open image in gallery Rightmove also said it is a challenging and crowded market for sellers, with the number of homes available on the market for sale at a 12-year high for the time of year and buyer affordability still stretched. ( AFP/Getty )

The Bank of England kept interest rates unchanged at 3.75 per cent last week – but average fixed mortgage rates have still been increasing in recent weeks amid rises in swap rates, which are used to price mortgages.

Finance experts said last week that fixed mortgage rates are influenced by financial markets’ expectations for what will happen, adding that home buyers are expected to be cautious and price-sensitive in the months ahead.

Rightmove said buyer demand is below this time last year as buyers grapple with affordability challenges.

Colleen Babcock, property expert at Rightmove, said: “Property prices have largely underperformed against the long-term average this year, but September is an exception.

“While buyers and sellers are returning to the market after the summer holidays to potentially fuel an autumn bounce, sellers face stiff competition from a 12-year high number of other homes for sale.

“With a large crowd of sellers chasing a smaller number of buyers, realism on pricing or a high-quality finish are absolutely key to attracting a buyer and making a sale.”

open image in gallery Rightmove’s analysis also indicated that 74 per cent of homes sold so far this year were priced right first time and did not need a later asking price reduction ( AFP/Getty )

Rightmove’s analysis indicated that a home for sale typically has around a six in 10 (61 per cent) chance of finding a buyer – but this varies significantly across Britain.

In Scotland, nine in 10 (91 per cent) homes for sale are finding a buyer, which is partly due to Scotland’s buying and selling practices, the website said.

In the North West of England, 71 per cent of homes are finding a buyer, compared with 56 per cent in the South East and 42 per cent in London, the analysis indicated.

Rightmove’s analysis also indicated that 74 per cent of homes sold so far this year were priced right first time and did not need a later asking price reduction.

Ms Babcock added: “It’s encouraging to see more buyers returning to the market as we move into autumn, with activity picking up as usual after a subdued summer.

“Whilst almost two-thirds of homes are still successfully finding a buyer, the chances of selling vary significantly depending on where you live.

“Over 90 per cent of homes that come to market for sale are selling in Scotland versus less than half in London, meaning those who want to sell will have to set their pricing according to local market conditions.

“Buyers continue to have plenty of choice and mortgage rates are increasing, so competitive pricing is still the biggest factor in attracting interest and securing a sale.

“Sellers who get the initial asking price right are giving themselves the best chance of standing out in a crowded market.”

open image in gallery Finance experts said last week that fixed mortgage rates are influenced by financial markets’ expectations for what will happen, adding that home buyers are expected to be cautious and price-sensitive in the months ahead ( AFP/Getty )

Matt Smith, a mortgage expert at Rightmove, said: “This month’s traditional uplift in buyer activity shows there’s still a strong underlying desire to move, but volatility in mortgage rates remains a significant challenge for many.

“Mortgage rates have risen again over the past month, adding further pressure to monthly budgets, and the uncertainty over what may happen to rates in the medium term is likely holding back some potential movers.”

Kevin James, managing director at Bradleys Estate Agents in the south west of England, said: “The summer months delivered better activity than expected in our areas, particularly for sellers who adapted their expectations to the affordability pressures in the market, and listened to advice to price realistically.

“As families now return from their holidays and the new school year begins, we’re seeing the traditional autumn uplift in demand.”

Marc von Grundherr, director of Benham and Reeves, said: “Pricing correctly from day one is absolutely vital, particularly in London where buyers have a huge amount of choice and very little patience for homes that look over-ambitious on price.

“That can sometimes mean having a difficult conversation with a seller at the outset, but an experienced agent should be prepared to have it.

“Launch too high and you risk wasting the strongest period of buyer interest, only to reduce later once the property has already started to look stale.

“Price is only part of the equation.

“Presentation matters, flexibility around viewings matters and, above all, sellers need to listen to the feedback the market is giving them.”

Celebrity hairdresser Chris Appleton has suggested his friend and client Kim Kardashian could be cheering him on from the studio audience as he takes part in Strictly Come Dancing.

The 43-year-old was paired with professional dancer Amy Dowden on Saturday’s launch episode of the BBC One entertainment show.

He will compete against stars including singer Delta Goodrem, former Love Island winner Dani Dyer and former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips.

Asked if Kardashian, whose reality TV show The Kardashians has featured Appleton, would attend a live show, he said: "Who knows? Watch this space, but I don’t know, anything could happen.

"I think being in Strictly, I’ve realised anything is possible and magic happens.

"I have no idea, I know a lot of people want to come to the show and we’re only allocated two tickets."

It comes after Kardashian posted on social media to support Appleton when his participation in the show was announced and also sent him flowers.

open image in gallery Kim Kardashian and North West present the award to Chris Appleton, Hair Artist of the Year Award recipient, onstage during The Daily Front Row's Seventh Annual Fashion Los Angeles Awards ( Getty )

The Leicester-born hairdresser added: “Kim’s so sweet, I mean, she’s been such an amazing person throughout my whole career.

“She’s obviously fantastic at what she does, but obviously I know Kim personally, and she’s just always been so kind, and she sent me a beautiful bouquet of flowers, which was just so kind of her to do, she didn’t have to.

“And she said, ‘break a leg’, and just commenting on my post when I did it, and that’s so nice of her to support me because she’s always been so supportive.

“But to do that, which is going above and beyond, it just says so much about who she is, she’s an amazing person.

“Like I say, she’s always been so supportive, I’m very lucky to work with her, and she’s my hair muse, she’s always been my girl.”

open image in gallery The hair stylist – who is best known for working with stars including Kim Kardashian and Jennifer Lopez – said he was counting down to appearing in the BBC series ( PA )

Appleton’s other celebrity clients include Sofía Vergara, Ariana Grande and Katy Perry.

He has previously been named a “Hair Star” by Vogue UK and his work has been showcased on covers and in major features for publications including Vogue, Harper’s Bazaar, Vanity Fair, Marie Claire, Grazia, L’Officiel Paris, and more.

The hair stylist also recently made the New York Times Best Sellers list for his memoir Your Roots Don’t Define You.

Appleton will return to Strictly in Saturday’s first live show on BBC One and iPlayer at 6.15pm.

Food and milk producers in England and Wales have come under increasing pressure from extreme heat and drought, and Scottish producers have said they are looking north to fill in the gaps.

The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, with five intense heatwaves alongside historic dry spells that triggered widespread drought declarations and hosepipe bans across much of the nation.

Thanks to the weather, farmers in England and Wales have seen poor grazing conditions, stunted harvests, and heat strain on livestock.

As a result, an Ayrshire-based organic dairy producer told the Press Association that it has seen a “quite dramatic” increase in demand for organic milk from businesses south of the border.

Mossgiel Organic Dairy founder Bryce Cunningham said he received three calls from businesses asking what milk his company could supply for the following week within the space of around 10 minutes.

Mr Cunningham said the level of interest was unprecedented for the farm and demonstrated how quickly the market had tightened, with businesses now looking further afield to secure supplies.

open image in gallery The increased demand comes as the UK milk market faces lower collections than 2025 due to the impacts of heat stress and drought ( Getty )

“The drought has caused serious supply issues across the dairy industry,” Mr Cunningham said.

“Organic milk is generally quite difficult to get at this time of year anyway, but the drought has amplified that.”

As of 11 September, Mossgiel Organic Dairy has sent approximately 56,000 litres of Scottish organic milk – or approximately two large milk tankers – south of the border to bolster supplies.

The company was asked to supply a further 40,000 litres, which it did not have available.

“In the dairy industry, (56,000 litres of milk) is relatively small beans, but in organics, it’s quite substantial,” he said.

“We’re obviously pleased to be able to help out, but it just shows you a sign of the times, you know, and how impactful this weather event has been.”

The increased demand comes as the UK milk market faces lower collections than 2025 due to the impacts of heat stress and drought.

According to Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB) figures, UK daily milk collections are currently running around 1.24 million litres (3.7 per cent) lower than the same week last year.

While Mossgiel has experienced some heat stress among its cows, Mr Cunningham said Scottish producers have largely avoided the worst effects of the weather this year.

open image in gallery Thanks to the weather, farmers in England and Wales have seen poor grazing conditions, stunted harvests, and heat strain on livestock ( Getty )

But he said there’s a “real concern” because these pressures ultimately affect farmers and food producers everywhere.

“The bigger worry for us all is that if this happens once in ten years, then that’s a hard thing to take, but you can recover from it,” he said.

“But what happens if this is the new normal? Is climate change hitting us quicker than we thought? We are in the middle of summer and we can’t graze animals and we can’t grow food because it’s too dry and too hot. So that’s a big worry that we’ve got for the future.”

The same pressures are being felt across other areas of food production, including fruit.

Scottish cider producers are watching the situation closely as growers south of the border face mounting pressure.

Angus Morrison, founder of Lost Orchards, said there has been a bumper crop for fruits in Scotland while the heat and drought has caused “calamity on the orchard crops for this year” down south.

“What we’re seeing is a really telling example of how climate change is beginning to affect where food can be grown and how businesses source it,” he said.

“We’re in constant dialogue with our friends south of the border, and the challenges being reported by growers in England this year show just how difficult prolonged heat and drought can be for the industry.”

Mr Morrison added: “English apple growers are considered some of the best in the world, with generations of knowledge and experience behind them, but even the best growers are having to contend with conditions that are becoming increasingly difficult to manage.”

Mr Morrison continued: “Whether it’s a long-term climate change pattern or not, is probably yet to be seen… but certainly the changing climate is helping the fruit growing in Scotland and other areas better than it is in the south and Europe for that matter.”

A father who lost 32st after being cautioned that his size endangered his life during open-heart surgery now believes he has the "best chance" of staying with his family.

Standing 6ft 8in tall, 46-year-old maintenance business owner Mark Bailey, from Stockton, Warwickshire, was nicknamed Tiny and was a "big lad" from a young age. Having been "on the heavier side" since childhood, he hit a peak weight of 48st 9lbs (309kg) aged 39, requiring 7XL tops and 72-inch waist trousers.

His weight soared after years of consuming 7,500 calories daily, including pasties and Mars bars for breakfast, McDonald’s lunches, kebabs for dinner, and unmonitored beer consumption.

A heart murmur diagnosis in October 2021 prompted the need for open-heart surgery, serving as a "wake-up call" to "be around" for his wife, Nicola Bailey, and their children, Kyla, 26, Byron, 23, and Kyson, 17.

Declining GLP-1 medication and weight loss surgery, he lost 28st (177kg) across four years through lifestyle changes ahead of his October 2025 operation. Following a successful procedure, he shed an additional 4st (25kg) and recently finished a 5km challenge for the Rugby Cardiac Rehabilitation team.

open image in gallery After a successful operation and recovery, Tiny has lost a further 4st (25kg) and managed to complete a 5km challenge this month to raise funds for the Rugby Cardiac Rehabilitation team that helped him rebuild his life ( Your Photo Finish/PA Real Life )

Tiny told PA Real Life: “When I had a chat with the cardiologist … she said if I had open-heart surgery at the weight I was, the chances of me coming off that operating table were very, very slim.

“I knew I got myself in this position, so I could get myself out of it.

“It’s frightening, but you can have such a good life afterwards and I’m already proving that now.”

Tiny said he got his “ironic” nickname of Tiny aged 10 because he has “always stood out in a crowd” for his height and weight.

“I’ve always been a food lover and it just escalated,” he said.

“I just never limited myself to anything, so I had what I wanted when I wanted it.”

On an average day, Tiny said he consumed around 7,500 calories, starting with a full English breakfast of five sausages, five rashers of bacon, five hash browns and five eggs, before having a packet of crisps, a soft drink and chocolate bars as a mid-morning snack.

For lunch, he tended to have McDonald’s, with his order consisting of a double quarter pounder, two double cheeseburgers, fries, mozzarella sticks and a large milkshake.

open image in gallery A routine scan in September 2025 confirmed his valve got worse so they could not put off the open-heart surgery any longer ( Your Photo Finish/PA Real Life )

His dinner was often an extra large doner kebab with cheesy chips and garlic bread, and he always finished the night with a packet of biscuits.

Tiny has had health complications over the years, including being diagnosed with the thyroid immune condition Graves’ disease at age 34, as well as sore knees, gallbladder issues and shoulder pain.

As a result, he tried “a few” ways to lose weight, including the carnivore diet, which is based mainly on eating meat and other animal products, and Slimming World, with some success.

But after being diagnosed with a heart murmur in October 2021, he was told he needed open-heart surgery and that his weight would pose additional risks.

Tiny said he was offered bariatric surgery to shrink his stomach and weight-loss jabs but declined both, as he did not want any further medical interventions.

Instead, Tiny “did a lot of research” and implemented a calorie deficit, cutting out biscuits and chocolate bars, and started going to the gym twice a week.

Within two years, he lost 18st (114kg) but said he still felt mentally and emotionally “rubbish” because he was experiencing breathlessness and “horrible palpitations” because of his failing heart health.

A routine scan in September 2025 confirmed his valve got worse so they could not put off the open-heart surgery any longer.

“The surgeon actually said my valve didn’t have six weeks left in it, so he agreed to cut short his holiday for me to get me fixed up,” Tiny said.

open image in gallery Mark Bailey, 46, a maintenance business owner from Stockton, Warwickshire said he has always been a “big lad” at 6ft 8in tall, and is widely known as Tiny. ( Your Photo Finish/PA Real Life )

On October 15, Tiny had the seven-hour surgery at University Hospital Coventry. He said his recovery was “really quite fast” and he was discharged after eight days.

Tiny started at the Cardiac Rehabilitation Service in Rugby for eight weeks from December, across 16 “very steady” and supervised sessions.

“The surgeon did a fantastic job and the nurses at Coventry Hospital were absolutely brilliant,” Tiny said.

“But Rugby Cardiac Rehabilitation went above and beyond.

“They gave me the confidence to know what my heart can and can’t take and how far I can push myself.”

As a way to say thank you to his rehabilitation team, Tiny completed the 5km Autumn Wolf wild muddy obstacle run – an off-road course through obstacles, mud and water – on September 11 this year.

Tiny said: “I absolutely loved it … and it was my own personal challenge to see how well this heart works.

“I was jumping off bridges, climbing up riverbanks, running through fields, rope climbing, climbing walls – all stuff that I never thought I’d be able to do again.

“But I’ve proven that I can do it and I really enjoyed it.”

Tiny now weighs 16st 11lbs (106kg), wearing a size large and 38in waist trousers, and has even lost two shoe sizes, going from a 15 to a 13.

open image in gallery Tiny said he got his “ironic” nickname of Tiny aged 10 because he has “always stood out in a crowd” for his height and weight ( Collect/PA Real Life )

Some people have jokingly started calling him Biggie, instead of his “less ironic” nickname Tiny, but he said it still works for his height.

Tiny’s average daily meals now consist of a shot of turmeric, ginger, cayenne pepper and apple cider vinegar first thing in the morning before a gym workout, high protein foods, as well as fresh fruit, vegetables and water throughout the day.

He wanted to thank his wife Nicola in particular, who he said has been his “rock” throughout, and he is thankful he can enjoy a future getting to know his 18-month-old granddaughter, Ellena.

“I love going to the gym or for a run with my wife and I enjoy the foods I eat,” Tiny said.

“I’ve given myself the best chance in life now and I’ve gone out my way to improve everything and make sure that I’m around for my kids and my wife.”

Looking back on his progress, he said: “I made a mistake by letting myself go by eating rubbish.

“It’s the same as having a car – if you put decent fuel in, it’ll last you a lifetime.”

Entries for the 2027 Wolf Run season are now on sale. For more information, visit: thewolfrun.com.

To donate to Tiny’s fundraiser, visit: gofundme.com/f/from-open-heart-surgery-to-the-wolf-run.

News.title: Michael Carrick will not survive unless Manchester United change
News.content:
But so passive was their football that is the way he felt in the moment. For a club with United’s “attack, attack, attack” tradition – becoming something of a distant memory as seasons pass – that is a damning as it gets.

Neville’s Sky paymasters will be delighted by his emotive, insulting, headline-grabbing language. But he of course exaggerated a point to make a point. United, and Carrick, were, indeed, far too passive, lacking aggression, urgency and belief. They just do not press. United did, for too long, play like a team of dummies.

Against Fulham they almost played walking football until they conceded, desperation kicked in and they chased the game to salvage a late draw.

It begs the question: what is Carrick doing with this team? Yes, he may have been let down by no defensive signings in the summer – even if he must have bought into the plan to prioritise a midfield rebuild – but he is far from absolved from blame.

He will cling to the response to Lisandro Martínez’s own goal, to striking a post twice in the first half from Matheus Cunha and Bruno Fernandes, to managing to avoid a third successive defeat in a week, which would have led to the crisis klaxon being sounded. Carrick can talk about how ridiculous it would be to question his position as head coach. But is it?

We now go into a three-week international break and the Premier League vacuum would have been filled by a debate over Carrick’s future, whether he is up to the job and another existential examination as to where United are heading. And who is to blame.

That still might happen. United did not lose. But they were not remotely good enough, as has been the case for most of the season. Their only league win in five was against newly promoted Ipswich Town, having lost to newly promoted Hull City. They have also drawn at Everton and now at Fulham, who started the day bottom of the table and remain winless. Apart from facing Manchester City, it has hardly been the most taxing of starts. Except they are down in 12th and have not played well at all.

News.title: Alisson’s brilliance takes the breath away to show way forward for Liverpool
News.content:
It proved to be the foundation stone from which Liverpool were able to build and inflict Bournemouth’s first home defeat since January. There are plenty of [valid] questions to ask of Liverpool’s attack at present but, defensively, it is starting to come together.

“It was a really good fight,” Alisson said, in that self-effacing way of his. “But we have to improve a lot – on the ball and sometimes off the ball as well but we improved in the second half. We adapted to the opponent and that’s what we are doing.”

Any manager with a well-drilled defence stands a chance of improving and that is what Liverpool are doing. Only four weeks ago the discussion was about how easy it was for teams to play through their middle – remember that chaotic afternoon at Newcastle to start? – but that is changing swiftly.

Since Iraola replaced Jeremie Frimpong with Araújo at right-back, three consecutive Premier League clean sheets have followed. Araújo, the Uruguayan on loan from Barcelona, revels in doing the dirty work while Jacquet, the £60m signing from Rennes, oozes quality.

“He’s [Jacquet] very young and adapted really well to the Premier League,” Iraola said. “The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to sub him. This was a step forward. He looked solid until the end. He’s in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development.”

News.title: All that money spent and Spurs do not have a proper striker or goalkeeper
News.content:
It was an excellent goal, but Kinsky got a good hand to it and a top goalkeeper would have pushed it around the post. On the evidence of the first half, when he made four saves, Suzuki would have also stopped the ball creeping into the net.

Suzuki cost Villa in the region of £30m and he looks a more than able replacement for Emiliano Martínez. Spurs, on the other hand, have not had a top-class goalkeeper since Hugo Lloris and it is a puzzle that so much faith has been placed in Kinsky.

Spurs spent most of the summer firmly denying any links to Jackson before Villa signed him from Chelsea for an initial £47.5m that could rise to £65m. Given the London club paid an initial £75m for Sávio and committed to a £60m obligation to make Omar Marmoush’s season-long loan permanent, Jackson might have been a relative bargain for them.

Asked if Tottenham had made a big mistake by failing to sign a proper number nine, head coach Robert De Zerbi said: “The transfer market was long. The situation changed many times. There was also the financial rules, at the end of the transfer market. And we had to respect the rules.

“We didn’t sell the players who we thought, in the beginning, there was the possibility, the chance to sell. There are a lot of reasons. I think the club and the coach, we are not sleeping, we know the characteristics of the players, we know everything. And if we didn’t make any different decisions, it was because we couldn’t.”

News.title: An A to Z guide to what’s in your laundry detergent
News.content:
Laundry is one of those jobs that most of us do on autopilot. Throw a load of washing and your favourite detergent into the drum and wait for the machine to work its magic. Perhaps you’ve never even thought to ask yourself what chemicals you’re putting in with your clothes.

In the UK, detergent brands are legally required to state the use of surfactants and enzymes (the main ingredients for stain removal) in a way that is easy to understand, but you may see additional compounds that leave you scratching your head.

Here, I break down the words on the back of the bottle to help you understand exactly what you’re putting in your washing. Given that I’ve just tested 26 laundry detergents and developed an app to help you clean your clothes better, I’m the best woman for the job.

Below, you’ll find the most common detergent ingredients listed A to Z. If you’ve got a burning question about a laundry buzzword, I should be able to help. Add any in the comments section below.

Anionic

There are two main types of surfactants: anionic and non-ionic. A surfactant has a hydrophilic head that loves water and a hydrophobic tail that hates it. Anionic surfactants have a negative charge on their head, which is what helps lift soils and stains from the fabric, though they’re not so good at getting rid of oils. They create a lot of foam but their effectiveness can be limited by minerals found in hard water, which is why they are paired with non-ionic surfactants.

Bio

Short for biological, this label means that a detergent contains enzymes. These are proteins that break down fats, starches and grease, so use bio formulations when you need to tackle stubborn food stains. They are effective at lower temperatures but they can be abrasive on sensitive skin. If your skin is easily irritated, opt for non-bio, instead.

News.title: Spitting row mars feisty Millwall-West Ham clash
News.content:
Millwall manager Alex Neil said after the game that fourth official Lewis Smith had confirmed a spitting accusation had been made.

Asked if he had spoken to Marschall about the claim, Neil replied: “I haven’t asked him about it. But it’s like anything else; I’m sure there’ll be footage of it, or not of it, if it didn’t happen.

“I’d be extremely surprised if Fil’s made an accusation and nothing’s happened. But that’s not really for me to deal with; I’m sure the authorities will deal with that.”

West Ham manager Nuno Espírito Santo said: “I’m aware of the allegation. I didn’t see the image; I didn’t speak with Taty. I cannot go much further on that.”

He added: “I’m going to try to look at the images.”

There were also ugly scenes at full time when players had to be separated at the end of a derby that had been at the centre of an unprecedented police operation.

There were six arrests as of 4pm on Saturday for offences including tailgating, assault on a police officer and entering or attempting to enter a stadium while intoxicated.

News.title: Bloodthirsty Brighton feast on rattled Arsenal
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of today’s Premier League 3pm kick-offs, with Brighton vs Arsenal the pick of the three matches.

Brighton are the league’s top goalscorers so far this season and have amassed the most expected goals, but the champions have the league’s best defence and are seeking five wins from five to start their title defence. There is some welcome needle between Fabian Hurzeler and Mikel Arteta, dating back to Declan Rice’s contentious second yellow for delaying the restart two years ago, as well as the Brighton manager’s comments about Arsenal’s style of play in March.

That 1-0 Arsenal victory at the Amex coincided with Man City dropping points at home to Nottingham Forest on a pivotal night in the title race. Bukayo Saka scored a deflected shot in the ninth minute, and Arsenal held on from there in an ugly but resolute display.

With Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz fit and firing, as well as the introduction of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes to Arteta’s midfield stable, Arsenal’s football has been more technical and enterprising so far this season. Brighton are one of the few teams who will back themselves to play through Arsenal’s press, which should make for an absorbing game.

Elsewhere, Newcastle are looking to bounce back from their shellacking at Leeds at home to surprise package Hull City. Mattias Jaissle’s team took four points from Liverpool and Spurs but there is concern about how many shots they are conceding. Hull remain unbeaten and continue to confound the odds and underlying data, but that surely cannot last forever.

Everton are also one of the division’s unbeaten teams, but will be targeting three points from a home game against Ipswich after three consecutive draws. Ipswich are sitting comfortably on six points after their win at Crystal Palace, though they did have the extra man for the majority at Selhurst Park.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Red Roses’ 39-match winning streak brought to end in Canada draw
News.content:
The record books will show that this meeting, a proper Test full of ebbs and flows, was neither. And, no matter the pre-match belief of England head coach John Mitchell, Canada are not on the same level of professionalism and funding as his side. Mitchell had brought back nine players, many of whom featured in last year’s World Cup final victory, after the thrashing of Australia last week with the expectation that the history of 2025 would repeat itself. Canada had other ideas.

“The plan on the field at the last scrum was to go for the win,” Canada captain Sophie de Goede said. “And then the message came on from the sideline to kick it out. In that moment you have to trust your coach and your coaching staff, and we’ll have a discussion about it later. If we had given away a penalty off the next breakdown, we’d be sitting here going, ‘Why didn’t you kick it out?’”

England’s downfall came at the set-piece, where their line-out malfunctioned and their scrum never gained dominance, in a tale which was not too dissimilar to last week. The hosts came second in the physical battle, too, which was uncharacteristic of them; losing Hannah Botterman to a shoulder injury did not help, either. All told, Canada just looked as though they wanted it a little bit more and maybe this was the wake-up call the Red Roses needed: when you are at the top, and at the top by a margin, every team want to be the one to dethrone you.

News.title: GPs summoned in Frankfurt as third malaria death reported
News.content:
Doctors in Frankfurt have been summoned for an urgent public health briefing after a third person died of malaria this week in the German city.

At least eight people have been infected with malaria in Frankfurt since July, when health officials suspect mosquitoes were brought into the country aboard an aeroplane, before biting multiple people and infecting them in and around the city’s airport.

Six of the cases, reported in July and August, have been amongst airport workers, two of whom died earlier in the summer.

But on Monday this week, two people living in the Schwanheim district, a neighbourhood close to the airport of around 20,000 people, were reported to have been infected with malaria – one of whom died on Thursday.

“We contacted all the GPs in Schwanheim directly earlier this week, as well as all the medical doctors from emergency departments and ambulance services and informed them about the current situation so that everybody is aware,” Dr Peter Tinnemann, Director of the Public Health Department for the city of Frankfurt, told The Telegraph.

The left-back, 22, celebrated his England recall this week with the winner in Newcastle’s 2-1 victory over Hull City.



The Toon star, who has penned a new contract until 2031, heads off for Three Lions duty with a point to prove having been forced to frustratingly watch this summer’s action back home with his mates.

Hall said: “Yeah, I was gutted. In football, you never take anything for granted, but I’d say I wasn’t necessarily expecting it, if I’m being completely honest. Obviously everyone has their own opinions and you’ve got to respect that.



“But as soon as the first couple of weeks were done, when I realised I wasn’t going to be there, I just had to think to myself that if I wasn’t a footballer, what would I be doing, and that’s supporting England.

“So I was just with my mates watching the games together and just being a fan.”



While it was misery for Hall, a host of current and former Newcastle team-mates did get the nod from Tuchel.

Hall said: “I was obviously supporting all of them with Dan [Burn] being there, Elliot [Anderson], Anthony [Gordon], and big Tino [Livramento].

“I was obviously buzzing for them and wanted all of them to do so well. So, when I was watching them and they were all playing really well, it obviously made me proud as well.

Hall produced another stellar display to help keep Hull at bay. Manager Matthias Jaissle, who went viral after the game for buying a Toon fan’s birthday meal after bumping into the party at a city restaurant, cannot wait to see what more the player can contribute to his team.

Sports.title: Man Utd run SIX KILOMETRES less than Fulham with Carrick’s men looking Premier League’s worst team without ball
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED players ran over SIX KILOMETRES less than their Fulham counterparts on Sunday.

Red Devils boss Michael Carrick insisted there was nothing wrong with the urgency and effort from his players in the 1-1 draw at Craven Cottage.



But club legend Gary Neville called United a “genuine disgrace“.

And the statistics back up the Sky Sports pundit rather than the man in the Old Trafford hot seat.



According to data collected by FotMob, United players collectively covered 110.2km – a full 6.5km less than Fulham‘s 116.7km.

Look into the other running metrics and it becomes even more worrying for Carrick.

Fulham covered a greater distance running, sprinting, and made 10 more overall sprints than their opponents.

Carrick could have been under serious pressure had Matheus Cunha not salvaged a draw with his deflected 89th-minute strike.

But he is by no means out of the woods after a flat performance and dropped points against a side who have not won in the Premier League all season.

SunSport Manchester United reporter Katherine Walsh said: “United are quite possibly the worst side in the Premier League at the moment out of possession.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“They were outworked, outmuscled, and were effectively accused of walking around the pitch by Gary Neville in his post-match interview as well as on commentary.

“Us in the press box, we couldn’t quite believe what we were watching after half-time – the lack of effort, the disjointedness as well. So that is a real problem.”

Carrick now has an extended international break to ponder his next move.



And Neville sent him a stern warning on Sky Sports, ranting: “Very rarely do I say a team doesn’t work hard or is lacking in effort. That’s the ultimate criticism you can give a group of players.

Sports.title: Mo Salah banned from driving for six months after ace caught speeding in £400k Rolls two days after he quit Liverpool
Sports.content:
Next

FOOTIE ace Mo Salah has been banned from driving after his £400,000 Rolls-Royce was clocked speeding.

The Egyptian forward failed to tell police who was behind the wheel of the electric Spectre when it was caught by a mobile camera in March.



It happened in Wilmslow, Cheshire, two days after he had dramatically announced he would be leaving Liverpool at the end of last season.

Salah, 34, the Premier League’s all-time top foreign scorer, did not respond to two court summonses sent to his £4million mansion.



He was convicted in his absence by magistrates in Warrington, Cheshire, last month of failing to identify the driver under the Single Justice Procedure.

A charge of exceeding the 30mph speed limit was withdrawn.

The Kop legend, who now plays for Turkish side Trabzonspor, was handed a six-month driving ban and £660 fine. He was also ordered to pay £120 in court costs and a victim surcharge of £264.

In 2022, Salah was clocked in his Ferrari F8 Tributo doing 63mph in a 50mph zone in Stockport. He got a £200 fine and three penalty points.

And he was filmed apparently using his mobile phone behind the wheel close to Anfield in 2018.

He was not prosecuted after police said there was “insufficient evidence”.

Sports.title: ‘They don’t like Man Utd to lose’ – Fulham boss Arbeloa says ‘every decision was for them’ in furious referee rant

FURIOUS Fulham head coach Alvaro Arbeloa could face a potential FA sanction after claiming officials “refused to let Manchester United lose” during their 1–1 draw.

Matheus Cunha‘s deflected 89th minute strike rescued a draw at Craven Cottage and delayed a full-blown crisis in the away dugout.



But Arbeloa, who replaced Marco Silva in the summer and is bookies favourite alongside Michael Carrick to be the first manager to be sacked, accused officials of being influenced by their apology to United after the Manchester derby injustice last Sunday.

Arbeloa was vexed that United received a free-kick for a foul on Harry Maguire 35 seconds before Cunha’s equaliser denied Fulham a first win of the season after five matches.



The Spaniard raged: “Every decision was for them and I knew after the game against Man City that they would not let Man Utd lose. We deserved a little bit more.”

“We were so, so close. We were a little bit unlucky again. We knew it would be difficult against this big team.

“We knew what happened last week. We have seen what the referee has been doing in all the matches, so it was a difficult game. And we were unlucky.”

Arbeloa felt the free-kick for Cesar Palacios’ foul on Maguire was soft and claimed ref Michael Oliver gave “all fouls” to United – because of the “error in judgement” by the officials who incorrectly awarded Erling Haaland‘s winner at Old Trafford.

In his later press conference, Arbeloa appeared to row back on his comments a tad – but still said he “was not really happy”.

He added: “My English is not so good. Maybe I explain myself so bad and I prefer not to say anything about the referees because you never know.”

Sports.title: Real Madrid issue furious statement amid extraordinary Jose Mourinho ref rant after derby defeat
Sports.content:
Real Madrid issue furious statement amid extraordinary Jose Mourinho ref rant after derby defeat

Atletico Madrid beat Real Madrid in a feisty derby on Sunday afternoon - but Jose Mourinho was left furious by the performance of the referee

View 3 Images Jose Mourinho after Real Madrid's derby defeat

Real Madrid launched a scathing attack on the refereeing team that oversaw their 2-1 derby defeat to Atletico Madrid. Alejandro Grimaldo put the hosts ahead with a second-half penalty at the Metropolitano after defender Dean Huijsen was sent off for bringing down Giuliano Simeone.

‌



Jonathan David then doubled Atletico’s lead before Antonio Rüdiger pulled a late goal back as Madrid dropped to fourth in the La Liga table. But just hours after the game concluded in the Spanish capital, Real released a statement that took aim at referee Miguel Angel Ortiz Arias and described some of the decisions given against them as "catastrophic".

‌



The statement read: “Real Madrid lost at the Metropolitano in a derby marked by the poor officiating of Ortiz Arias, who failed to send off Cuti Romero in the first half for stepping on Bellingham's knee (despite reviewing the play on the monitor) and Kang-In Lee for stepping on Valverde's left ankle. Both decisions shaped the match, which was decided in the second-half in favor of Atletico.

‌



“Until the 30th minute, the game had very few dangerous plays. But from that point on, controversy took over the derby. In the 35th minute, during a contested ball, Bellingham got to the ball before Cuti Romero, and the Atletico defender planted his studs into the left knee of the Madrid player. Ortiz Arias initially booked our player but was called by Trujillo Suarez to review the incident on the monitor.

“After watching the replay, he rescinded the card from Bellingham and issued a yellow card to the Atletico defender instead of sending him off. Nine minutes later, the referee made another crucial error by not penalizing Kang-In Lee for a challenge on Valverde, where he struck him with his studs on the left ankle. Ortiz Arias was close to the incident but did not show a red card (or even a yellow card) to the Atletico player, nor was he alerted by Trujillo Suarez on this occasion.

“In the 50th minute, Ortiz Arias awarded a penalty against Huijsen for a foul on Giuliano and showed the Madridista a yellow card. After being advised by Trujillo Suarez, he went to review the play on the monitor and this time decided to send off Huijsen. Grimaldo converted the penalty to make it 1-0.

“In the 59th minute, the score became 2-0 after a goal by J. David. In the 76th minute, Madrid had a chance to make it 2-1 with a one-on-one opportunity for Diomande against Oblak, who came out on top.

‌



View 3 Images Jonathan David celebrates after scoring for Atletico Madrid (Image: (Dennis Agyeman/Europa Press via Getty Images))

“However, our team did score in the 89th minute with a header from Rudiger following a free kick taken by Bernardo. From then until the final whistle, Mourinho's side pushed for an equalizer but were unsuccessful.”

While Jose Mourinho began his press conference with pictures of two fouls committed by Atleti players that he said should have been red cards. Mourinho opted to focus on two first-half incidents. The first was was when Cristian Romero was shown a yellow card for treading on Jude Bellingham's knee, while Lee Kang-in escaped punishment for a crunching challenge on Federico Valverde.

‌



"The story of the game is here," Mourinho said. "They're two clear red cards. With the difficulties we had afterwards, with 11 versus 10 (players), you could imagine what it would have been like (for us) for 50 minutes with 11 versus nine.

View 3 Images Jose Mourinho argues with Miguel Angel Ortiz Arias (Image: (Alberto Gardin/NurPhoto via Getty Images))

"It's the CTA (the referee's committee). It's all been very strange. It's a referee who, at 41, doesn't have international experience. I don't know why he was the referee. The poor guy came here and couldn't cope with the pressure.

"But for (the VAR) there's no pressure, at (RFEF HQ) Las Rozas there's no pressure. Or maybe there is and we don't know...That combination, a poor referee, who's only done small games, and a VAR with a big history. Congratulations to the CTA."

He then added: "The penalty at Real Sociedad [for Atletico] is laughable. The penalty for Barcelona is laughable, the non-sending off (for Barcelona) against Athletic Club. So many things together...I thought I'd find a different league to the one I left (in 2013), and people told me no, and they explained why. But we'll fight."

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

They are also in keeping with a mood at a club which demands and expects better. The fans even turned on Carrick in the way they booed the substitution of Kobbie Mainoo at a time when they were chasing an equaliser.

Eventually, they got the leveller courtesy of Matheus Cunha’s deflected shot which was in keeping with their performance. It came after a big stroke of luck which was barely deserved.

‌



The goal at the other end which had put Fulham ahead came after Lisandro Martinez put through his own goal in real Keystone Cops fashion. It was laughably bad.

United desperately needed a win to lift the spirits and change the mood around Carrick going into a three-week international break. That will now feel painfully long.

View 3 Images Matheus Cunha's late deflected strike rescued a point for Manchester United at Fulham (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Sir Alex Ferguson was looking on from the posh seats and he must be wondering what on earth has gone wrong with United’s latest experiment.

Doesn’t this sound all too familiar? Club legend comes in to give United a lift, gets the desired effect and then - surprise, surprise - the next season is much harder to manage. This time it is Carrick and before it was Ole Gunnar Solskjaer.

It is happening again. And then, in the background, you have got joint United owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe making a fool of himself again.

‌



It was Ratcliffe making damning remarks about the country being “on the slide” in an interview about the Government failing businesses.

Honestly, for such an intelligent man his lack of self awareness is incredible. Talk about timing. You might want to get your own affairs in order first, Sir Jim. What a plonker.

But that is what United have come to. They spend millions, buy without much of a plan and leave themselves with a creaking defence marshalled by Harry Maguire who, at 33, showed his age as he lost his balance and crashed into a crate of bottles on the touchline.

‌



View 3 Images Lisandro Martinez put through his own goal to put Fulham ahead (Image: Getty Images)

Chasing after Fulham’s Josh King and Alex Iwobi must take it out of you. Fulham deserved more than a draw and the result at least takes them off the bottom and leaves Tottenham rock bottom going into the international break.

And that is the point. United’s first five fixtures - Hull, Ipswich, Everton, Manchester City and Fulham - was quite a friendly start. And they have blown it.

‌



Yes, they did OK first half as Bruno Fernandes hit the post and Cunha’s looping effort also hit the woodwork. But Fulham were good and are improving under Alvaro Arbeloa.

Fulham were the better team from the start of the second half. The opening goal came after 63 minutes. Calvin Bassey intercepted Mainoo’s loose pass, strode forward and his shot was parried by Senne Lammens only for Martinez to deflect the rebound into his own net.

Finally United showed some heart. They pushed forward in the closing stages and nicked a point in the last minute. Typical United. Cunha’s shot deflected off David Affengruber for an equaliser.

Sports.title: Late Matheus Cunha goal rescues point for miserable Man Utd at Fulham - 5 talking points
Sports.content:
Late Matheus Cunha goal rescues point for miserable Man Utd at Fulham - 5 talking points

FULHAM 1-1 MANCHESTER UNITED: The Red Devils head into the first international break of the window with just one Premier League win to their name following a disappointing draw at Craven Cottage

View 3 Images Matheus Cunha was the hero for Man United at Craven Cottage (Image: Getty Images)

Manchester United were rescued from another defeat by a late Matheus Cunha goal against Fulham.

‌



Michael Carrick's men struggled to find any rhythm in West London and fell behind as Lisandro Martinez put through his own net midway through the second half. Despite seemingly heading for defeat, Cunha popped up late on with a deflected effort to salvage a point.

‌



It leaves the Red Devils with just one win to their name and in the midst of their worst-ever Premier League start. Fulham in the meantime are still waiting for their first win under new boss Alvaro Arbeloa.

‌



Here are all of the talking points from Craven Cottage.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Lammens saves United

Michael Carrick's side were indebted to their goalkeeper before the break, with Fulham having a number of opportunities to take the lead. Youngster Josh King had a couple of chances of his own, albeit saw good efforts saved by Senne Lammens.

Sander Berge also went close with a low effort that was parried by the Belgian. Alex Iwobi was also among the players to threaten United's goal throughout the first half as it lived a charmed life.

View 3 Images Senne Lammens was the only Man United star to leave Fulham with credit (Image: Getty Images)

‌



King continues to sparkle

Despite being just five games into the new campaign, this already looks like the season of Josh King at Craven Cottage. The Fulham academy graduate has established himself as a crucial player under Alvaro Arbeloa.

And his performance against United showed once more why he is so highly rated. King's movement is that of an elite ball carrier, while he was also a goal threat against the Red Devils.

He also showed the maturity of a senior player as he dictated instructions to his far more experienced teammates. King looks set to go to the very top.

‌



It's just a shame that he walked away with one blot on his copy book, that being a perceived dive towards the end of the first half.

Martinez mare

For all of Fulham's attacking verve, it was actually a United player that put through his own net to put the home side in the lead. The Red Devils failed to get the ball clear, with Matheus Cunha losing out.

Defender Calvin Bassey set his sights from range and saw his effort saved by Lammens. But the ball bounced back off Argentine defender Martinez and into the bottom corner.

‌



View 3 Images Lisandro Martinez was the guilty party at Craven Cottage (Image: Getty Images)

Cunha rescues United in Sesko absence

There was some bad news for United before the game with striker Benjamin Sesko ruled out through injury ahead of kick-off. And despite having not started a Premier League game this season, his absence was felt.

United lacked a focal point throughout the game, with Marcus Rashford and Bryan Mbeumo stationed out wide, while Cunha dropped deep. Not having Sesko on the bench also limited Carrick's options as he attempted to turn the game around.

‌



But to his credit, Cunha still managed to find enough space on the edge of the area to draw United level with his deflected effort.

United's rotten start goes on

Before the trip to Craven Cottage, United had endured their joint worst-ever start to a Premier League season. And despite having found an equaliser, it is still hugely disappointing.

The Red Devils were second best for large chunks of the game as they struggled to match their hosts' insensity and desire.

Article continues below

The draw leaves them 12th in the Premier League table with just five points from five games heading into the international break. It is certainly not the return United chiefs will have wanted after giving Michael Carrick the reins on a full-term basis. He has some questions to answer over the next few weeks.

Sports.title: Gary Neville slams worst Man Utd display EVER after Fulham goal - 'Absolutely pathetic'
Sports.content:
Gary Neville slams worst Man Utd display EVER after Fulham goal - 'Absolutely pathetic'

Gary Neville was left astounded by the way Manchester United conceded against the Cottager and the ex-defender did not hold back on his thoughts

View 2 Images Gary Neville launched a stinging criticism of Manchester United (Image: Dennis Goodwin/ProSports/Shutterstock)

Gary Neville labelled Manchester United's start to the second half as "the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen" the club play. Fulham took the lead after half time in a goal strewn with errors by the Reds.

‌



It began with Matheus Cunha being easily dispossessed by Calvin Bassey, who drove forward with the ball and forced a save out of Senne Lammens. The Reds goalkeeper was then caught in two minds after Lisandro Martinez tapped the ball back to him.

‌



He seemingly could not decide whether to save the ball with his foot or with his hand and by the time he made up his mind, the ball was already in. After the goal was conceded, Neville tore into his former side while commentating for Sky Sports.

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

He said: “I’ve watched Manchester United since the age of five and that’s the worst 15 minutes I’ve ever seen them play. Absolutely pathetic. They have walked for 15 minutes and you get what you deserve in a football match.”

When the camera panned to Michael Carrick, Neville added: "Maybe there will be a reaction but I've never seen a lack of effort for 15-20 minutes like I have just seen there. What must he be thinking? He probably cannot believe what he has watched in that last 15 or 20 minutes. He's got to act now."

‌



Neville most likely saw the goal coming as he was anything but impressed with how United started the second half. Before Martinez prodded the ball into his own net, Neville said: "It's a few minutes of the blue mannequins playing against the white mannequins and then it switches around, bizarre football match.

"They won't go anywhere with a lack of urgency like this. I don't know if it's fear, lack of complacency, they're just not working hard."

View 2 Images Martinez's own goal came after some poor United defend (Image: 2026 Getty Images)

‌



United did manage to get an equaliser through Matheus Cunha as the game headed towards the 90-minute mark. The Brazilian struck the ball from just outside the box and watched his effort deflect off David Affengruber and trickle past the wrong-footed Bernd Leno.

His fortuitous goal rescued the Reds from a third consecutive loss in all competitions. Carrick's side came into the match having lost to Manchester City last week and 3-2 to Brighton and Hove Albion in the League Cup.

After the match, former United ace Ashley Young tore into United, saying: "They were too slow. They were walking, they were jogging, there was not enough urgency in the game."

Sports.title: Michael Carrick explains Benjamin Sesko absence vs Fulham as Man Utd suffer fresh blow
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick explains Benjamin Sesko absence vs Fulham as Man Utd suffer fresh blow

Benjamin Sesko didn't travel with the Manchester United squad for their Premier League clash with Fulham and Michael Carrick has confirmed the reason for his absence

View 2 Images Manchester United were without Benjamin Sesko at Fulham (Image: James Gill - Danehouse/Getty Images)

Manchester United are assessing Benjamin Sesko after the striker picked up an injury, Michael Carrick has confirmed. Sesko, 23, missed Sunday's clash with Fulham, having not travelled to London with the rest of Carrick's squad.

‌



The Slovenia international was subbed off in the second half of Wednesday's woeful 3-2 loss at home to Brighton in the Carabao Cup. It's possible that the setback is a reoccurrence of the shin injury which he first sustained during a clash with Liverpool in May and ruled him out of pre-season.

‌



When asked for an update before kick-off at Craven Cottage, Carrick replied: "A little bit of an assessment at the moment. He pulled up after the game the other day with a little bit of pain, so we'll have to see how he is."

‌



Sesko featured in United's first six matches of the season, starting two. He scored in games against Everton and Sabah.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Sesko is now a doubt for his country's Nations League fixtures against Scotland, North Macedonia and Switzerland during the international break. The ex-RB Leipzig star was called up by Slovenia manager Bostjan Cesar earlier this week.

Carrick hoped to have Sesko at his disposal for what was billed as a must-win game, as Matheus Cunha started up front instead. After mustering just four points from their opening four Premier League games, the pressure was on the Red Devils boss.

"I know the club, I know the role, I know what's expected here in terms of playing at a certain standard, playing at a certain level, achieving certain things on the pitch," Carrick said.

‌



"In terms of future and ownership and how long I've got in the job, that's just totally not in my thinking, not one part of it. Like, how long I've got. It's ridiculous to think that way in a position that I'm in, that's just not on the radar.

Should Manchester United have signed a striker? Have your say in the comments section.

Article continues below

"I understand what we need to achieve and where we need to be as a football club for the owners, what they expect, for the supporters as much as anything… there's not [much] more important for me than what they expect and what they want to see. I get all that.

"It's two or three games that we haven't had certain results and two or three games too many because I really hate losing. But that doesn't mean that the world caves in. In some minds, it does. It can't for us because we've got to perform, we've got to get wins and we've got a lot of games to plan for. That's exactly what we're doing."
