What Central Puerto does. Central Puerto S.A. engages in the electric power generation activities in Argentina. It operates in three segments: Electric Power Generation From Conventional Sources, Electric Power Generation From Renewable Sources and Forest Activity, and Management and Operations of Thermal Plants. The company's power generation assets include combined cycle, gas and steam turbine, co-generation,…

The Deal Behind It

Central Puerto paid US$25 million for its stake in AbraSilver, a Canadian mining company, in 2024. After the project won approval under the government’s investment regime, it sold the stake for US$163 million, The Rio Times reported on 19 September.

The regime, known as RIGI, was created by the 2024 Ley Bases reform law to attract large investments. It offers qualifying projects a 25% income tax rate, 30 years of regulatory stability and gradual freedom to keep export dollars abroad.

Caputo confirmed the Diablillos approval on 27 February, AbraSilver said in March. The opposition deputy Rodolfo Tailhade questioned the transaction as soon as the sale became public.

Critics also point to Nicolás Caputo, a businessman described in the press as the minister’s cousin and once a Central Puerto shareholder. La Nación reported in December 2022 that he had sold his stake of nearly 3%.

A Second Complaint by the Same Lawyer

Cassola filed a separate complaint on 7 September against Caputo, Energy Secretary María Tettamanti and other officials. It concerned Southern Energy’s admission to RIGI, which she linked to a firm sanctioned for operating in the Falklands, Noticias La Insuperable reported.

The two cases are distinct and neither has produced a finding. Together they show the investment regime turning into a legal battleground, not only an economic policy.

Strains Inside Milei’s Camp

The government’s political committee fell into crisis after Senator Patricia Bullrich said the votes to abolish the PASO primaries were not there. La Política Online reported the row on 17 September.

Abolishing the PASO, Argentina’s compulsory open primaries, is a goal of Karina Milei, the president’s sister and chief of staff. Bullrich, a former security minister, now leads the ruling party’s senators.

Infobae reported that Bullrich sat at the political table with Karina Milei and adviser Santiago Caputo two days before the row. She later complained she had not been told about spending cuts in disability policy.

Milei keeps only 39% of the voters who backed Bullrich in 2023, La Política Online reported. La Nación found his support among them fell eight points from August.

Congress Asked to Approve 26 Military Exercises

The government also sent Congress a bill to authorise 26 combined military exercises with foreign forces, Mendoza Post reported on 19 September. Registered as 0011-PE-2026, it covers September 2026 to August 2027.

The constitution and Law 25,880 require congressional approval for foreign troops to enter and Argentine troops to leave. In August the government had already authorised four exercises by decree, including Fraterno with Brazil and Viekaren with Chile.

The full list of exercises and partner countries has not been published. The bill joins a crowded agenda for a Congress where Milei’s party lacks a majority.

What Comes Next

Judge Lijo will decide whether the complaint is forwarded to a prosecutor and investigated. A prosecutor can then order evidence to be gathered or ask for the case to be closed.

For foreign investors, the case matters less for its legal prospects than for what it says about RIGI’s politics. The regime was designed to promise stability, and every controversy tests that promise.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the complaint against Luis Caputo about? It asks whether he improperly approved tax benefits for AbraSilver’s Diablillos project to benefit Central Puerto, which then sold its stake. It alleges fraud, breach of duty and misuse of privileged information. Has Caputo been charged? No. A complaint asks a court to investigate, and no prosecutor, charge or finding had been announced by Sunday. What is RIGI? RIGI is Argentina’s incentive regime for large investments, created by the 2024 Ley Bases. It offers a 25% income tax rate and 30 years of regulatory stability. How much did Central Puerto make? It paid US$25 million for its AbraSilver stake in 2024 and sold it for US$163 million after the project’s RIGI approval. Why is Milei’s coalition divided? Senator Patricia Bullrich said the votes to abolish the PASO primaries were missing, which the president’s sister Karina Milei wants. Polls also show Milei losing support among Bullrich’s 2023 voters.

Sources: La Política Online, on the complaint against Caputo, The Rio Times, on Central Puerto’s AbraSilver sale, Noticias La Insuperable, on the Southern Energy complaint, La Política Online, on the political committee crisis, La Nación, Poliarquía poll, Mendoza Post, on the military exercises bill

World.title: Argentina Household Loan Delinquency Hits 12.9%, Highest Since 2004
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts — The record. Delinquency on bank loans to Argentine families reached 12.9% in July 2026, the highest since 2004. — The comparison. A year earlier, in July 2025, the same rate stood at 5.6%, according to the central bank. — The companies. A private Fidelitas report counted 57,045 firms in arrears in July, almost 12% of active companies. — The mission. An IMF mission arrives Monday 21 September for the third review of the US$20 billion programme. — The targets. The programme set a 2026 primary surplus target of 1.4% of GDP, missed in the first half. — The ranking. Goldman Sachs placed Argentina last of 28 countries in an AI adoption ranking, below 10%.

Delinquency on bank loans to Argentine families reached 12.9% in July 2026, the highest level since 2004, according to the central bank. A year earlier the same measure stood at 5.6%, so the share of borrowers behind on payments has more than doubled in twelve months.

The figure lands days before an International Monetary Fund mission arrives in Buenos Aires on Monday 21 September. That team will run the third review of Argentina’s US$20 billion loan programme, agreed in April 2025, examining reserves and the government’s fiscal accounts.

The central bank in Buenos Aires, whose data show household loan delinquency at its highest since 2004 (Photo: Claudio Elias, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

A Record for Household Borrowing

The Banco Central de la República Argentina, the country’s central bank, publishes delinquency data each month. Its July figures, reported by Infobae and MDZ on 18 September, show 12.9% of family credit in irregular payment status.

That is up from 5.6% in July 2025, an increase of 7.3 percentage points in a single year. The last time the rate was this high was 2004, more than two decades ago.

The same reports put company delinquency at 3.6% in July. Households are therefore falling behind roughly three and a half times as often as firms.

Why Families Are Falling Behind

The rise has been steady rather than sudden. The rate was 2.94% in February 2025 and 11.2% a year later, according to Cadena 3, which described a quadrupling.

By April 2026 it had reached 12.1%, and by May 12.8%, where it held in June after 19 straight monthly rises, Infobae reported. July’s 12.9% resumed the climb.

Economists cited in Argentine media link the trend to consumer credit that expanded quickly while real incomes lagged. When wages do not keep pace with repayments, households that borrowed in better conditions begin to miss instalments.

Companies in Arrears

A private report by Fidelitas, a local financial consultancy, estimated that 57,045 companies were in irregular payment status in July 2026. That is almost 12% of Argentina’s roughly 480,000 active firms, according to Infobae, C5N and MDZ.

The same report put the year-on-year increase at 56.5%. Between January and July 2026 alone, the count of firms in arrears rose 18.7%.

The trajectory is steep: 28,258 companies in January 2025, 48,078 in January 2026 and 57,045 by July. The figure comes from a private consultancy using official data, not from a published central bank statement.

The IMF Review Opening Monday

The International Monetary Fund is the Washington-based lender that agreed a US$20 billion programme with Argentina in April 2025. Its staff mission arrives on Monday 21 September for the third review of that arrangement.

The review will focus on two things: the central bank’s purchase and accumulation of foreign reserves, and the government’s primary fiscal surplus. The 2026 programme targets US$10 billion in currency purchases and a primary surplus of 1.4% of gross domestic product.

Argentina has already exceeded the reserves goal. The central bank has bought more than US$14.2 billion and accumulated about US$9 billion in net reserves, above the programme’s benchmarks.

The fiscal side is harder. The government missed its first-half commitment, Infobae reported, making the budget outcome a central question for the visiting team.

What the Mission Means for Markets

A successful review keeps Argentina inside the programme and its scheduled payouts flowing. The second review, approved in May 2026, released about US$1 billion and took total disbursements to about US$15.8 billion.

The size of any disbursement tied to this third review is not confirmed. Under the programme’s schedule, reviews from 2026 onward are semi-annual, with about US$714 million pencilled in for each remaining review.

For ordinary Argentines, the more immediate question is credit. With 12.9% of family loans in arrears, banks tend to tighten lending.

Households hoping to borrow for a home, a car or a small business then find it harder to qualify. Companies behind on their bank debts face the same squeeze on new credit.

Argentina Last in AI Adoption Ranking

Separately, a Goldman Sachs research report ranked 28 countries by what it calls implied adoption of artificial intelligence. Argentina came last, with just under 10% of its population using AI tools, Infobae reported on 19 September.

The countries at the top, with adoption near or above 20%, include France, the United States, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Germany and Norway. The report does not clearly identify a single first-placed country.

Radio Mitre noted that Argentina’s adoption rate is lower than Brazil, Mexico, Chile and Colombia among the emerging economies covered. The ranking measures use of AI tools, not investment or industrial capacity.

The Wider Picture

Argentina’s delinquency problem and its AI gap point in the same direction: an economy recovering unevenly. Reserves are rebuilding, but the fiscal target was missed and household finances remain strained.

The IMF mission will deliver its assessment in the coming weeks. Its conclusions will shape how much external support Argentina can count on through 2027, and how quickly credit can start flowing again.

Frequently Asked Questions

How high is delinquency on family loans in Argentina? The central bank reported 12.9% of bank credit to families in irregular payment status in July 2026. That is the highest level since 2004 and compares with 5.6% a year earlier. How many Argentine companies are behind on payments? A private Fidelitas report counted 57,045 companies in arrears in July 2026, almost 12% of roughly 480,000 active firms. The figure comes from a consultancy using official data, not a published central bank statement. Why is an IMF mission going to Argentina? The mission arrives on Monday 21 September for the third review of Argentina’s US$20 billion loan programme agreed in April 2025. It will examine foreign reserve accumulation and the government’s fiscal surplus target. Has Argentina met the programme’s targets? The central bank has exceeded the reserves goal, buying more than US$14.2 billion against a US$10 billion target. The government missed its first-half fiscal commitment, which the mission will examine. Where does Argentina rank on AI adoption? A Goldman Sachs report placed Argentina last among 28 countries, with just under 10% of the population using AI tools. Countries at the top, including France and the United States, are near or above 20%.

Sources: Infobae, 18 September 2026: family delinquency reaches 12.9%, MDZ, 18 September 2026: family and company delinquency rates, Infobae, 15 September 2026: 57,045 companies in arrears, Infobae, 17 September 2026: IMF mission and programme targets, TN, 10 September 2026: IMF confirms mission for third review, Infobae, 19 September 2026: Goldman Sachs AI adoption ranking, Cadena 3, 27 April 2026: family delinquency quadruples in a year

World.title: Buenos Aires Blackout Cuts Power to About 600,000 Customers
World.content:
Argentina · Energy

Key Facts — What happened. A blackout hit Buenos Aires and its northern suburbs on the evening of Saturday 19 September. — How big. At the 21:45 peak, Edenor had 519,472 customer accounts without power and Edesur 78,125. — Where. Belgrano, Palermo, Recoleta, Núñez and Vicente López were among the districts that went dark. — The cause. Edesur blamed a failure outside its own network; no official cause had been given by Sunday. — The street. Dead traffic lights brought traffic chaos across the northern half of the city. — What comes next. The electricity regulator, ENRE, is expected to establish the cause and any liability.

A large part of Buenos Aires went dark on Saturday night, as a blackout spread across the capital’s northern districts and suburbs. At its peak, about 600,000 customer accounts were without electricity.

Traffic lights failed across wide stretches of the city, and buildings from Palermo to Vicente López lost power. By Sunday, neither the distributors nor the regulator had given an official explanation.

Avenida 9 de Julio in Buenos Aires at night; on Saturday about 600,000 customer accounts across the north of the metropolitan area lost power (Photo: Raphael Henrique Figueira, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

How Big the Outage Was

At 21:45, the worst moment, Edenor had 519,472 customer accounts without service and Edesur had 78,125, Infobae and teleSUR reported. Several outlets, including TN, put the total at about 600,000 users.

These figures count electricity accounts, not people. One account can serve a whole household or a business, so the number of residents affected was considerably higher.

Edenor distributes power in the north of the city and the northern and western suburbs. Edesur, controlled by Italy’s Enel, serves the south of the city and the southern suburbs.

Which Neighbourhoods Went Dark

Alberto News listed Belgrano, Colegiales, Villa del Parque, Palermo, Recoleta, Villa Crespo, Villa Urquiza and Saavedra. It also named Munro and Vicente López, just beyond the city limits.

Publimetro added Núñez, La Paternal, Flores, Floresta, Caballito, Villa Santa Rita, Villa Devoto and Villa General Mitre. The list covers much of the north and west of the capital.

Several of these districts are among the most densely populated in Buenos Aires. Palermo, Belgrano and Recoleta are also where many foreign residents, embassies and international firms are based.

What Caused It

Edesur said the interruption was due to a failure in the system outside the company, TN reported. Data from ENRE, the national electricity regulator, showed that the cut began in Edenor’s area and then reached Edesur’s.

Xinhua reported that the outage hit mainly the northern part of Greater Buenos Aires. No report identified the substation or transmission line involved.

A failure outside a distributor’s own network usually points to high-voltage transmission. That distinction matters, because it decides which company answers to the regulator.

Who Runs the Grid

Argentina’s high-voltage lines are operated mainly by Transener, while the wholesale market company Cammesa dispatches power across the national system. The distributors take over at the local level and deliver electricity to homes and businesses.

Edenor has been controlled since 2023 by a group of local businessmen, including José Luis Manzano, Daniel Vila and Mauricio Filiberti. Edesur is majority-owned by Enel, the Italian utility.

When a fault starts upstream of the distributors, responsibility can fall on the transmission operator instead. Edesur’s statement placed the fault outside its own network without saying where.

Chaos on the Streets

Dead traffic lights caused chaos at intersections, TN reported, and videos showed whole blocks without light. The cut came on a Saturday evening, when restaurants and streets are busiest.

Buenos Aires city has about three million residents, and the wider metropolitan area about 15 million. A cut on this scale can reach lifts, water pumps and mobile phone masts as well as homes.

A Grid Under Scrutiny

Large outages have hit the Buenos Aires area repeatedly in recent summers, usually during heatwaves. A major failure in a mild September evening, with demand far below its peak, will draw closer questions.

President Javier Milei‘s government has sharply raised electricity tariffs since 2024 while cutting subsidies. Consumers paying more will expect a more reliable service in return.

For the distributors, big outages can bring fines and compensation payments to customers, set by the regulator. No penalty for Saturday’s blackout had been announced by Sunday.

A Reminder of 2019

Argentines remember 16 June 2019, when a transmission failure left almost all of Argentina and Uruguay without power. That blackout lasted most of a day and reached tens of millions of people.

Saturday’s outage was far smaller and limited to one part of one metropolitan area. It still showed how a single failure can darken some of the busiest districts of a city of millions.

What Comes Next

ENRE is expected to establish where the failure began and which company was responsible. Its findings will determine whether customers are entitled to compensation.

ENRE publishes live outage data by distributor and by district on its website. Outlets used those figures to track Saturday’s cut as it spread.

Customers whose appliances were damaged can file a claim with their distributor and, if it is refused, with ENRE. The regulator has handled such claims after previous large outages.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did the Buenos Aires blackout happen? It happened on the evening of Saturday 19 September 2026, with the peak at 21:45 local time. How many people lost power? About 600,000 customer accounts lost power at the peak: 519,472 with Edenor and 78,125 with Edesur. The number of people affected was higher, because one account can serve a household. What caused the blackout? Edesur said the failure was outside its own network, and the cut began in Edenor’s area. No official cause had been given by Sunday. Which areas were affected? Mostly the north and west of the city and the northern suburbs, including Belgrano, Palermo, Recoleta, Núñez, Caballito and Vicente López. Can customers claim compensation? Customers can file claims for damaged appliances with their distributor and then with the regulator, ENRE. Any wider compensation depends on the regulator’s findings.

Sources: Infobae report on the AMBA blackout, teleSUR English report on the blackout, TN report on the outage and traffic chaos, Xinhua report on the northern area impact, Alberto News list of affected districts, Publimetro report on affected neighbourhoods

World.title: New Costa Rica Law Requires Wildlife Crossings on Public Infrastructure
World.content:
Costa Rica now has a law requiring wildlife crossings on public infrastructure projects, but the regulation that will actually put it into practice could take more than two years to arrive. The rule requires new road, bridge and other infrastructure projects to incorporate mechanisms allowing wild species to move safely across routes that would otherwise fragment their habitat, but before any of that happens the National System of Conservation Areas and the Ministry of Public Works and Transport still have to jointly write the technical regulation defining procedures, responsibilities and criteria for applying it.

Once that regulation takes effect, the conservation agency will then have up to 24 months just to identify the natural corridors wildlife use and the most vulnerable points on existing roads, meaning construction itself is still years away. The law took a long road to get here. It was filed in the legislature back in 2022 by then deputy Ariel Robles Barrantes and spent four years moving slowly enough that it nearly expired under the four year shelf life Costa Rican bills carry before automatic archiving.

Lawmakers voted 53 to 0 in June to extend it just before that deadline, and the bill finally cleared final approval in August with unanimous support. That gap between broad political agreement and years of inaction is a pattern environmentalists and officials both recognize. An environmentalist inside MOPT itself, Andrea Ávila, who runs the ministry’s transportation infrastructure project, has been candid about the reason nothing moved for years before the law passed.

She said every wildlife protection measure taken until now came from individual institutional initiative rather than obligation, and did not rule out a lack of political interest, since no law required new construction projects to include such measures. She specifically pointed to Lanamme, the University of Costa Rica’s highway research institute, saying it makes recommendations nobody follows because they carry no legal weight.

A wildlife biologist from the National University’s conservation institute made a similar point, saying the missing piece was never a shortage of impact studies but a legal framework forcing institutions to act on them. That track record matters because it suggests the coming regulatory delay has less to do with a lack of technical groundwork and more to do with institutional follow through. Much of the mapping work the new law assigns SINAC up to 24 months to complete already exists in some form.

A group tied to Universidad Latina compiled more than 19000 roadkill records dating back to 1996, and one 20-kilometer stretch of route 253 in Guanacaste alone was estimated to see around 7000 roadkill incidents annually as of 2019. Panthera, the University of Costa Rica and the Las Pumas rescue center separately tracked wild cat deaths and found 676 felines, jaguars, pumas, ocelots and margays among them, killed on Costa Rican roads between 2012 and 2025, with more than 4200 animals of all kinds struck between 2013 and the present.

Lanamme has also already developed and field tested a methodology for identifying exactly the kind of crossing points the new regulation calls for. Researchers working along the Barbilla Destierro biological subcorridor as part of the Jaguar Corridor Initiative compared roadkill and wildlife sighting data between a paved and an unpaved section of the same road as far back as 2015, documenting jaguar and margay crossings and raccoons using existing culverts.

A separate scientific guide on wildlife friendly roads, developed jointly by conservation and transportation researchers, has been informing individual projects like the route 32 expansion to Limon since 2014, where aerial rope crossings for monkeys and underground tunnels were installed based on monitoring data from that period. Follow up monitoring across existing structures has recorded 59 wildlife species safely using them, though researchers note some sensitive species such as the margay and spider monkey still show limited evidence the current designs work well for them.

None of that existing work resolves the underlying question of how quickly MOPT and SINAC will move once the regulation is actually written, but it does complicate the idea that a two year timeline for identifying priority corridors reflects how much work remains. Much of the mapping this law calls for has already been done piecemeal by university researchers and conservation groups over more than a decade, without a legal mandate forcing anyone to act on it. Whether the regulation leans on that existing research or starts largely from scratch may end up determining whether the two year estimate holds or stretches further.

World.title: Heavy Rains Hamper Access to Irazú Volcano and Costa Rica’s Caribbean
World.content:
Heavy rains have disrupted travel to two of Costa Rica’s most important tourism areas after a landslide affected the road toward Irazú Volcano and falling debris forced the closure of Route 32, the main highway connecting San José with the Caribbean. The most serious incident was reported last night on National Route 219 in Oreamuno, Cartago, where a large landslide blocked part of the road leading toward Irazú Volcano following hours of heavy rain.

An initial emergency report indicated that around 30 people may have been left isolated by the landslide, prompting the Costa Rican Red Cross to send rescue crews and basic emergency units to the area. However, by late Saturday night authorities had not confirmed that anyone needed to be evacuated, and there were no reports of injuries connected to the incident.

Emergency officials activated the Municipal Emergency Committee in Oreamuno, while the National Road Council, police and rescue personnel were sent to evaluate conditions and determine what would be needed to clear the road. As of this morning, authorities had not publicly confirmed whether Route 219 had been completely reopened or whether all of the people initially reported as isolated had been able to leave the area.

The uncertainty is important for anyone using Route 219 as its the main road used to reach Irazú Volcano National Park from Cartago, as well as communities including Cot, Tierra Blanca and Potrero Cerrado. The road had already experienced problems earlier in September because of heavy rain, making the latest landslide another reminder of how quickly conditions can change on Costa Rica’s mountain routes during the rainy season.

The problems were not limited to Cartago. Route 32, the main highway between San José and Limón, was also closed last night after heavy rain caused material to fall onto the road in the mountainous section of the highway. The closure was announced shortly before 7 p.m., and drivers were advised to use alternate routes, including Route 10 through Turrialba, Route 126 through Vara Blanca or the Bajos de Chilamate–Vuelta de Kopper connection.

Route 32 is one of our most important transportation corridors, taking drivers between the Central Valley and Caribbean destinations such as Puerto Viejo, Cahuita and Tortuguero, while also serving as the principal land connection to the Caribbean ports.

The highway has suffered repeated closures this rainy season because of landslides, falling rocks and saturated hillsides, particularly through the mountainous section near Braulio Carrillo National Park. Last night’s problems followed the passage of Tropical Wave 45, which brought heavy showers and thunderstorms to several parts of Costa Rica while being influenced by the Intertropical Convergence Zone.

Although the tropical wave has moved through by now, unstable weather is expected to continue today, with more afternoon showers and thunderstorms possible in the Central Valley and other parts of Costa Rica. That means travelers heading toward Irazú Volcano, the Caribbean or other mountainous areas should check road conditions before leaving and be prepared for sudden closures if heavy rain causes additional landslides.

For anyone planning to go to Irazú Volcano National Park today, the main issue is the condition of Route 219 rather than volcanic activity, and you should confirm that the road is passable before making the drive from Cartago. The same applies to anyone traveling between San José and the Caribbean, where Route 32 can reopen quickly after crews remove debris but can also close again if rain destabilizes surrounding slopes.

Costa Rica is in one of the wettest times of its rainy season, and saturated ground makes steep mountain roads especially vulnerable to landslides even after the heaviest rain has ended. Authorities are continuing to monitor conditions, and further road restrictions remain possible if strong afternoon storms return.

World.title: Belize’s flag rises high as Shyne Barrow receives 2026 Global Ambassador Award at the Caribbean Music Awards Show in Trinidad
World.content:
Belize’s flag rises high as Shyne Barrow receives 2026 Global Ambassador Award at the Caribbean Music Awards Show in Trinidad

By Hugh O’Brien: On Saturday, September 19th, 2026, Belize stands proud as former Music Ambassador and Grammy Award winning recording artist, Shyne Barrow, received the 2026 Global Ambassador Award in Trinidad and Tobago. The award was presented to Shyne in person during the Caribbean Music Awards Show held at the National Academy of Performing Arts (NAPA) in Port of Spain, Trinidad. The regional music awards show is normally held in New York and the organization made history on Saturday night by hosting the award ceremony in the Caribbean for the first time.

Being named the 2026 Global Ambassador at the Caribbean Music Award honors Shyne’s rise as an internationally recognized artist who helped bring the sound and influence of Caribbean talent to audiences around the world. It also recognizes his journey from recording artist to political leader and advocate for Belize and the Caribbean.

The honour celebrates both chapters of a life few has bragging rights to. As a Belizean artist, Shyne made his mark on the global music industry at the turn of the millennium with a distinctive voice and presence that helped define an era, bringing the sound and influence of Caribbean talent to audiences around the world from the biggest stages in hip hop.

Then came the second act. Years later, Shyne carried that influence into public service, going on to serve as Party Leader of the United Democratic Party, Leader of the Opposition in House of Representatives and, as noted by the awards organization, using his platform to advocate for Belize and its people.

In expressing his gratitude Shyne said “While my talents have been recognized by the Grammy’s and the American Music Awards, nothing compares to the recognition of my Caribbean sisters and brothers. As a son of Belize and child of the Caribbean, the foundation of my Music career is rooted in rhythms of the Land of the Free by the Carib Sea.”

“Initially they called me Shabba due to my heavy baritone and ability to recite every song from the great Shabba Ranks line for line. As an artist I aspired to be like Shabba, Super Cat, Bounty Killa, Beanieman and Buju Banton….but as a human being I wanted to be like Bob Marley. His songs saved my life! They gave me hope, calm, love and peace in world of constant war in Brooklyn Vietnam.” (“Brooklyn Vietnam” is a metaphorical term used by Shyne and other rappers to describe the rough, dangerous environment of Brooklyn, New York, during the crack epidemic and crime wave of the 1980s and 90s”.

According to Shyne, history shows that he always took Belize and the Caribbean with him, in his music and his interviews. “I live to do for Belize what Bob Marley did for Jamaica”, he posted on social media.

Shyne’s musical journey took off in 2000 when he released his platinum-certified self-titled debut album, followed by the gold-certified “Godfather Buried Alive” in 2004 in which he said “My dream came true while I was living a nightmare, when I was able to do a song, Quasi OG, with my all time hero Bob Marley and the Wailers.” Shyne has also worked as a performer, writer and producer with major artists including Usher, Lil Wayne and The Notorious B.I.G.

This special regional recognition comes as Shyne continues his return to the stage in celebration of the hip-hop and reggae’s golden eras with his “2622 LGND” tour, featuring reggae icon Barrington Levy, rap legend Lil’ Cease and Belizean artists Stig Da Artist and DJ Rampage.

And in reflecting on his life, including time spent in Brooklyn and incarcerated, Shyne said that this is “testament that the sun rises after the long night of suffering”.

For Belize, the recognition lands as another remarkable international spotlights on the Jewel, and it could not have come at a better time, almost on the eve of our Independence day celebrations on Monday, September 21.

As we celebrate our 45th year of Independence, let’s celebrate a son of the soil whose name has travelled as far as any Belizean’s ever has. From the record booths of New York to the floor of the National Assembly, and now to a regional stage at NAPA (the National Academy of Performing Arts), Trinidad’s premier music institution, built to honour.

Breaking Belize News (BBN) joins Belizeans in congratulating Shyne on being named the 2026 Global Ambassador at the Caribbean Music Awards.

We also extend congratulations to the other Honorees and Nominees, including Calypso Rose who received the Elite Calypso Honor, recognizing her six-decade career and Jamaican dancehall artiste Patra, who received the Lifetime Achievement Award for her influence in dancehall and reggae.

World.title: My Journey: A Story of Survival, Strength and the Fight for Accountability
World.content:
My Journey: A Story of Survival, Strength and the Fight for Accountability

The views expressed in this article are those of the author and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

CONTRIBUTED: In January 2025, my life changed in ways I could never have imagined.

I was diagnosed with tumors in my womb while also experiencing several painful personal losses. Before I could properly process one heartbreak, I found myself facing another. I underwent treatment twice, including chemotherapy that was physically and emotionally devastating. It was a horrible experience, but I fought through it with the hope that better days were ahead.

In September 2025, I had my womb removed. I believed that perhaps the worst was finally behind me. Unfortunately, another frightening medical diagnosis soon followed.

Doctors discovered three herniated discs in my cervical spine. I was told that the compression was extremely severe—approximately 90 percent against my spinal cord—and that I urgently needed surgery.

I trusted a doctor friend who arranged for a neurosurgeon from another country to come to Belize to perform the surgery along with him. Wanting to remain close to my home and family, I decided to have the operation in Belize.

It became a decision that changed my life forever.

I woke up from surgery paralyzed.

The neurosurgeon left Belize the following morning. Another doctor examined me and assured me that my movement would eventually return. After only a few days, I was sent home because I was told that nothing else could be done for me except therapy.

I had to be transported home in an ambulance.

A hospital bed was loaned to me, and my nightmare continued within the walls of my own home. I was completely helpless and unable to perform even the most basic tasks for myself. My family and friends became my hands, my strength and my support. They cared for me around the clock, along with a wonderful nurse whose compassion helped carry me through some of my darkest days.

Those months were cruel.

Every day demanded more strength than I knew I possessed. I waited for the recovery I had been promised. I hoped, prayed and endured the pain, fear, frustration and humiliation of suddenly losing my independence.

From the first week after my surgery in November, I began paying for daily therapy. The cost has been enormous, but I continued because I was determined to regain as much movement and independence as possible.

Three months after the surgery, I still saw no meaningful improvement on my right side. Even more painfully, I had neither seen nor heard from the neurosurgeon again.

I knew I needed answers, so I travelled out of the country to seek another medical opinion. During that follow-up, I was told something deeply disturbing: I should have undergone another MRI approximately one month after the procedure.

No one had told me.

I arranged to have the MRI that very same day. Twenty-four hours later, the results came back—and they were horrifying.

The MRI showed significant damage to my spine. I was told that the original operation had not been completed and that there was still pressure on my spinal cord. I now needed another surgery if I was to have a chance of walking and recovering further.

Desperate to understand the full extent of my condition, I sent the results to doctors in the United States and to several specialists in Guatemala. Their conclusions were consistent: there was irreversible damage to my spine, and no one could say how much recovery I would ultimately achieve.

My second spinal surgery was in March by an amazing neurosurgeon in Guatemala City.

Almost a year later, I am still paying for daily therapy. Through determination, prayer, professional care and the unwavering support of my family and friends, I have made progress. I am now walking with a cane—but my journey is far from over.

I still require another major spinal surgery in an attempt to relieve the remaining pressure and address the damage caused by what I believe was incomplete and negligent medical care. Each spinal operation can cost more than $50,000, not including travel, accommodation, therapy, medication and the loss of income and independence.

The physical damage has been devastating, but so have the emotional and financial consequences.

Why are patients left to carry these burdens alone? Why are doctors not required to provide proper follow-up care? Why was I sent home without the necessary testing, monitoring or answers? Why have I never heard from the neurosurgeon again? Who is responsible for the errors made medical doctors from abroad? Most importantly, why are medical professionals whose actions—or lack of action—cause life-changing harm not being held accountable by the Ministry of Health?

Something must be done.

No patient should enter an operating room expecting healing and wake up to a lifetime of disability without answers, follow-up care or accountability. No family should have to watch someone they love suffer while wondering whether the outcome could have been prevented.

Now, I am preparing to face what I pray will be my final surgery. I am afraid, but I am also stronger, wiser and more determined than I was before. I share my story not because I want pity, but because I want awareness, accountability and change.

To everyone reading this: please seek a second opinion. Seek a third and a fourth if necessary. Ask questions. Request copies of your medical records and imaging. Research your surgeon and the facility where your procedure will take place. Make sure there is a clear plan for follow-up care, and never be afraid to speak up when something does not feel right.

Your life, your health and your future are worth protecting.

This is not the journey I chose, but it is the journey I am surviving. I will continue fighting—for my recovery, for answers and for every patient who deserves safe, responsible and accountable medical care.

World.title: PUP endorses Pablo Cawich and Belmopan slate for 2027 municipal elections
World.content:
PUP endorses Pablo Cawich and Belmopan slate for 2027 municipal elections

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The People’s United Party has formally endorsed Mayor Pablo Cawich and his team to contest the March 3, 2027 municipal elections in Belmopan.

Supporters and invited guests gathered in the capital on Friday, September 18, for the PUP 7 Endorsement Convention and Municipal Campaign Launch.

Cawich was endorsed alongside Florita Botes, Coretta Banner, Lawrence Tush, Sannie Cal, Radin Santos and Christopher Enriquez. The team was sworn in by PUP Chairman Henry Usher.

The event also featured addresses from United Women’s Group National President Carla Bradley, Belmopan Area Representative Oscar Mira and Prime Minister John Briceño.

Briceño used his remarks to rally party supporters around the upcoming municipal campaign, speaking about the PUP’s record while also acknowledging periods when the party had fallen short.

Cawich is seeking a second term as mayor after winning the office in 2024. Official Elections and Boundaries Department results show he received 3,127 votes in that election, while the PUP captured the entire Belmopan City Council.

The PUP says its candidates across Belize are preparing to contest the March 3, 2027 municipal elections.

World.title: El Salvador’s dramatic crime decline sparks question: Should Belize adopt similar policies?
World.content:
El Salvador’s dramatic crime decline sparks question: Should Belize adopt similar policies?

By Breaking Belize News Staff: El Salvador’s dramatic transformation in public security is again generating discussion across the region, raising a question for Belizeans: Should Belize adopt any of the crime fighting policies used under President Nayib Bukele?

Claims circulating online describe a 98 percent reduction in homicides in El Salvador. Official Salvadoran figures show a similarly dramatic long term decline. The country’s homicide rate fell from 106 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2015 to 1.3 per 100,000 in 2025. Officials recorded 82 homicides in 2025.

Bukele’s government credits its Territorial Control Plan and the state of emergency introduced in 2022 with breaking the power of violent gangs. More than 90,000 people have been detained since the emergency measures began.

The results have attracted attention in Belize, where violent crime remains a persistent concern. Belize Police Commissioner Dr. Richard Rosado reported 91 murders in 2025, compared with 92 in 2024.

However, El Salvador’s approach has also generated serious controversy.

Human Rights Watch says gang violence has declined markedly, but has documented allegations of arbitrary detention, torture, enforced disappearances and serious violations of due process during the state of emergency. Salvadoran authorities have defended their security strategy as necessary to dismantle gangs that once controlled communities.

That leaves an important debate for Belize. Could elements such as stronger intelligence gathering, tougher action against organized gangs, improved investigations and greater police presence be adapted locally while maintaining constitutional protections and due process?

What do you think? Should Belize adopt some of El Salvador’s tough crime fighting policies, or should Belize pursue a different approach to violent crime?

World.title: Belize remembers Father of the Nation George Price on National Service Day
World.content:
Belize remembers Father of the Nation George Price on National Service Day

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belizeans are remembering the life and legacy of the Right Honourable George Cadle Price as the country observes National Service Day and the 15th anniversary of his passing.

A wreath laying ceremony was held at Price’s final resting place at Lord’s Ridge Cemetery in Belize City as part of the official programme of events.

Opposition Leader Tracy Taegar Panton, who attended the ceremony, said the occasion was one of solemn remembrance of the former Prime Minister’s life and contribution to Belize.

Official wreaths were laid on behalf of the Governor General, Prime Minister, Chief Justice, Leader of the Opposition, Mayor of Belize City, National Celebrations Commission and the Price family.

Price served as Belize’s first Prime Minister following Independence in 1981 and is widely recognized as the Father of the Nation.

Panton used the occasion to call for renewed commitment to values she associated with Price, including humility, service and nation building.

The remembrance comes as Belize prepares to celebrate its 45th anniversary of Independence on Monday, September 21.

World.title: Taiwan Ambassador joins Belize’s State of the Nation Address and citizenship ceremony
World.content:
Taiwan Ambassador joins Belize’s State of the Nation Address and citizenship ceremony

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Taiwan’s Ambassador to Belize, Lily Li Wen Chi, joined Cabinet members and members of the Diplomatic Corps for Belize’s 2026 State of the Nation Address in Belmopan on September 15.

The annual address was delivered by Prime Minister John Briceño and focused on several national issues, including economic development, affordability, energy security, education and the country’s wider development agenda.

Following the event, Ambassador Chi said she was pleased to attend and expressed confidence that Belize will continue moving toward a brighter future.

The September 15 programme also included a citizenship ceremony marking Belize’s 45th anniversary of Independence.

During the ceremony, 45 new citizens were officially sworn in and presented with nationality certificates, matching the country’s 45 years of Independence.

The symbolic ceremony formed part of the wider national activities leading up to Independence Day on September 21.

The event brought together senior government officials, diplomats and newly naturalized Belizeans as the country reflected on its progress and future priorities.

World.title: Belize and Greece explore stronger cooperation during bilateral meeting
World.content:
Belize and Greece explore stronger cooperation during bilateral meeting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize and Greece are looking at ways to deepen diplomatic cooperation following a bilateral meeting between Foreign Affairs Minister Francis Fonseca and Greek Ambassador Nikolaos Kotrokois.

Fonseca met with Kotrokois, Ambassador of the Hellenic Republic to Belize, for discussions focused on strengthening relations between the two countries.

According to information from Belize’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, the exchange explored opportunities for greater cooperation in areas of mutual interest as well as increased engagement in multilateral forums.

Kotrokois serves as Greece’s ambassador to Mexico with concurrent accreditation to Belize and several other countries in the region.

Belize’s foreign policy framework places emphasis on strengthening bilateral and multilateral relationships, promoting trade and tourism, and advancing national development priorities through international cooperation.

The meeting forms part of Belize’s ongoing diplomatic engagement with international partners as both countries look for opportunities to expand their relationship.

World.title: 3,000 rural Belize households to get electricity under US$23.75 million IDB programme
World.content:
3,000 rural Belize households to get electricity under US$23.75 million IDB programme

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Approximately 3,000 rural households in Belize are expected to receive electricity for the first time under a new US$23.75 million financing package approved by the Inter American Development Bank.

The IDB says the Rural Electrification Program will expand the electricity network while also introducing solar photovoltaic mini grids, battery energy storage systems and smart meters in communities where conventional grid connections may be difficult.

The financing package consists of a US$20 million IDB loan, a US$2.75 million nonreimbursable investment grant and a US$1 million grant from the Low Carbon Energy Fund.

The programme will particularly target rural communities with high proportions of Indigenous people and migrants.

According to the IDB, the investment is intended not only to bring electricity into homes but also to improve living conditions and create economic opportunities in rural Belize.

The programme will finance the design, construction and installation of solar mini grids with battery storage and smart metering technology. Distribution networks will also be expanded to connect households and community facilities.

The IDB says the programme will additionally strengthen Belize’s capacity to plan, operate and maintain rural electrification investments while encouraging productive uses of electricity.

It marks the IDB’s first energy sector operation in Belize.

The US$20 million loan carries a 25 year repayment period, a 5.5 year grace period and an interest rate based on SOFR.

World.title: WATCH: Rain fails to dampen spirits at PNP annual conference in Westmoreland
World.content:
SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — Persistent showers of rain failed to dampen spirits at the People’s National Party’s (PNP) historic 88th Annual Conference on Sunday, as thousands gathered at Independence Park in Savanna-la-Mar. Marking a significant departure from tradition, this year’s staging is the first time in the party’s history that the national conference is being hosted outside of Kingston.

​Under the theme, “We Put People First,” the PNP intentionally chose Westmoreland as the host venue, a symbolic decision to stand in solidarity with the parish most severely impacted by Hurricane Melissa.

​Despite the torrential downpours that began around 3:30 pm, the atmosphere remained buzzing. Hundreds of vendors lined the venue, erecting makeshift stalls on the perimeter while walking vendors maneuvered through the dense crowds inside and outside the park.

​Entrepreneurial vendors, anticipating the bad weather, quickly capitalizsed on the changing conditions. Rain cloaks and umbrellas became the day’s hottest commodities, though not without controversy. Some vendors raised umbrella prices up to $1,000, drawing sharp criticism from drenched patrons who openly accused the sellers of “making poor people suffer just like the prime minister.”

​As each heavy wave of rain battered the open-air venue, concerns mounted among attendees over whether the historic gathering would be washed out, how long the programme could persist, or if key proceedings would be curtailed.

​As of publication time, party leader Mark Golding had not yet arrived at the venue, leaving patrons sheltering under umbrellas and awnings, anxiously awaiting his keynote address and wondering if the weather will hold for the remainder of the historic event.

World.title: ‘Burnt out’: St Mary farmers bemoan wipeout of crops due to bush fires
World.content:
Farmers in St Mary are counting the mounting losses of weeks of bush fires – worsened by prolonged dry conditions – that have swept through agricultural communities, destroying crops, irrigation equipment and farm infrastructure.

Farmer Owen Hanchard said large sections of the parish have been affected by fires that have moved across mountainsides and into farming areas, leaving some properties almost unrecognisable.

“Most of St Mary is being gutted by fire,” Hanchard said. “There was this huge fire that I don’t know where it started from, but it has traversed along the mountainside and all over the place.”

He said one farm he visited was severely damaged, with irrigation equipment and other resources destroyed.

“The place was burnt out, unrecognisable,” he said. “I used some of our equipment because we have our water hose and certain things here that’s used to irrigate the farm. They were burnt up.”

Hanchard said the fires have continued in several communities, including Mount Regale, Rock River and Clarke Castle, with some areas difficult for firefighters to access because of the remote and rugged terrain.

“Some of the areas that it has been going, it’s so remote, though the fire unit would have come there, they cannot get access to those places,” he said. “So, it’s like all they can do is just watch it burn.”

What’s worse, he said efforts to fight the fires have been complicated by low water levels in rivers, limiting the ability of residents to pump water to contain the flames.

“The river has gotten so low that they had a pump; they were trying to pump some water to see if they could maybe expend the fire, but it didn’t work,” he said.

Hanchard said while his own farm suffered losses, other farmers have been hit much harder.

“Mine was impacted, but not as severe as other persons. I’ve lost some cane and some plantain,” he said.

He praised the Jamaica Fire Brigade for responding to calls, but noted that the terrain often prevented them from reaching the affected areas.

“The (Jamaica) Fire Brigade really turned up,” he said. “I can remember four consecutive times when I was over there that they came. But having come, there’s nothing that they could have done because of how the terrain is.”

Another farmer, Dave Evans, who operates a nine-acre farm, said the impact has been devastating after more than three months of drought conditions left crops vulnerable.

“This drought has been here for over 13 weeks. It dry up everything around it and we lose the crops them, we lose the plants them, but the fire now take set,” Evans said.

He explained that some of the fires are fuelled by dry vegetation and strong winds.

“We have firestorm from Friday. We have been having firestorms every day,” he said. “When it reach nine to 10 o’clock, the fire just generates.”

Evans said sparks from burning bamboo and other dry material have helped spread the fires, causing widespread destruction.

“It burn a greenhouse for me, it burn all the pipes them,” he said. “We have corn we plant, we lose everything because them push up and then them just suffocate and dead.”

He said his farm has lost nearly all of its production, including plantain fields, corn crops, irrigation pipes and drip hoses.

“The fire just come and blow through the plantain walk and burn down the plantain walk dem so we basically on ground zero because even if you did have the young crops dem weh should be pushing up now, everything burn out. Weh the sun nuh do, the fire come finish them,” Evans said.

The farmer said he has also been forced to relocate some farming activities closer to the river in an effort to continue production.

“My yam field, we have to leave them land there and come near to the river,” he said. “I lose the greenhouse, I lose the pipe, I lose 36 lengths of inch and a half pipe, not talking about drip hose.”

Evans said firefighters have been focused mainly on protecting homes because of the number of communities affected, but many farms remain difficult to access.

“The fire trucks don’t have access to the farms,” he said. “Most of the farms are not really near the road, so the farms just leave and burn out.”

He said farmers have been trying to save what they can by removing equipment and wetting areas around storage facilities, but many crops and farming materials have already been lost.

“We try to pull up some of the water pipes and the things them, but you can’t save nothing out in the farm,” he said.

Evans acknowledged that the Rural Agricultural Development Authority (RADA) has visited some affected farms to assess the damage, but said additional fires have since destroyed more agricultural areas.

The farmers are calling on the Government and the wider public to provide some relief and support as they work to recover from what they describe as one of the most damaging fire periods they have experienced.

World.title: Pregnant in State care
World.content:
BEFORE her sister died she expressed one wish for her daughter — that she would not become a teen mother. Her loving sibling says she tried desperately to honour that wish, eventually placing her niece in State care when she became increasingly difficult to manage at home, only to later learn that the 16-year-old had become pregnant while at Maxfield Park Children’s Home.

Heartbroken, she now feels as though she has failed both her sister and her niece. However, she said her pain has been compounded by her anger over not being provided with timely updates on matters related to her now-pregnant niece.

According to her, she was told that the teen had “consensual sex” with another ward of the State while residing at the Corporate Area children’s home. However, the teen was already about six weeks pregnant when her aunt was told of the pregnancy in July.

The aunt told the Jamaica Observer that a few days before she was formally notified by a representative, her niece had sent her a message saying that she had something to tell her, but never revealed what that was. She suspects that the teen may have intended to tell her that she was pregnant, which has led her to question whether staff at the facility were aware of the pregnancy but failed to immediately inform her.

Shortly after learning about her niece’s pregnancy, the aunt said she went to the children’s home hoping to see the 16-year-old, only to be told that the teenager had been transferred to another facility. While she admitted to previously being informed that a transfer was pending since Maxfield Park was not equipped for pregnant teens, she said she was not told when it would be actioned or the new location to which the teen would be moved.

On a separate occasion, she learned that her niece had been arrested for allegedly assaulting an individual at a children’s home in Montego Bay, St James. However, this news did not come from the teenager’s caseworker, but from the police who called to make contact with the family.

In fact, the aunt said much of what she knows about her niece’s whereabouts and well-being has come through the grapevine from friends and contacts within various agencies, who have tried to help her piece together what has been happening with the child in State care.

The aunt said the experience has been both heartbreaking and infuriating. She described the lack of communication from the teen’s caseworker and various children’s homes as unacceptable.

“I am so angry. I don’t even know how to explain this feeling, but I am hurt about it. I am torn up about it,” she told the Sunday Observer.

She said that following her sister’s death in 2023 she became the guardian of all four of her children. She said her niece was very problematic and bounced around from one family member to the next. She said the teenager was eventually placed in State care in Falmouth, Trelawny, but when the facility was damaged during the passage of Hurricane Melissa, she returned home.

However, her behaviour did not improve. She said her niece continued to rebel, eventually engaging in self-harm.

The family then decided to put her back in State care, where her aunt said she believed the teen would be surrounded by qualified professionals who would ensure her care and safety. Instead, the teenager got pregnant and was allegedly subjected to abuse.

The teen’s uncle said he was informed by the pregnant teen that she was locked outside of a home at which she was residing in Montego Bay, with no food, water, or shelter. He alleged that his niece also faced verbal abuse and neglect at the childcare facility.

“It’s wrong,” he said, repeating the phrase three times for emphasis.

“It’s an abuse of power. It’s abusing the child; it’s abusing the family. We want legal action taken against the various institutions that are responsible, and for there to be some [restitution] for her, because she does not have the capacity to take care of a child. The State has not done its duty so, therefore, the State has to take responsibility for that,” he insisted.

A returning resident, the uncle said it is depressing to see what Jamaica has become.

“We don’t understand the trauma that a person who lives abroad has to go through. To come back to Jamaica and see the same stupidness going on between our own people when we should know better that it is wrong. We should know better,” he said, demanding accountability.

Meanwhile, the aunt is heartbroken that she did not get to keep the promise she made to her sister.

“Me feel like me fail. When I told them to take her back, that was the main reason why I gave her back because I never wanted her to be a teen mom. I wanted her to have an education and get something out of life. Being a mother at this age wasn’t for her. Mi never want that. Mi feel like me fail my sister. Every day me feel like me a fail. I keep saying, ‘Where am I going wrong?’,” said the distraught aunt.

“There are nights when I lie down in my bed, and I cry uncontrollably because I can’t cry in front of the kids…me have to try and make these kids not see that aunty a break. Mi tired,” she said, her voice heavy.

She said the latest information she’s received is that her niece is at a correctional facility in Kingston, where she is being held in relation to the alleged assault.

She said she’s sent a letter to the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) demanding answers as to why she was not kept in the loop regarding her niece’s care, but has yet to receive a response.

She hopes the matter shines light on the realities of how children are treated in State care to bring about change.

“Them nah watch them, and they are not doing them job. They are negligent,” she said.

“I want people to know what is going on in State care. I want them to know that these are the people that we have looking after our kids because we can’t look after them. It cannot continue,” she told the

Sunday Observer.

Executive director and co-founder of Eve for Life Joy Crawford said the situation is extremely difficult to understand.

A non-government organisation that focuses on the sexual and reproductive health, rights and well-being of the Jamaican girl child, the head said the teen has received support from the organisation. According to Crawford, the teen has a history of abuse and self-harm and had been placed in the facility to ensure her safety and care.

“For her to go into State care for care and protection and nurturing and then for her, within eight months, to have had a report that she is currently pregnant while being a ward of the State, it is difficult to understand the sequence of events and the things that the State had in place to ensure her safety and protection.

“What is as problematic is that, based on the interaction and the support that we have been lending to her aunt, who is her current legal guardian, is the missing alarm, the missing accountability, the missing engagement from the State actors and their responsibility to the family and to this young girl. They need to actually answer key questions and say what is going to be in place for this young woman and her child that is coming, as well as what is the restitution for her being harmed, abused, neglected, and becoming pregnant while in State care,” said Crawford.

She insisted that there are some serious questions to be answered.

“I am aware that the aunt had sent a letter to the CPFSA for which, to my knowledge, she has still not yet gotten a response. That, for me, now is tantamount to being the worst part of this story, because we have a duty, as Jamaica, to answer this family about what has happened to their relative while in State care,” she told the Sunday Observer.

The director said the non-government institution is concerned about how privately run homes care for wards of the State and the interventions that are taken when they are harmed.

“While we understand that Eve for Life is not a legal guardian, or we don’t have legal jurisdiction over the families that we work with and the children…we are legitimate child protection partners in Jamaica, playing a role for a group of young people who are vulnerable. We are the sole representative of them in the education system, in the childcare protection system, and in their communities, and I think from that perspective we have a duty to be very invested in what happens to them,” said Crawford.

She advocated for swift intervention, adding that the family deserves answers.

“The family should be in the know and should be brought to the table. There should be some State acknowledgement that there has been grievous harm done to this young woman while under the watch of the Government,” she stressed.

World.title: Jamaica’s slavery petition packed with years of research
World.content:
Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange stands in front of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council building in London, England, holding the historic reparations petition document filed to His Majesty King Charles III on September 7.

Jamaica’s petition inviting King Charles III to refer to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council questions regarding Britain’s seizure, transportation, chattelisation, and enslavement of the island’s ancestors from the mid-17th century to 1834 is packed with heavy and emotive information gathered through extensive research conducted over at least 17 years.

“It is estimated that over a period of more than 300 years, at least 15.4 million Africans were forcibly captured and transported across the Atlantic. It is recorded that approximately 1.2 million people were transported to Jamaica alone,” the petition states in the opening section outlining the background to the application.

Filed on September 7, 2026 by a delegation headed by Culture Minister Olivia Grange, the petition gives overwhelming information about the cruelty and inhumane treatment meted out to captured Africans who were sold into slavery.

“The staggering numbers of those who arrived in Jamaica, chilling in themselves, obscure the additional detail of the significant numbers of Africans who were killed, in particular on the infamous ‘Middle Passage’. Mortality rates on the ‘slavers’, that is the ships that transported the enslaved, were extremely high in the early years of the trade in enslaved persons. By way of example, on arrival in Jamaica in 1732, the Saint Michel recorded a shocking mortality rate of 96.5 per cent,” the petition states.

“The depravity of the mercantile enterprise that systematically transformed humans into commodities was laid bare in a 1783 case about another slaver, the Zong (Gregson v Gilbert 99 ER 629). Serious navigational errors caused the voyage of the ship to become protracted, and to imperil all onboard. A number of the 442 enslaved Africans who started the journey died en route.

“The poor physical condition of those still alive as the vessel neared Jamaica meant that as ‘perishable goods’, they would have little resale value on arrival. A deliberate decision was made by those in charge of the ship to drown some 134 captive Africans in three batches. The ship’s owners argued, in order to make good a claim for insurance, that this calculated decision was not murder. Rather, the argument went, it was merely the preservation of healthy ‘cargo’ by removing the contaminants; by disposing of the frail and the infirm. There was, according to the case report in Gregson, only ‘the throwing overboard of goods, and of part to save the residue’,” the petition states.

It points out that the story of the Zong “stands figuratively for the horror of the whole slavery era”, as only 208 of the original 442 captive Africans on the Zong — a 53 per cent mortality rate — made it to Jamaica.

“Many were flung overboard still handcuffed, with some opting to jump rather than be pushed to their deaths,” the petition points out, adding that those who died are commemorated by the Zong Monument in Black River, St Elizabeth, and the episode is remembered by Jamaicans, and those of Caribbean ancestry all over the world “as evidence of Imperial Britain’s disregard for the very humanity of captive Africans, the forebears of Jamaicans of African descent”.

In the application, Jamaica is contending that transatlantic chattel slavery dehumanised people of African descent and its impact is not limited by national boundaries.

“It has caused and contributed to the enduring perception of those of African descent as inferior and has helped to entrench corrosive notions of racial hierarchy. Its dependence upon extreme violence, in order to subjugate, is reflected in the excessive use of force against black people in many countries with significant African and Caribbean diasporic communities. Unsurprisingly, in both the United Kingdom and the USA, there is a disproportionate use both of force and of incarceration, against people of African descent,” the petition states.

It gives as an example, ‘The Lammy Review’, published in 2017 and authored by former British Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy, which found that people of African descent accounted for 12 per cent of the adult prison population, and over 40 per cent of those in youth custody, despite representing just three per cent of the general population.

The review — an independent study examining the treatment of and outcomes for black, Asian, and minority ethnic people in England and Wales’ criminal justice system — noted that “these statistics reflect a level of disproportionality greater than that recorded in the United States at the time”.

Essentially, Jamaica wants the Privy Council to:

* make a determination as to “whether transatlantic chattel slavery, as practised in Jamaica, was in fact ever lawful under English law, or whether it was offensive to the fundamental principles of the common law and to certain express statutory provisions of the Westminster Parliament”;

* determine “whether the said forced transportation and chattel enslavement was a breach of relevant international obligations”, which include “those arising out of general principles of law, the peremptory prohibitions of slavery, torture, racial discrimination and crimes against humanity and obligations derived from other sources of international law”; and

* determine “whether there is a legal obligation on the part of the United Kingdom to provide a reparatory remedy to the people of Jamaica, as descendants of those subject to these dehumanising practices, and as a community of persons on whom the practices have had indelible, and continuing, negative effect”.

The petition notes that Jamaica is prevented from commencing inter-state litigation against the United Kingdom before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) under Article 36(2) of the ICJ Statute in relation to the harms resulting from transatlantic chattel slavery.

“This is because of the United Kingdom’s reservation, under Article 36(2), which states that the United Kingdom does not accept the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ in respect of disputes ‘with the government of any other country which is or has been a member of the Commonwealth’,” the petition states.

World.title: Excellence In Music honoured
World.content:
Agent Sasco, one of the evening’s awardees, displays his certificates.

Some of reggae-dancehall’s unheralded trailblazers were recognised at the Excellence In Music Ceremony, which took place at Courtleigh Auditorium in New Kingston on September 15.

Among them were keyboardist/organist Ansel Collins, famous for creating the classic Double Barrel and Stalag rhythms. Noel Davy, who crafted the Sleng Teng beat that sparked dancehall’s digital age in 1985; and Neville Hinds, who played organ on Mother And Child Reunion, Paul Simon’s 1972 hit single.

The event, previously known as the Grammy Certificate Ceremony, was organised by Back 2 Da Future Music Ltd, a London-based company operated by Kennedy Mensah. It saw 95 artistes, producers, musicians and studio engineers who contributed to Grammy-winning or nominated projects, being acknowledged with certificates and plaques.

Two days before the ceremony, Collins received a plaque at his Portmore home from Mensah for playing on Pressure Drop, Toots And The Maytals’ 1971 hit song. It was certified silver in 2024 by the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) for sales of 200,000 units.

On Tuesday, Davy was presented with certificates for playing on Damian Marley’s 2005 Grammy-winning album Welcome to Jamrock. He received similar plaques for playing on Awake and As I Am, Julian Marley’s Grammy-nominated albums.

Hinds was awarded a gold plaque for Negotiations And Love Songs, a 1988 compilation of Simon’s biggest hits which include Mother And Child Reunion.

Guitarist Dalton Browne, who died in 2020, was one of the evening’s big winners. His daughter Abisha was presented with a silver plaque from the BPI for playing on Wayne Wonder’s 2003 album

No Letting Go.

His family also received certificates for contributing to Grammy-nominated albums by Wayne Wonder (No Holding Back), Jimmy Cliff (Breakout), The Wailing Souls (Equality), Luciano (A New Day), Buju Banton (Friends For Life and Rasta Got Soul), Freddie McGregor (Anything For You), Judy Mowatt (

Working Wonders), Beenie Man (The Doctor) and Gregory Isaacs (Mr Cool, Private And Confidential, Brand New Me, and Isaacs Meets Isaac — Gregory Isaacs and King Isaac).

Cleveland “Clevie” Browne, his younger brother, took home Grammy Certificates for Rock Steady (No Doubt), Black Magic and Jahmekya (Ziggy Marley and The Melody Makers).

Wycliffe “Steely” Johnson, Clevie’s partner in the production duo Steely and Clevie, was awarded a gold disc for co-producing Dawn Penn’s gold-selling single, You Don’t Love Me (No, No, No). He died in 2009.

Posthumous recognition was for Gregory Isaacs, who died in 2010. His wife, June, accepted silver plaques for Night Nurse, his 1982 album and song. She also received certificates for four of his albums nominated for Best Reggae Grammys — Mr Cool, Private and Confidential, Brand New Me, and

Gregory Isaacs and King Isaac — Isaacs Meets Isaac.

Singer Richie Stephens, one of the evening’s performers, was another multiple winner. He was the recipient of five Grammy Certificates and three BPI-certified discs.

One of the discs was a platinum plaque for Rihanna sampling his Sail Away rhythm for her 2016 global hit Work.

Among the event’s highlights was veteran deejay Flourgon accepting a platinum plaque for Miley Cyrus’s 2013 song We Can’t Stop, which sampled his 1988 hit single We Run Things. He joked that the financial settlement he received from the well-publicised lawsuit he brought against the pop singer for using his song without permission allowed him to purchase a house. That home is emblazoned with “We Run Things”. He then paid tribute to his mother with a rousing performance of Glory.

Mensah, born in London to Ghanaian parents, was pleased with the event.

“I am elated! The most satisfying aspect was the ‘apprecilovtion’ that we bore witness to [and] the fact that many of our recipients have never been celebrated like this before,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

It was the second year that Back 2 Da Future Music Ltd collaborated with the BPI and American company, The Royalty Network Inc, for the ceremony.

A BPI platinum plaque was presented to deejay Agent Sasco for appearing on rapper Kendrick Lamar’s

To Pimp A Butterfly hit song; a Grammy Certificate for working on the album of the same name; and a second Grammy Certificate for Sean Paul’s Live N Livin.

Delly Ranx earned a triple platinum plaque for Dutty Rock’s 2002 album. He produced one of the Grammy-winning set’s songs, Ganja Breed which features Chico.

Aidonia received a platinum plaque for his song, Fi di Jockey, being sampled by will.i.am and Cody Wise for their 2014 hit It’s My Birthday.

Reggie Stepper (Reggie Henriques), whose 1991 song Co-Oonuh was sampled for Mercy, Kanye West’s 2012 song, received a gold disc.

Other winners were saxophonist Dean Fraser, who received Grammy Certificates for playing on The Wailers’ I.D., Toots and The Maytals’ True Love, and Mek Wi Dweet by Burning Spear.

Singer Glen Washington was awarded certificates for collaborating with Capleton and Third World on their albums Still Blazin and Ain’t Giving Up, respectively.

Engineer Chester Walker was awarded a platinum disc for working on Tease Me, Chaka Demus and Pliers’ 1993 hit single. His colleague, Roland McDermott, was recognised with Grammy Certificates for a similar role on Still Blazin, Awake, As I Am and The Cure by Jah Cure.

Singer Brian Gold accepted Grammy Certificates for harmony work on Maxi Priest’s Fe Real and Protoje’s A Matter of Time.

Producer Victan “Teetimus” Edmund got Grammy Certificates for Buju Banton’ Friends For Life and Bounty Killer’s Ghetto Dictionary: The Mystery.

World.title: …CPFSA tried to separate wards before pregnancy
World.content:
The Child Protection and Family Services Agency provides residential childcare services, which includes direct responsibility for the operation and management of eight government children’s homes and places of safety and the monitoring and licensing of another 40-plus private homes.

THE Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) has confirmed that a 16-year-old ward of the State has been impregnated by another ward while in its care, noting that the agency had implemented several unsuccessful preventative measures to keep the two apart.

The revelation comes amid concerns from the teen’s aunt, whose name is being withheld to protect the child, who complained about a lack of communication from the CPFSA regarding her niece’s pregnancy, movements between childcare facilities, and the teen’s arrest while in State care.

In a detailed response to questions from the Jamaica Observer, the agency said the facility’s management at Maxfield Park Children’s Home in the Corporate Area had identified the developing relationship between the 16-year-old and the male ward, who is also 16 years old, but both teenagers repeatedly denied that they were involved.

“Subsequently, various control measures were put in place to keep them separated and specially supervised while on property. Both wards were consistently defiant of these measures. At the time [the teen’s] pregnancy was discovered, arrangements were already being made to transfer the male ward to another facility as part of broader efforts to separate them,” the agency said in its response.

The agency said separation efforts were still ongoing when the pregnancy was discovered on July 6, 2026.

According to the agency, the pregnancy was discovered after the teen girl told a staff member that she was concerned she might be pregnant because she had missed her menstrual period. The teen was reportedly taken to the facility’s clinic and a doctor confirmed the pregnancy.

The CPFSA told the Sunday Observer the matter was also reported to the police, and the teen girl was taken to the Centre for Investigation of Sexual Offences and Child Abuse (CISOCA) for an assessment.

“CISOCA advised that [the teen] was over 16 years old at the time of conception and indicated that, based on the information she provided, the relationship was consensual. As such, there was no further action they could pursue in relation to a sexual offence investigation at that time,” said the agency.

The aunt and another family member were reportedly notified of the pregnancy on July 10, 2026 during a meeting with the teen’s caseworker at the CPFSA’s Kingston office.

According to the agency, the option was provided for the aunt to take the teen into her custody, but the aunt refused. They said the aunt was then informed that the teen would be transferred as her current facility was not equipped to handle pregnant teens.

In relation to the teen’s arrest charges, the agency said the 16-year-old was arrested on September 7 for reasonable suspicion of unlawful wounding at the Irwin Police Post. The agency said the teen’s grandmother and aunt were contacted by the police to be present when the teen gave her statement.

According to the CPFSA, it was not until the following day, September 8, that its officers were informed that an adult was needed to collect a statement from the teen.
