World.title: Pashinyan’s salary to nearly double as Armenian civil servants set for pay rises from 2027
World.content:
Salary increases for public officials in Armenia

From 1 January 2027, senior Armenian officials will receive higher salaries. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, for example, will earn 2,662,000 drams ($7,353), up from the current 1.5 million ($4,143). Deputy prime ministers’ salaries will rise to 2,163,000 drams ($5,975), from 1,289,000 ($3,560).

The increases will apply not only to the executive branch, but also to the legislative and judicial branches. The state budget will allocate 25 billion drams ($69 million) for this purpose. The government has already approved the draft. Parliament must now approve it.

“How does this public official live? How does he buy a suit and a watch? We never assess the negative impact [of this factor] on the development of our state. But the effect is highly negative. If we do not solve this problem, it will lead to disasters,” Nikol Pashinyan said during a discussion of the draft.

The ruling party views the decision as a reform. The prime minister said he was confident that failing to implement the project would mean “keeping Armenia stuck in place and continuing to subordinate the logic of the state to the logic of corruption”.

However, the opposition warns that such decisions will further deepen the sense of social injustice.

“Citizens often become disillusioned and leave the country not only because of economic difficulties, but also because of a sense of injustice,” former MP Garnik Danielyan said.

Salary increases in figures

Under the proposed amendments to the law “On remuneration for persons holding public office”:

the president of Armenia will earn 2,662,000 drams ($7,353), up from the current 1,664,000 drams ($4,596);

the speaker of the National Assembly will earn 2,496,000 drams ($6,895), up from 1,497,600 drams ($4,137);

MPs will earn up to 1,497,600 drams ($4,137), up from 832,000 drams ($2,311);

the president of the Constitutional Court will earn 2,412,800 drams ($6,665), up from 1,664,000 drams ($4,596);

the prosecutor general will earn 1,830,400 drams ($5,056), up from 1,248,000 drams ($3,447);

the ombudsman will earn 1,830,400 drams ($5,056), up from 998,400 drams ($2,758).

Governors, deputy ministers and deputy speakers of parliament will also receive higher salaries.

The stated amounts include taxes and other mandatory payments.

Ruling party representative’s assessment and opposition response

Eduard Aghajanyan, an MP from the ruling party, told journalists:

“The public administration system has consistently faced difficulties attracting highly qualified specialists. The issue became particularly acute after the 2018 revolution, when the logic of working within the system changed radically. Systemic corruption was eradicated, and the motivation mechanisms were completely restructured.

At the same time, pay levels made the public administration system unattractive to highly qualified professionals.

We have been at the helm of government for eight years now. I believe that the decision to address this issue is somewhat overdue.

I welcome the government’s decision. I am confident that it will produce the desired results in attracting highly qualified professionals.”

Former MP from the opposition Armenia bloc Garnik Danielyan wrote on his Facebook page:

“According to official data for 2024, Armenia’s poverty rate stands at 21.7%. One in four children lives in poverty, while thousands of families continue to face severe social hardship. People struggle to meet their basic needs. Moreover, in the 21st century, Armenia has recorded cases of people dying from hunger.

In your 2021 election programme, you [addressing the authorities] promised to halve the poverty rate by 2026. Poverty has not declined. But you yourselves are now living better. You no longer buy vacuum cleaners or televisions on instalment plans. Instead, you are accumulating assets.

Of course, no one objects to high salaries for public officials. But given this level of poverty, should the priorities not be addressing social problems, creating new jobs and ensuring decent living conditions for people?

And this is happening while Armenia’s public debt has already exceeded $14 billion. Housing and employment remain critical issues for thousands of Karabakh Armenians. Hundreds of people still live in temporary shelters, and many are forced to buy groceries on credit.

Clearly, political calculations also lie behind this decision — namely, preserving loyalty within the state system.”

Comments from Armenian residents on social media

The decision to raise the salaries of senior public officials has sparked heated discussions on social media. Most users criticised the authorities. Here are some of their comments:

“Of course, raising the salaries of civil servants and public officials is important. But we must not forget a phenomenon that is shameful for Armenia. Librarians receive the lowest salaries [75,000 drams — $208]. Raise them!”

“After spending days and nights thinking about the people, the ‘democratic’ government decided to raise its own salaries by 60–80%. Meanwhile, citizens earning 80,000–150,000 drams ($220–414) can continue entering shops full of goods. As prices rise rapidly, they must painfully choose whether to buy food for their child or shoes for themselves.”

“They are setting their salaries higher than those of members of the British royal family. And they are paying for all this with our taxes. They will bleed us dry. This is only the beginning.”

“The [prime minister] claims that raising his salary and those of other officials is necessary to prevent a catastrophe. According to this passionate speaker, a ‘catastrophe’ is when someone asks where an official got his suit or watch. I wonder who will ask him what he plans to spend those 2,662,000 drams — around $7,400 — a month on, considering how expensive he is for the state. For nine years now, you have paid neither rent nor utility bills, car expenses, petrol or maintenance costs.”

Salary increases for public officials in Armenia

World.title: Tbilisi condemns “presidential election” in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region
World.content:
Georgia condemns Russia over South Ossetia election

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry condemned the so-called “presidential election” held on 18 September in the Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia), calling it a violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

According to the ministry’s statement, “the opening of polling stations by Russia in the occupied territory without the consent of the Georgian government is a gross violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and another manifestation of Russia’s policy aimed at the de facto annexation of Georgia’s regions.”

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry said that holding the so-called election violates fundamental norms and principles of international law and cannot legitimise the occupation regime in Tskhinvali or change the region’s status under international law as part of Georgia.

“Holding any so-called elections in Georgia’s occupied territories, which are under military occupation and the effective control of the Russian Federation, while internally displaced persons and refugees are not given the opportunity to return to their homes safely and with dignity, is illegal and cannot have any international legal consequences,” the ministry said.

Tbilisi also condemned Russia’s decision to open polling stations for the Russian State Duma election in occupied Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region from 18 to 20 September.

The Foreign Ministry called on the international community to properly assess and condemn Russia’s actions and ensure an appropriate international legal and political response.

“Georgia continues to call on the international community to firmly protect Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders and support a peaceful resolution of the conflict,” the statement said.

On 18 September, snap “presidential elections” were held in Russian-occupied “South Ossetia”. Four candidates took part.

However, calling it an “election race” would only be accurate in a very loose sense, as it was clear from the outset that the overwhelming favourite was so-called “acting president” and “prime minister” Marat Kambolov, who arrived in the region from Russia in May 2026.

Unlike Kambolov, the other three candidates were residents of South Ossetia. But that was where their advantage ended. Most experts described them as “technical candidates” — people who were not seriously trying to compete for the presidency:

Zurab Kokoev, leader of the Unity party;

Kazbek Kodoev, an independent candidate and adviser to the rector of South Ossetia University;

Murat Valiev, a candidate nominated by the Patriots of Alania party and an employee of the state security service.

None of them campaigned among the population. They presented their views on the development of so-called South Ossetia only during live televised debates.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenia’s anti-corruption campaign: law on confiscating illicit assets takes effect
World.content:
Armenia’s law on confiscating illicit property

A large-scale anti-corruption campaign is unfolding in Armenia . As part of the campaign, the state is confiscating assets belonging to members of the country’s former financial and political elite.

The authorities say they are moving from high-profile political accusations to a systematic effort to recover illegally acquired property. The list of people accused of corruption whose numerous properties and business assets have been frozen includes former Armenian president Robert Kocharyan , Prosperous Armenia party leader Gagik Tsarukyan, and former finance minister and ex-head of the State Revenue Committee Gagik Khachatryan. Prosecutors accuse those involved in these high-profile cases of money laundering, bribery and abuse of office.

At the same time, the debate in Armenia goes beyond how they managed to amass such wealth. It also concerns whether the process complies with the law, whether the authorities apply the law equally to everyone, and whether the confiscated property is genuinely being returned to the people.

About the law

Armenia’s Law on Confiscation of Property of Illicit Origin has been in force since 2020. The authorities adopted it “to strengthen the fight against corruption and restore social justice”. The law applies to assets worth more than 50 million drams ($132,120). It allows the state to confiscate property if its owner cannot prove that the income used to acquire it came from legal sources.

According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, between 2018 and the first half of 2026, the state and local communities recovered assets worth approximately 304 billion drams (around $840 million). More than two-thirds of that amount — about $562 million — was recovered over the past three and a half years.

Comment from lawyer Aram Orbelyan

“The Law on Confiscation of Property of Illicit Origin contains fundamental contradictions. In international practice, confiscation models are clearly separated. One involves checking declarations: if a person cannot explain their income, the state confiscates the property. The other involves confiscation following proof of a crime. Our lawmakers, however, have mixed everything together into complete confusion.

The grounds for an investigation are chaotic. Half of the provisions are linked to criminal cases, including cases that authorities have suspended or closed on non-exonerating grounds. The other half allows officials to launch confiscation proceedings based simply on ‘operational information’. As soon as any intelligence report appears, law-enforcement agencies immediately begin examining a person’s property, going back as far as 1991.”

The factual vacuum of the 1990s

“What political statements describe as ‘plunder’ is often impossible to prove in court because the circumstances of that era were different. In the 1990s, non-monetary transactions, including agricultural exchanges, were widespread. There was no clear system of tax and customs control. Vehicle databases only appeared in the early 2000s, while electronic tax records emerged in 2013.

Moreover, the law at the time did not require businesses to keep documents for more than five years. This has naturally created an information vacuum today. Young prosecutors fail to take this historical context into account, leading to dead ends in court.”

Intrusion into private life and the political context

“The extent of the intrusion into private life raises serious questions. The law allows investigators to examine years of bank statements belonging to any relatives of a person under investigation. As a result, investigators and prosecutors gain access to strictly personal spending unrelated to corruption: where people went on holiday, what they ordered in cafés and what illnesses they received treatment for.

Society sees this mechanism exclusively as a ‘law to recover what former [authorities] stole’. Legally, however, the law should target corruption as such, rather than individuals. To ensure that anti-corruption tools do not appear politically selective, they must operate universally. They should apply to all elites, regardless of their current political status or affiliation with the ruling camp.

Authorities must examine both the past and the present transparently, without politically motivated cases, while taking limitation periods and the economic realities of earlier years into account. The process should objectively target illicit property, rather than serve as a selectively applied repressive tool.”

Comment from Varuzhan Hoktanian, an expert at Transparency International’s Anti-Corruption Centre

“The law sparked legal disputes from the outset, which led to a review of its constitutionality by the Constitutional Court. The court, in turn, sought an expert opinion from the Venice Commission. International experts offered two key recommendations. First, the confiscation of property for the benefit of the state should take place through separate civil proceedings, rather than criminal prosecution resulting in imprisonment. Second, some responsibility for proving the lawful origin of assets should fall on the owner.

It is often extremely difficult to prove that property has a corrupt origin. For example, Kocharyan’s case involves the signing of government decisions. For the charges to stand, the prosecution must prove that he deliberately approved specific decisions in the expectation that the assets would eventually pass to his family. This is extremely difficult to establish, so the evidence often appears unconvincing. The situation is compounded by the absence of a mandatory declaration system in the 1990s. As a result, it is now virtually impossible to confirm that property was acquired legally.”

Discrimination or fight against corruption?

“Applying legal mechanisms exclusively to one group of people discredits the anti-corruption institution itself, turning the law into a tool of political pressure. Attempts to deprive opponents of financial resources by seizing their property create a risk of completely clearing the political field. If this is combined with double standards during elections — harsh punishment, including arrests, for vote-buying while ignoring the abuse of administrative resources — the system of checks and balances itself collapses. Ignoring any of these abuses leads to dictatorship.”

What happens to confiscated property?

“The legal question is only one side of the problem. The question of what happens to confiscated property after the state receives it is no less important.

I recall a similar confiscation from Soviet history — the dekulakisation campaign of the late 1920s and early 1930s. We later learned about the grave consequences it caused, including the Holodomor. As it turned out, the party nomenklatura ultimately received everything that the authorities had seized. Today, these assets could likewise pass to new wealthy individuals or another nomenklatura. Once again, ordinary people would receive nothing.

When people talk about confiscating property, they mean both financial assets and movable and immovable property. For example, someone may have built a luxurious house and live in it. If we return to the Soviet example, after the October Revolution, the authorities seized property from wealthy people and turned luxury homes into communal apartments. That will not happen in our case. No one plans to move an ordinary citizen into someone else’s mansion. This raises the question: who received the mansion belonging to formerprimeministerformer prime minister Hovik Abrahamyan, or the Golden Palace hotel in Tsaghkadzor?

The situation is also problematic here. Even if a new wealthy owner buys these properties, a change of government could lead to their seizure again, with the authorities claiming that the original confiscation was unlawful.

Moreover, the phrase ‘returning property to the people’ sounds somewhat abstract to me. The trend shows that confiscated real estate goes not to the people, but to another wealthy person close to the authorities. And the public will ask: ‘What do we get out of it?’

Let me give you an example. There used to be a kindergarten in our courtyard. A newly wealthy owner acquired it through an illegal transfer. If the state takes the building back today and restores its former status as a kindergarten, then yes, that would mean ‘returning it to the people’.

In other cases, this could become a vicious circle in which each successive government dispossesses the previous one. This is quite dangerous, especially in the context of investment. Investors should not have to fear that the authorities might dispossess them tomorrow.”

How can confiscated funds be used?

“As for monetary confiscations, the seized funds go into the budget, into what is known as a ‘common pot’. It is unclear how the authorities then spend this money. These are not earmarked revenues, so the authorities decide how to use them.

It would be better to classify these revenues as earmarked funds and regulate them by law, directing the money towards social programmes designed to improve citizens’ welfare.”

Armenia’s law on confiscating illicit property

World.title: Poll: Do Abkhazia residents consider voting in Russia’s State Duma elections important? Video
World.content:
Russia’s State Duma elections will take place on 20 September. As most residents of Abkhazia hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, they can also take part in the vote. In the republic, which has a population of 250,000, as many as 35 polling stations have opened, and campaigning is in full swing.

Ahead of the election, we asked residents of Sukhum whether they planned to vote and whether they believed doing so would make a real difference.

The poll produced highly contradictory responses. Some people do not want to spend their day off voting in another country. Others consider it very important because, “if things go badly in Russia, things will get very hot here in Abkhazia too”.

Rustam: “For some reason, Russia is placing great importance on Abkhazia at the moment, and they really want all residents to take part in these elections. Perhaps it does not even matter how people vote, because there is no alternative. What matters is showing the turnout — that people are actively and collectively going to the polls, thereby acknowledging the assistance Russia provides to Abkhazia.

Personally, I will not vote because I see no point in it. If the [Yabloko party] had not been barred from the election, I would definitely have voted. Or I would have supported the Communists. As things stand, I do not want to spend my day off that way.”

Eliso: “I will definitely go to the polls and vote.

I will not say whom I will vote for. But as a Russian passport holder, I have the right to influence the composition of the State Duma, because the decisions made there directly affect us.

As a woman and a future mother, I want Abkhazia residents with Russian citizenship to be able to receive child benefits. I believe this bill should be among the first issues considered by the new parliamentary term.”

Timur: “I always vote in every election, both ours and Russia’s. My choice may almost never win, but I want to feel involved and have at least some opportunity to influence events. Russia directly affects us, and by voting I make my small contribution to what is happening in Abkhazia today.”

Almaskhan: “I will not vote. I never take part in elections and I am not interested in politics. I do not even know which parties are currently running or what they decide. Everything is done without us anyway. We live in a reality that we simply have to adapt to. It is impossible to change anything with a ‘tick’ on a ballot — everything has already been decided.”

Liana: “I will see how things go on Sunday, but I am not particularly keen. I do not even know whom to choose. The only party I hear about is United Russia, because its s are everywhere. Everyone says it is the strongest party. And Kiriyenko (the Kremlin’s overseer of Abkhazia — JAMnews) is a member, so apparently everything here is done through them. If I go, I will probably vote for them.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Will Abkhaz vote in Russia’s State Duma elections?

Abulfat Ismayilov (60 kg), Mahir Abbasov (81 kg), and Joshgun Abdullayev (90 kg) won bronze medals.

Azerbaijan is represented by 30 judokas at the World Championships.

World.title: Grapes, wine and music — this is how festival in Azerbaijan's Shamakhi concludes (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 20. The Grape and Wine Festival continued today in Shamakhi.

The festival was held on the grounds of the viticulture and winemaking complex of Şirvan şərabları LLC in the village of Meysari, where various wine brands were represented with their own pavilions. Guests had the opportunity to visit the pavilions and taste different types of viticulture and winemaking products.

Visitors learned about the traditions of viticulture and winemaking and also took part in various entertainment and show programs.

During the event-filled day, guests enjoyed performances by our Eurovision representative Dilara Kazimova, Teymur Suleymanbeyli, People's Artist Zulfiya Khanbabayeva, as well as DJ Kamon.

Entertainment activities for different age groups added a special touch to the festival program throughout the day. Visitors took part in various competitions and quizzes.

The Organizing Committee presented certificates to the organizations represented at the festival.

The festival's youngest guests were not forgotten either. A children's entertainment area, an interactive program for children, and activities with animators were organized at the venue.

The festival was organized by the Shamakhi District Executive Authority, Abqora restaurant, and the Nasimi Gardens complex.

The festival aims to promote local grape and wine production, increase the export potential of wine products, and inform the general public about the history of viticulture and winemaking in Azerbaijan, as well as the work being carried out in this field.

World.title: New 'blanket' Safe Work rules not practical, say miners and farmers
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Farmers and miners in Western Australia are nervous about new workplace safety rules that will reduce accepted exposure levels of dust and certain chemicals from December 1.

New rules set by Safe Work Australia (SWA) will reduce the safe exposure limit for hundreds of dusts, fumes and chemicals found in Australian workplaces.

The change is designed to protect workers, but industry groups say some new limits are so low there is no practical way to measure them.

Farming groups are warning the new rules could disrupt grain harvest and are calling on the government to intervene.

Most grain storage in Australia relies on phosphine to keep out insects. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Jo Prendergast)

West Australian Grain Group chair Alastair Falconer said farmers were alarmed SWA's accepted exposure limit for the fumigant phosphine will be slashed by 80 per cent.

"It's concerning, and I'm not sure if there's equipment that can measure such [new] low levels," he said.

Mr Falconer said the grain industry relied on phosphine to keep insects out of stored or exported grain, but said the new rule "almost renders phosphine unusable".

Exports play a big role in Australia's $33 billion grain industry, but many importing countries will reject entire shipments if insects are found due to biosecurity laws.

Grain dust limits more than halved

Mr Falconer said the new exposure limits for grain dust, including oats, wheat and barley had been more than halved.

He said the industry was scrambling to find information on how to measure grain dust exposure, and how to comply with the new regulations.

"To be honest, I wasn't aware of what our grain dust limits were until now," he said.

"When we're blowing down harvesters, we're cleaning out our own silos, what exposure is that giving us, how do you measure exposure when you're blowing down a harvester, and what's the correct PPE to use to make sure you don't go over this new limit.

"I think we need a three-year delay on implementing [the new rules] while industry can do more research on are these levels appropriate, or how we manage them into the future?"

Grain dust is an inevitable part of harvest operations. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Jo Prendergast)

Rules to protect workers

In a statement, Safe Work Australia said workplace exposure limits were used to protect workers and the revised workplace exposure limits reflect current scientific evidence and independent expert advice.

Safe Work said it conducted public consultation in 2019-2021, and the new limits were agreed by work health and safety ministers and published in April 2024 for implementation on December 1, 2026.

"Safe Work Australia recognises there are questions about how limits for phosphine and other airborne contaminants are applied in practice and is working with industry stakeholders and other government agencies, including the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority and the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, to support a consistent understanding of the requirements," the statement said.

"Compliance is assessed through personal air monitoring of workers, rather than measuring levels of an airborne contaminant at a fixed location."

Safe Work pointed to more information on its website.

The new standards are set by Safe Work Australia, but will be implemented by states legislation.

In August, WorkSafe Victoria said it would delay workplace exposure limits for 15 airborne contaminants, including phosphine, until December 1, 2029.

Grain industry groups met with West Australian Agriculture Minister Jackie Jarvis last week raising concerns about phosphine and grain dust compliance.

New Safe Work rules slash acceptable exposure to manganese dust. (Supplied)

The minister told the ABC she was seeking more information from the impact of the new phosphine limits on the grains industry.

More than 600 substances are covered by the new workplace exposure limit (WEL) system, with exposure limits tightened for about 250 of them.

The WEL defines the maximum level of airborne contaminant that most people can be exposed to without harming their health.

Blanket approach does not consider individual challenges

Mining groups have requested government modify or delay the new rules before December 1.

Association of Mining and Exploration Companies chief executive Warren Pearce said Safe Work had taken a "blanket" approach, which was not always practical to implement.

"It's important for workplace safety and worker safety, but in some cases it doesn't take into account the challenges of certain ore bodies or certain minerals," he said.

"There are issues in minerals such as manganese, we're concerned we won't be able demonstrate that we can get beneath that limit because there's not an ability to measure at that level.

"There will be operations that won't be able to meet those limits, but there are other pathways to continue operations.

"We've seen tragic stories emerge over many decades with asbestos and more recently silica, so it's really important we approach this from a worker safety perspective.

" We're willing to do everything we can possibly do to ensure that's possible and minimise risk in this space, but there needs to be an ability to tailor to individual operations. "

Mr Pearce said it was impossible to eliminate dust in mining, but industry used a range of tools such as protective equipment, pressurised cabs, dust monitoring and watering to reduce dust and exposure as much as possible.

In a statement, Minerals Council of Australia CEO Tania Constable said the proposed changes had significant implications across a range of Australian industries.

Miners say it will not be possible to measure for new workplace rules, due to come into effect on December 1. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

She said Safe Work Australia was consulting with affected industries, and MCA was providing input.

"This is an opportunity to ensure health objectives and all technical, scientific and implementation considerations are fully assessed before any final decisions are made and recognises the complex science and the practical ability of the minerals industry and other sectors to implement these limits," she said.

"These issues are particularly important in mining, where workplace exposure limits must be supported by reliable measurement methods, proven risk controls and practical implementation pathways across diverse operating environments."

World.title: Man dies after being towed by quad bike in regional NSW
World.content:
A man in his 20s has died after hitting a goalpost while being towed by a quad bike at a recreation reserve in regional New South Wales.

Emergency services were called to the reserve on Osborne Yerong Creek Road, at Osborne, about 70 kilometres west of Wagga Wagga, just after 2:30pm on Sunday.

Police said the man was seriously injured after being towed by the quad bike and hitting a goal post on the oval.

Bystanders provided first aid before emergency services arrived, but the man died at the scene.

He is yet to be formally identified.

Community in shock

The small rural and farming community has a population of fewer than 30 people.

Lockhart Shire Council Mayor Peter Sharp said the community was in shock and the crash would ultimately affect everyone.

"Osborne is a very tight-knit community, and it's a profound tragedy that's going to affect the community a great deal," Mr Sharp said.

He said the two men involved in the incident were members of the football club, which is central to the region's social calendar.

Lockhart Shire Council Mayor Peter Sharp

"It brings the community together, when farming times are tough it's a place we can go and talk about things.

"Everybody who is a member of the footy club would have known the young men involved."

Mr Sharpe said the council was working with the local health district (Murrumbidgee Health District) to organise counselling for people in the community who needed support.

Driver charged

Police arrested the quad bike driver, a 20-year-old man, after the crash.

He was taken to Wagga Wagga police station for mandatory testing, where he was charged with dangerous driving occasioning death, driving in a dangerous manner and negligent driving occasioning death.

He was granted conditional bail and is due to appear in the Wagga Wagga Local Court on Wednesday, September 23.

World.title: Mother confirmed a suspect in alleged domestic violence stabbings
World.content:
The death of a five-year-old boy, and the stabbing of two other children in the Blue Mountains is being treated as an alleged domestic violence incident, police have confirmed.

Emergency services were called to the scene at Valley Heights near Springwood about 1pm on Sunday after walkers discovered the group of four in a parked car.

The five-year-old boy died at the scene, while two younger children and a 42-year-old woman were found with stab wounds.

Police are in contact with the father of the children. (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

They underwent surgery and remain in hospital in a critical condition.

The woman, who police say is their mother, has not been charged.

NSW Police Deputy Commissioner Peter McKenna said all children were siblings, with the 42-year-old now a suspect in the domestic violence-related matter.

"I can state that the female is the mother of all three children and is a suspect," he said.

He said police will allege the woman's injuries were self-inflicted.

Deputy Commissioner McKenna said the four were found in what appeared to be a "random" location, and investigations into the incident were ongoing.

He said the woman was not previously known to police.

Deputy Commissioner McKenna said the father was supporting his two children in hospital.

'Horrific' weekend in NSW

The incident followed three other alleged domestic violence-related deaths in NSW over the weekend.

Police say two women, aged 90 and 23, were fatally stabbed in separate incidents at homes in Bondi Beach in Sydney, and Kooringal in Wagga Wagga.

A third woman, aged 70, was found dead at a property in the state's Northern Tablelands region.

A 31-year-old man has been charged over the fatal stabbing of a 23-year-old woman in Kooringal. (ABC News: Rachel Holdsworth)

Deputy Commissioner McKenna said the community had been heavily affected by the incidents.

"In my career, I don't think I have seen a weekend like this or a 48-hour period," he said.

"Such tragedy, such horrific events that have touched the whole community."

Deputy Commissioner Peter McKenna says the incidents are affecting the community. (ABC News)

He said none of the alleged offenders charged over the incidents were previously known to police.

"Because they weren't known to us, means we weren't in a position to be in the preventive space," he said.

"Four different incidents, all completely separate, all with tragic outcomes, just shows that domestic violence doesn't know postcodes, doesn't know what people do for a living.

"If people out there have any concerns about anyone, we would encourage them to speak up and report matters so that we can get into this space and can try and prevent these matters from occurring."

'Unacceptable levels' of violence

Full Stop Australia provides support for people affected by domestic and family violence, with CEO Karen Bevan saying it had been a "really tough morning" for those working in the space.

"I think everyone in NSW is waking up feeling overwhelmed by what can look like an insolvable problem," she said.

"We're thinking as a community, we all have to rise to this and start to think about how we can make a difference."

Katy Gallagher says domestic violence requires a whole of community response. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Federal Minister for Women Katy Gallagher said domestic violence prevention continued to be a priority for government.

"There is no easy solution, if there was one we would have already put it in place," she said.

"More money's part of it, we're doing that but again it's a whole of community response that's needed to end violence and to stand up and talk about the level of violence in our community right now, which is at unacceptable levels."

World.title: Harry and Meghan's treatment echoes Diana's, her brother says
World.content:
Princess Diana's brother says Prince Harry and his wife Meghan should be given official security because the media now treats them much the same way as it treated his sister in the years leading up to her death.

Princess Diana was 36 when she was killed in a 1997 Paris car crash while being pursued by photographers on motorbikes.

Her death sparked an outpouring of grief and a reckoning over whether the media, which splashed details of Princess Diana's life across front pages for years, bore some responsibility.

Prince Harry and his wife Meghan recently returned to the United Kingdom after six years in California. (AP: Jonathan Brady)

Earl Spencer has been speaking to the media in the lead-up to the publication of his book about his sister, which is critical of her former husband, the now-King Charles.

"From a security aspect, as an uncle who's seen his sister die in very, very preventable circumstances, I would veer towards protection," Earl Spencer said of Harry and Meghan when speaking to the BBC.

He said the tabloid treatment of Diana, and Harry and Meghan, could be "really, really unpleasant", and that it was "beholden on people" to learn from that experience.

Spencer's book makes international headlines

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, has made headlines around the world because it includes accusations about Charles making incendiary comments in the days after the princess's death.

In the book, Earl Spencer accuses Diana's former husband, the then-prince of Wales, of sounding "giddily elated" in the hours after her death.

Earl Spence also writes that an angry Charles had told him that the world would forget Diana soon enough.

In a rare move, the palace has hit back by saying the king is "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ⁠ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Asked by the BBC how he could prove the conversations had taken place, Earl Spencer said he had included a specific line in his much-lauded eulogy at Diana's funeral to counter the comments, ending it by saying she would "never be extinguished from our minds".

Earl Spencer has been speaking to the media in the lead-up to the publication of his book about Diana. (Supplied: BBC)

Earl Spencer said he had written the book, ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death, to celebrate her life.

He said their childhood never had a dull moment. "We both have ADHD," he said. "She was never diagnosed, but clearly we did."

The publication of the book and the surprise return of Harry and Meghan to Britain after six years living in the US pose a challenge for King Charles, who is still undergoing treatment for cancer.

Princess Diana's family accused the royals of showing a lack of support or care towards her before her death, a charge that was repeated by Harry and Meghan about their personal experience before they quit royal duties in 2020 to move abroad.

'I'm telling the truth': Diana's brother on king's 'monstrous' phone call Princess Diana's brother has doubled down on his swathe of explosive claims about Britain's royal family, insisting he is "telling the truth", and suggesting the king is "embarrassed".

Prince Harry has criticised the British government's decision to strip him and his family of automatic police protection afforded to other senior royals since he quit royal duties.

Following a long-running legal battle, that is now under review.

Earl Spencer, who recently hosted the couple, has serialised his book through The Daily Mail, just months after Prince Harry lost an expensive privacy lawsuit against the tabloid.

Earl Spencer said his revelations about King Charles would not come as a surprise to Prince Harry or his older brother, heir-to-the-throne Prince William, and he said while he knew many more details about the king, he had chosen not to include them.

Reuters

World.title: She went missing after leaving the ANU Bar in 1980. The mystery remains
World.content:
Elizabeth Herfort was last seen walking through the centre of Canberra on June 13, 1980.

What happened to her after that remains a mystery, despite repeated attempts to raise awareness over the years.

According to police, Ms Herfort had been out socialising with friends at the Australian National University Bar in Acton.

It is believed she left the venue to catch a bus home, and a person matching her description was seen walking along Vernon Circle and Commonwealth Avenue between 9pm and 9:45pm.

But the 18-year-old never made it home.

Seeking 'successful prosecutions'

Now, the ACT government is offering a reward of up to $500,000 for information that leads to the successful prosecution of the person — or people — responsible for Ms Herfort's disappearance.

Rewards of up to half a million dollars are also being offered for four other unsolved cases — including that of Keren Rowland.

Ms Rowland was 20 years old when she went missing on February 26, 1971 — the night of the Royal Canberra Show.

The government said her remains were discovered at the Air Disaster Memorial nearly three months later.

Canberra woman Keren Rowland was 20 years old when she died in 1971. (Supplied)

David Abuoi, also known as Gabrielle Malak Arok, was last seen on the morning of July 10, 2012, in Canberra's CBD.

He was 35 years old when he disappeared.

Police suspect he was murdered.

David Abuoi was last seen on London Circuit in Civic in 2012. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

Megan Louise Mulquiney, who started work at 8.30am on July 28, 1984, at Big W in the Woden Shopping Centre, also remains missing.

The 17-year-old was last seen standing outside the western entrance of Woden Plaza about noon that day.

"She was due to catch a bus home from the Plaza, however never arrived home," the government statement said.

Megan Louise Mulquiney has been missing since 1984. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

Troy Hugh Forsyth was 17 years old when he was fatally struck by a panel van while walking home with friends along Kent Street in Deakin in the early hours of Sunday March 1, 1987.

Police never found the panel van nor its driver despite what they called an "exhaustive" investigation, and that case remains open.

Troy Forsyth's mother Valerie Tompkins (left) and his sister Vanessa Forsyth (right) with Sergeant Jason Kennedy in 2012, at the site where Mr Forsyth died. (Kathleen Dyett)

'A strong incentive'

The government said if the disappearance or death of each of these individuals was the result of criminal action, "any witness or person with relevant information may be eligible for a reward".

Police have been unable to locate the driver of the vehicle that struck and killed Troy Forsyth. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

Police, Fire and Emergency Services Minister Marisa Paterson said it was hoped the reward would motivate someone to come forward.

"The ACT government is pleased to be able to offer these rewards for information that leads to a resolution for these families," Dr Paterson said.

"The families of these five people have never given up hope of getting answers regarding what happened to their loved ones."

ACT Chief Police Officer Scott Lee said these five cases were the most likely to have witnesses or information that could assist police.

ACT Chief Police Officer Scott Lee says there is a chance someone knows something despite the passage of time in each case. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"As we continue to review, reconsider and re-examine each of these matters, we acknowledge that significant time has passed for some of these investigations," he said.

"But that doesn't mean there isn't someone out there that knows what happened.

" One small piece of information may be all that's required to lead us to the answers we seek. "

Police suspect missing Canberra woman Laura Haworth 'met with foul play' Police believe Canberra woman Laura Haworth, who's been missing for more than 16 years, has "met with foul play".

These five cases are in addition to three existing unsolved homicides that had rewards announced in 2012 — the murders of Kathryn Grosvenor in 2002, Susan Winburn in 2004 and Frank Campbell in 2005.

Anyone with any information about any of these eight matters is being urged to provide their details to Crime Stoppers.

"While information can be provided anonymously, to be eligible for any reward requires the person providing the information to supply their details and speak with police," the government statement said.

World.title: Two men charged over what is believed to be Tasmania's largest ice bust
World.content:
Police in Tasmania's north-west have seized 17 kilograms of the drug ice, believed to be the largest single seizure of the drug in the state.

Tasmania Police said officers, including those from the state's Joint Organised Crime Task Force, the local drugs and firearms unit and the Special Operations Group, intercepted two vehicles at a beachside car park near Burnie on Friday.

"As a result of the interception, police located and seized 17kg of methamphetamine, which is estimated to have a street value of about $8.5 million," Tasmania Police said in a statement.

A New South Wales man, 40, and a Hobart man, 41 — who police allege is a member of an outlaw motorcycle group — were taken into custody.

Police said during a search of the vehicles and subsequent searches at other locations, about $100,000 in cash was also found, which they allege is "directly linked to the trafficking of drugs into Tasmania".

The two men have been arrested and charged with trafficking in controlled substances and will appear in the Devonport Magistrates Court today.

"The seizure of these 17 kilograms of methamphetamine is one of the most significant seizures ever by Tasmania Police for illicit drugs," Detective Inspector Troy Morrisby said.

"We know by seizing the drugs, it will prevent catastrophic harm to individuals and the broader community."

He said the investigation was continuing.

"Although this seizure is an outstanding result, we will be continuing to take steps against the broader criminal network, both in Australia and overseas who participated in this importation and we anticipate further arrests."

Inspector Morrisby said the Joint Organised Crime Task Force, made up of Tasmania Police, the Australian Federal Police, Australian Border Force and other federal agencies had achieved "several significant results since its inception nearly two years ago".

"This is yet another example of what these partnerships achieve when working collaboratively.

"Organised crime groups should be under no illusion the JOCTF [Joint Organised Crime Task Force] will continue to identify, investigate and dismantle criminal networks seeking to profit from drug harm in Tasmania."

World.title: Converse pulls sneaker ad critics say includes racist imagery
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The sneaker company Converse has removed a social media ad that sparked outrage among critics who viewed it as evoking the Ku Klux Klan (KKK) and lynching.

The Instagram ad photo showed K-pop singer Karina wearing a skirt and holding a pair of Chuck 70 X sneakers.

The ad has since been removed by Converse. (Supplied: Converse)

Critics lashed out online, saying a white triangular image created by lighting on the skirt resembled a KKK hood and the way she held the sneakers made them look like the dangling feet of a lynching victim.

Converse, owned by Nike, issued a statement apologising and said it had removed the ad.

"We're sorry," the statement said.

"We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognise that we got this wrong. We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared.

" This should not have happened, and we will do better. "

Converse, based in Boston in the United States, declined to answer questions seeking additional information, including how the company screened ads before they were posted and how the ad was approved.

Karina and her management company, SM Entertainment Group, did not immediately respond to messages through their Instagram accounts.

Corporations 'failing the same test'

Retailers and top fashion brands have issued a string of apologies over the years for products and advertising criticised for being racially insensitive.

Last month, US retailer Target Corporation pulled a children's Halloween costume from its shelves after widespread social media backlash, apologising for selling a garment that critics said evoked racist minstrel caricatures.

The Converse photo sparked swift criticism, including calls to fire staff involved in the ad and boycott the company.

In a slew of social media comments, posters questioned how the ad could have cleared the company's advertising vetting process.

Other commenters defended Converse, saying they did not believe it was intentional.

Converse issued a statement saying the company understood why the image was "deeply upsetting". (AP Photo: Charles Krupa, file)

Civil rights attorney Lee Merritt, who is based in Texas, posted on Instagram that Converse's apology "doesn't undo what got past legal, marketing and leadership at every step".

"We keep having this conversation because corporations keep failing the same test," he wrote.

" Do better means catching this before it airs — not after we're offended. "

Converse, founded in Malden, Massachusetts, in 1908, makes the iconic Chuck Taylor All Star sneaker.

It was first released in 1917 as a non-skid basketball shoe and, in 1934, added Taylor's signature, after the basketball player promoted the sneaker, according to the company's website.

AP

World.title: Motorists warned of dangers of picking flowers on busy WA highway
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The popular drive between Bunbury and Busselton, about 200 kilometres south of Perth, has become more scenic, with the median strips awash with blooming everlasting flowers.

But Main Roads WA has criticised the risky behaviour of motorists who are pulling over on the Bussell Highway to grab handfuls of the flowers.

Regional director Dominic Boyle urged people to leave the flowers alone and not create unnecessary hazards on the road.

"We'd really discourage that behaviour," he said.

"Not just because it's illegal to pick these flowers, but also they are putting themselves in danger."

Everlastings between Busselton and Bunbury. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Mr Boyle said the decision to plant flowers, rather than shrubs, to revegetate the median strip on the Bussell Highway, was unusual.

Everlastings were chosen because they were hardy and would improve soil quality.

"We're received some really positive feedback about their use on this project," he said.

However, reports of ardent flower pickers stopping to gather blooms have alarmed the agency.

"There's a big safety concern. We also want to make sure that seed gets back into the soil," Mr Boyle said.

"So we really encourage people just to keep themselves safe and to leave these flowers alone."

Everlastings require little care and thrive in sandy soil. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Enjoy them, don't pick them

The City of Bunbury has also planted the everlastings on its road reserves and the flowers are proving popular.

Bunbury Deputy Mayor Cheryl Kozisek took a positive approach to reports of flower theft.

"I think it's a real compliment that people are picking them," she said.

" I wouldn't encourage it immensely, but everlastings are beautiful — enjoy them. "

Everlastings have also been planted on roadsides in Bunbury. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Illegal picking an issue throughout region

South West Wildflower Society's Kelly Paterson said people illicitly picking wildflowers was an issue throughout the region.

"I've seen people sneakily picking flowers, and it's pretty clear that they know they are doing the wrong thing," she said.

"It's a disappointing thing to see.



"Taking those flowers before they are able to set seed means that seed is not going into the seed bank to produce additional plants in the future."

Commercial flower seed supplier Jen Egerton-Warburton said picking wildflowers on other people's land was not on.

Jen Egerton-Warburton supplies everlasting seeds to buyers across Western Australia from her Kojonup farm. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

"It's kind of rude really, isn't it? Someone else has planted them, for you to go and pick them, so I don't think it's appropriate.

"I don't think it's appropriate to pick any wildflower in Western Australia that is not in your garden.

"If people want to pick wildflowers, grow them at home."

Everlastings are protected wildflowers in Western Australia. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

The Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions said Western Australia's native everlastings were protected.

"It is an offence to take native flora, including wildflowers, from Crown land, public reserves and road verges without lawful authority," a spokesperson said.

Penalties can be significant, with fines of up to $50,000 for unlawfully taking native flora and up to $500,000 if critically endangered flora is involved.

World.title: ASX slides lower as oil prices, bond yields weigh on Wall Street
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slides lower as oil prices, bond yields weigh on Wall Street Stan Choe Updated September 21, 2026 — 10:01am ,first published September 21, 2026 — 5:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has opened in the red after Wall Street capped an up-and-down week with a mixed finish for US stock indexes on Friday, as elevated bond yields and oil prices weighed on the market. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 38.8 points, or 0.4 per cent, to 8692.4 in early trade. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.21¢. The S&P 500 inched 0.2 per cent higher after drifting between modest gains and losses for much of the day. The benchmark index also posted its second straight weekly loss. Wall Street had a mixed session to close an uneven week. AP The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added 0.4 per cent.



The majority of stocks on Wall Street fell, and helping to weaken them was rising pressure from the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5 per cent from 4.94 per cent late Thursday after it topped the 5 per cent level early this week for the first time since 2023. Higher yields slow the overall economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, from the US government to people looking to buy houses to businesses wanting to build AI data centres. They also tend to undercut prices for stocks and other investments. Related Article Superannuation Super contributions surge more than a third after budget tax changes Yields have been climbing in a long march since the COVID pandemic knocked them nearly to zero in 2020. The ascent has accelerated recently because inflation has remained stubbornly high for years. Inflation is well above 3 per cent by several measures. It worsened due to higher oil prices caused by the war with Iran.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, got to nearly $US110 early this week, up from a little over $US70 in July. It has been seesawing since. It briefly dropped below $US102 in overnight trading before erasing much of the loss and settling at $US103.87, down 0.9 per cent from the day before. Rising oil prices have pushed gasoline prices to $US4.47 per gallon, up from $US3.20 per gallon a year ago, according to AAA. That is tightening the squeeze on household budgets. Diesel prices are at a record $US6.45 per gallon and that has a more direct impact on shipping costs for everything from groceries to clothing. High inflation has been raising expenses for everyone, and more companies are giving details about how much. Steel maker Nucor said late Thursday that it expects to report an increase in profit from its steel mills business in the third quarter from the second because it’s able to charge higher prices. But it’s also having to absorb higher costs. It gave a forecast for overall profit in the third quarter that fell short of analysts’ expectations, and its stock sank 6.3 per cent.



Berkshire Hathaway edged up 0.1 per cent after famed investor Warren Buffett said he’s giving up his role as chairman of the company. Buffett already gave up his role as CEO of the company, where he built a reputation for buying stocks at relatively cheap prices and being patient with his investments. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Why higher interest rates are the new normal Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Elsewhere on Wall Street, General Motors fell 5.1 per cent and Qualcomm dropped 5.8 per cent. Among stocks that gained ground were Coinbase Global, which climbed 11.7 per cent for the biggest gain among S&P 500 stocks, and Robinhood Markets, which climbed 9.1 per cent. In stock markets abroad, indexes slumped across Europe, including drops of 1.5 per cent for the CAC 40 in Paris and 1.5 per cent for London’s FTSE 100.



Wall Street will get a key update this week on the US housing market, along with a regular weekly unemployment update. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: The Brownlow is Nick Daicos’ to lose, but these players could cause a shock
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLBrownlow Medal The Brownlow is Nick Daicos’ to lose, but these players could cause a shock Scott Spits Updated September 21, 2026 — 9:34am ,first published September 17, 2026 — 12:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Download your round-by-round Brownlow guide With Nick Daicos expected to not only romp to a massive Brownlow Medal win but have it secured by as early as the round 19 votes are read out, tipsters are having to get more creative than normal. Perennial contender Marcus Bontempelli and Geelong star Bailey Smith are favoured to fill the podium spots – but comfortably behind Daicos. Beyond those three, trying to identify a “surprise packet” is the next task. Brownlow Medal contenders Marcus Bontempelli, Nick Daicos and Bailey Smith. Artwork: Monique Westermann Our footy scribes and experts have had a crack, and the predictions are varied. Melbourne ruckman Max Gawn is one favoured name, but otherwise it’s a lottery. Think Hawk Jai Newcombe, Gawn’s teammate Kysaiah Pickett, Izak Rankine, Tim Taranto and Ollie Dempsey. Yes, even Dempsey and Taranto. No-one has lobbed for star Saint Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera, even though The Age’s Phantom Brownlow (see below for the leaderboard) has Nas polling nine best-on-grounds from just 17 games.



What our experts say Jake Niall

1. Nick Daicos (Collingwood)

2. Marcus Bontempelli (Western Bulldogs)

3. Luke Jackson (Fremantle)

Surprise packet, and why: Jai Newcombe. The Hawthorn midfielder and co-captain stood out in a team that made the top four. Luke “the Unicorn” Jackson was nothing short of brilliant for the Dockers. AFL Photos Caroline Wilson

1. Nick Daicos (Collingwood)

2. Bailey Smith (Geelong)

3. Caleb Serong (Fremantle)

Surprise packet: Luke Jackson deserves to be up there and a surprise only because he would be the first genuine ruckman since Jim Stynes last century to win it. Jimmy Bartel

1. Nick Daicos (Collingwood)

2. Marcus Bontempelli (Western Bulldogs)

3. Bailey Smith (Geelong)

Surprise packet: Will Ashcroft is a dominant, goal-kicking midfielder and has been a key driver of Brisbane’s run home.



Libby Birch

1.Nick Daicos (Collingwood)

2. Will Ashcroft (Brisbane Lions)

3. Marcus Bontempelli (Western Bulldogs)

Surprise packet: Luke Jackson. His athleticism and versatility make him one of the most dominant players in the competition, but it is his ability to influence games as both a ruckman and an extra midfielder that has really stood out this season. Will Ashcroft fires off a handball. AFL Photos Wayne Campbell

1. Nick Daicos (Collingwood)

2. Marcus Bontempelli (Western Bulldogs)

3. Jai Newcombe (Hawthorn)

Surprise packet: Tim Taranto. His team only got three wins, which means it’s hard to see him polling enough threes to challenge, but Taranto is always under the eye of the umpires and was a standout for his team. Michael Gleeson

1. Nick Daicos (Collingwood)

2. Patrick Cripps (Carlton)

3. Max Gawn (Melbourne

Surprise packet: Caleb Serong. As a midfielder for the minor premiers he’ll poll well. Max Gawn had one of his best seasons, and that’s saying something.



Sam McClure

1. Nick Daicos (Collingwood)

2. Marcus Bontempelli (Western Bulldogs)

3. Bailey Smith (Geelong)

Surprise packet: Isaac Heeney will poll more votes than you expect him to. And more than the AFL would like. Calum Jaspan

2. Bailey Smith (Geelong)

3. Marcus Bontempelli (Western Bulldogs)

Surprise packet: Ollie Dempsey. An absolute livewire all season for Geelong. One of the cats’ most consistent stars. Has flashy moments the umpires will remember. Emma Kearney

1. Nick Daicos (Collingwood)

2. Bailey Smith (Geelong)

3. Jai Newcombe (Hawthorn)

Surprise packet: Will Ashcroft. He’s been the dominant mid for Brisbane all year. Snubbed by the all Australian panel, but key stats indicating he is in the elite bracket of the competition. Hawthorn co-captain Jai Newcombe figures in our expert predictions. AFL Photos Hannah Kennelly

1.Nick Daicos (Collingwood)

3. Bailey Smith (Geelong)

Surprise packet: Will Ashcroft. He missed out on All-Australian, but don’t be surprised if you see Ashcroft in the top five. The dual Norm Smith medallist has had a strong season again, but might face some stiff competition from teammate Lachie Neale.



Marc McGowan

Surprise packet: Max Gawn. The champion ruckman had a career-best season in terms of possessions, played for a team that won 15 games and no longer has to compete against two generational midfielders for votes. A top-five finish is a distinct possibility. Scott Spits

1. Nick Daicos (Collingwood)

2. Marcus Bontempelli (Western Bulldogs)

3. Bailey Smith (Geelong)

Surprise packet: Izak Rankine’s hot form late in the season could push him to a high spot on the leaderboard. Why is Nick Daicos so favoured? “Ladies and gentlemen, please put your hands together for this year’s Brownlow medallist … Nick Daicos.”



Those are the words you will almost certainly hear on Monday night. Perhaps the biggest question now is – at what stage of the count will the Collingwood star be confirmed as a first-time medallist? Will Daicos reach the unbeatable stage at round 20, still with a month of votes to be counted? Or will the 23-year-old dynamo, the hottest of hot favourites, have to endure a nervous flutter or two in the final few rounds? World.title: ‘Unimaginable grief’: Child dead and two critical after Blue Mountains stabbing caps weekend of horror
World.content:
The stabbing death of a preschool-aged child in the Blue Mountains capped a brutal spate of domestic violence-related deaths in NSW over the weekend, when four people were killed in separate incidents and two small children were left fighting for their lives. Cyclists stumbled upon three children under the age of five and their mother in her 40s, all suffering stab wounds, on Waratah Road, Valley Heights, near Springwood early on Sunday afternoon, just minutes after the violence had unfolded, police believe. Loading The children were inside a car that had partially turned into a vacant block, near a fire trail leading into the national park, and the woman was outside the car nearby. Those at the scene applied first aid while calling emergency services, but by the time the ambulances arrived a short time later, one of the children, aged 5, was already dead. Police say the mother is a suspect, but charges have yet to be laid in relation to the incident.



Residents of Waratah Road are familiar with tragedy. It is not uncommon for them to hear sirens on the Great Western Avenue that runs parallel to Waratah Road, or for rescue services to use the fire trail to reach people who have suffered misadventures in the park. Historically, bodies have been dumped in the area. Neighbour Peita Davies said everybody on the street knew one another, and the woman and the children were not believed to be locals. They did not match the physical description of anyone who lived on the street. The street had been strangely silent throughout the violent event, she said. “Nobody heard anything,” Davies said. “We all want to know how they ended up here.”



Another resident, Glenn Lyall, said he initially assumed when he saw police in the street that there had been a car crash. “I could see a hatchback on an angle and two cyclists pointing, and I thought the car had hit one of the cyclists,” Lyall said. It was only later that he learned the nature of the injuries. Police attend a crime scene on Waratah Road in Valley Heights after a stabbing incident that left one child dead and two other children and a woman in a critical condition. Sitthixay Ditthavong A child’s car seat rests on the ground. Sitthixay Ditthavong Superintendent John Nelson, the Blue Mountains area commander, said the woman was not known to police, and that the children’s father had been told, but no further details would be released until the wider family had been contacted.



“You can imagine receiving that tragic news. That person is at work, going about their business, and they’ve had this information provided to them,” Nelson said. “All of Sydney, people are just going about a lovely Sunday afternoon and to be confronted with this is traumatic and tragic for anybody.” The children were taken to the Children’s Hospital at Westmead in a critical condition, and the woman was taken to Westmead Hospital, where her condition was also critical. Loading The incident became the fourth domestic violence-related incident in 24 hours. A woman was found decapitated in her home and an elderly woman had been allegedly stabbed to death in Bondi by her grandson, who said he was suffering the side effects of Ozempic.



Premier Chris Minns, who will address the media on Monday, said just hours before the stabbing incident that his thoughts were with the families and communities of the three women who died on Saturday. “These are shocking crimes and families are today dealing with unimaginable grief,” Minns said. On Saturday, about 9.35pm, police were called to a domestic violence incident at Mole Creek in the state’s north, where they were told a 27-year-old man had entered a property and tried to steal a vehicle before assaulting the 74-year-old male home owner. Sergei Mitnik was arrested after he allegedly stabbed his grandmother in Bondi on Saturday. TNV The younger man was arrested and police then went on to search the neighbouring property, where they found the body of a 70-year-old woman, which appeared to have been decapitated, sources not authorised to speak publicly confirmed. Part of the property was also damaged by fire.



The man, alleged to be the woman’s son, was taken to Tenterfield police station, where he was charged with murder. He was refused bail and will face court tomorrow. Just hours earlier, a woman in her 90s was fatally stabbed in a Bondi apartment in the early evening, just metres from a busy pedestrian thoroughfare and the beach. Sergei Mitnik, 47, had been estranged from his 90-year-old grandmother Valentina Spivak. He was arrested on Saturday and was charged on Sunday with domestic violence murder. “This is an extremely serious matter,” Javid Faiz, solicitor for Mitnik, told this masthead. Faiz said Mitnik would need to be assessed by psychiatrists, as he was suffering side effects from weight-loss drug Ozempic.



Related Article Crime Three women allegedly murdered in horror weekend across NSW after Bondi stabbing “His Honour accepted that those concerns warranted further assessment by appropriately qualified medical professionals, and those assessments will now be undertaken,” he said. Mitnik did not apply for bail and it was formally refused on Sunday. Earlier on Saturday, at a home in Kooringal, a suburb of Wagga Wagga, a 23-year-old woman was fatally stabbed inside a home, allegedly at the hands of her partner. Emergency services responded about 11.45am on Saturday.



NSW Ambulance paramedics and police officers performed CPR on the woman, but she died at the home. An 18-year-old was arrested at the scene, but was later released without charge. Police launched a search for a second man, who fled the residence before the arrival of emergency services. Police will allege in court that he was the woman’s partner. Later on Saturday, about 8.30pm, the man was arrested at another home in Kooringal. The 31-year-old was taken to Wagga Wagga police station, where he was charged with domestic violence murder. One woman was killed by an intimate partner every 11 days in 2024-25, according to recent data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.



Of the 48 women killed in domestic homicides in that period, 32 were killed by their intimate partner, seven by a parent, eight by their child and one by another relative. Police are encouraging anyone with dashcam or phone footage of the area around the time of the report to contact Springwood Police Station or CrimeStoppers on 1800 333 000. With Rachel Rasker If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: ASX slides lower as oil prices, bond yields weigh on Wall Street
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slides lower as oil prices, bond yields weigh on Wall Street Stan Choe Updated September 21, 2026 — 10:01am ,first published September 21, 2026 — 5:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has opened in the red after Wall Street capped an up-and-down week with a mixed finish for US stock indexes on Friday, as elevated bond yields and oil prices weighed on the market. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 38.8 points, or 0.4 per cent, to 8692.4 in early trade. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.21¢. The S&P 500 inched 0.2 per cent higher after drifting between modest gains and losses for much of the day. The benchmark index also posted its second straight weekly loss. Wall Street had a mixed session to close an uneven week. AP The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added 0.4 per cent.



The majority of stocks on Wall Street fell, and helping to weaken them was rising pressure from the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5 per cent from 4.94 per cent late Thursday after it topped the 5 per cent level early this week for the first time since 2023. Higher yields slow the overall economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, from the US government to people looking to buy houses to businesses wanting to build AI data centres. They also tend to undercut prices for stocks and other investments. Related Article Superannuation Super contributions surge more than a third after budget tax changes Yields have been climbing in a long march since the COVID pandemic knocked them nearly to zero in 2020. The ascent has accelerated recently because inflation has remained stubbornly high for years. Inflation is well above 3 per cent by several measures. It worsened due to higher oil prices caused by the war with Iran.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, got to nearly $US110 early this week, up from a little over $US70 in July. It has been seesawing since. It briefly dropped below $US102 in overnight trading before erasing much of the loss and settling at $US103.87, down 0.9 per cent from the day before. Rising oil prices have pushed gasoline prices to $US4.47 per gallon, up from $US3.20 per gallon a year ago, according to AAA. That is tightening the squeeze on household budgets. Diesel prices are at a record $US6.45 per gallon and that has a more direct impact on shipping costs for everything from groceries to clothing. High inflation has been raising expenses for everyone, and more companies are giving details about how much. Steel maker Nucor said late Thursday that it expects to report an increase in profit from its steel mills business in the third quarter from the second because it’s able to charge higher prices. But it’s also having to absorb higher costs. It gave a forecast for overall profit in the third quarter that fell short of analysts’ expectations, and its stock sank 6.3 per cent.



Berkshire Hathaway edged up 0.1 per cent after famed investor Warren Buffett said he’s giving up his role as chairman of the company. Buffett already gave up his role as CEO of the company, where he built a reputation for buying stocks at relatively cheap prices and being patient with his investments. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Why higher interest rates are the new normal Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Elsewhere on Wall Street, General Motors fell 5.1 per cent and Qualcomm dropped 5.8 per cent. Among stocks that gained ground were Coinbase Global, which climbed 11.7 per cent for the biggest gain among S&P 500 stocks, and Robinhood Markets, which climbed 9.1 per cent. In stock markets abroad, indexes slumped across Europe, including drops of 1.5 per cent for the CAC 40 in Paris and 1.5 per cent for London’s FTSE 100.



Wall Street will get a key update this week on the US housing market, along with a regular weekly unemployment update. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Former Toplace lawyer, Strathfield Labor councillor Sharangan Maheswaran to resume evidence
World.content:
Sharangan Maheswaran, who was a former top executive for disgraced Sydney property developer Jean Nassif has been accused of lying over how a large cheque was handed to a Liberal Party operative.

The day kicked has kicked off with lawyer-turned Toplace executive Maheswaran being grilled over whether he was involved in handing over the cheque for $148,500 to Charles Perrottet, a brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet.

Sharangan Maheswaran arrives at the ICAC on Monday to resume giving evidence. Sitthixay Ditthavong

The ICAC has previously heard that Charles Perrottet sent a text to Nassif in January 2021 asking to pick up “assistance” for “upcoming preselections”.

The ICAC has heard evidence that Maheswaran - a former Labor member of Strathfield Council - potentially gave Perrottet the cheque at the Longueville Hotel.
